title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: A sphere gives the simplest example
text:
A sphere gives the simplest example
Constrain a nonzero vector to the sphere \(\lVert w\rVert_2=R\). Differentiating \(\lVert w+tZ\rVert_2^2=R^2\) at \(t=0\) gives the tangent condition
\[
\langle w,Z\rangle=0.
\]
Let \(g\) be the ambient loss gradient. Its tangent projection is
\[
g_T=g-\frac{\langle w,g\rangle}{R^2}w.
\]
Under a Euclidean displacement budget \(\lVert Z\rVert_2\leq\epsilon\), the constrained linear problem has solution
\[
Z_*=-\epsilon\frac{g_T}{\lVert g_T\rVert_2}
\]
when \(g_T\ne0\). Choose zero if \(g_T=0\). This follows because a tangent displacement pairs with \(g\) exactly as it pairs with \(g_T\), and Cauchy-Schwarz solves the remaining support problem.
The ambient gradient need not be tangent. We did not assume scale invariance of the loss here. The tangent condition comes from the weight constraint itself.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: A tangent step is still only locally on the sphere
text:
A tangent step is still only locally on the sphere
For tangent \(Z\),
\[
\lVert w+Z\rVert_2^2=R^2+\lVert Z\rVert_2^2.
\]
The trial point leaves the sphere by a second-order amount. A radial retraction brings it back:
\[
\mathcal R_w(Z)=R\frac{w+Z}{\lVert w+Z\rVert_2}.
\]
Its derivative at zero returns \(Z\), so it agrees with the tangent displacement to first order. It is not an assertion that a finite straight step lies on a curved surface.
For \(w=(1,0)\) and \(Z=(0,1/2)\), the trial point is \((1,1/2)\) and the retracted point is \((2,1)/\sqrt5\). The rotation is \(\arctan(1/2)\approx26.57^\circ\). More generally,
\[
\tan\theta=\frac{\lVert Z\rVert_2}{R},
\qquad
\lVert\mathcal R_w(Z)-w\rVert_2=2R\sin(\theta/2).
\]
Tangent length, arc length \(R\theta\), and chord length are close for small steps. They are different finite-step quantities.



A tangent displacement leaves the unit circle at a trial point. Radial retraction returns it to the circle while preserving its new direction. The tangent length, rotation angle, and chord length are distinct.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: The Stiefel constraint preserves more than one length
text:
The Stiefel constraint preserves more than one length
For \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) with \(m\geq n\), the column Stiefel constraint is
\[
W^\top W=I_n.
\]
It fixes each column length and every pairwise column inner product. Differentiating gives
\[
W^\top Z+Z^\top W=0.
\]
Under Frobenius geometry, the tangent projection of an ambient matrix \(G\) is
\[
\Pi_W(G)=G-W\operatorname{sym}(W^\top G),
\qquad \operatorname{sym}(A)=\frac{A+A^\top}{2}.
\]
The removed term is Frobenius-orthogonal to every tangent matrix. A fixed Frobenius-radius support step therefore normalizes \(\Pi_W(G)\), just as in the sphere example.
A convenient retraction is
\[
\mathcal R_W(Z)=(W+Z)
\left[(W+Z)^\top(W+Z)\right]^{-1/2}.
\]
For tangent \(Z\), the Gram matrix in brackets is \(I+Z^\top Z\), which is positive definite. The retracted matrix has orthonormal columns and equals \(W+Z\) to first order.
The row-orthonormal version applies when the matrix shape calls for it. A rectangular matrix cannot generally have both orthonormal rows and orthonormal columns. The orientation of the constraint is part of the specification.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: A different tangent norm changes the support problem
text:
A different tangent norm changes the support problem
Replacing the Frobenius budget by a spectral budget gives
\[
\min_Z\langle G,Z\rangle_F
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
W^\top Z+Z^\top W=0,
\quad\lVert Z\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\epsilon.
\]
This is not the unconstrained polar problem from Part 6. Projecting an ambient polar factor is not automatically its solution.
For a small counterexample, set \(W=I_2\) and
\[
G=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The tangent matrices are skew-symmetric. The ambient polar factor is
\[
P=\frac1{\sqrt{10}}\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\-1&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its Frobenius tangent projection is \(J/\sqrt{10}\), where \(J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). This has operator norm \(1/\sqrt{10}\) and support value \(1/\sqrt{10}\). The feasible tangent matrix \(J\) has operator norm one and support value one.
For descent, negate these directions. Projection after dualization wasted available budget in this example. Renormalizing repairs this particular two-dimensional case, but that is not a general derivation of a constrained spectral oracle.
This is why manifold methods must solve the support problem for their actual tangent set and norm. The operations do not come with permission to commute.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: A sphere, an oblique set, and Stiefel are different constraints
text:
A sphere, an oblique set, and Stiefel are different constraints
A Frobenius sphere fixes one total matrix length while allowing its singular values and column lengths to redistribute. An oblique constraint fixes each column length, while leaving the angles between columns free. Stiefel additionally fixes those angles to be right angles.
For example,
\[
W=\begin{pmatrix}1&\cos\phi\\0&\sin\phi\end{pmatrix}
\]
has unit columns for every \(\phi\). At \(\phi=60^\circ\), its singular values are \(\sqrt{3/2}\) and \(\sqrt{1/2}\), so its condition number is \(\sqrt3\). As \(\phi\) approaches zero, it becomes nearly rank deficient despite retaining both column lengths.
A weight constraint can therefore remove useful functional freedoms, not merely redundant coordinate scales. Whether it preserves an architecture’s function class needs a separate argument. The later shared-gain examples will make that issue concrete.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: What the optimizer must specify
text:
What the optimizer must specify
A complete constrained update needs a weight set, its tangent directions, a norm or metric on those directions, and a finite-step return map. It also needs an account of optimizer memory when the base update has a momentum state.
Fixing only the weight radius leaves the update geometry unspecified. Fixing only the update norm leaves the weight trajectory free to drift. The choices can cooperate, but they answer different questions.
Next we examine a wrapper that explicitly controls both weight and proposal norms, and ask what that control does and does not say about angular schedules.

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: Try staying on the constraint set
text:
Try staying on the constraint set

On a radius-two sphere, take a tangent displacement of length one. What is the rotation after radial retraction?
Verify that \(W^\top\Pi_W(G)+\Pi_W(G)^\top W=0\) whenever \(W^\top W=I\).
Why does the projected polar factor in the \(2\times2\) example fail to maximize spectral-unit support?



Answer sketches


\(\theta=\arctan(1/2)\approx26.57^\circ\). The tangent length is one, not the angle in radians.
Substitute the projection formula. The remaining expression is \(W^\top G+G^\top W-2\operatorname{sym}(W^\top G)=0\).
It equals \(J/\sqrt{10}\), while \(J\) itself remains feasible and gives a larger pairing with \(G\).

title: Constraining weights, constraining motion
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Jeremy Bernstein, Modular Manifolds (2025), especially the sphere example and Manifold Muon discussion, separates weight constraints, tangent norms, support directions, and retractions. Its spectral manifold problem should not be replaced silently by a Frobenius projection.
Bernstein and Newhouse, Modular Duality in Deep Learning (ICML 2025), Section 3, supplies the normed support framework. The Stiefel tangent identity and polar retraction above follow by differentiation and direct Gram-matrix calculation under the stated column convention.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: The gradient first acts as a measuring device
text:
The gradient first acts as a measuring device
Let \(L(W)\) be differentiable, with matrix gradient \(G=\nabla L(W)\). Its first-order change along a perturbation is
\[
\mathrm dL_W[\Delta W]
=\langle G,\Delta W\rangle_F
=\operatorname{tr}(G^\top\Delta W).
\]
At this point, \(G\) represents a linear functional: give it a proposed update and it reports a scalar slope. The Frobenius pairing is how we write that derivative in matrix coordinates. It does not require us to measure the size of an update with the Frobenius norm.
Let \(N\) be our chosen norm on perturbations. For a radius \(\epsilon>0\), choose the update that minimizes the linear model:
\[
\min_{N(\Delta W)\leq\epsilon}\langle G,\Delta W\rangle_F.
\]
The constraint is the missing definition of steepest. Without it, a negative linear slope can be made arbitrarily negative just by scaling up the step.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: The dual norm is the support value
text:
The dual norm is the support value
Define the dual norm by
\[
N^*(G)=\max_{N(D)\leq1}\langle G,D\rangle_F.
\]
Because a norm ball is symmetric, minimizing over a radius-\(\epsilon\) ball gives
\[
\min_{N(\Delta W)\leq\epsilon}\langle G,\Delta W\rangle_F
=-\epsilon N^*(G).
\]
If \(D_*(G)\) is a maximizing unit-ball direction, one optimal update is
\[
\Delta W_*=-\epsilon D_*(G).
\]
The dual norm gives the best linear decrease per unit budget. The maximizing direction tells us how to attain it. Those are different outputs of the same support problem.
This is standard normed steepest descent. Boyd and Vandenberghe’s Section 9.4 develops the geometric interpretation, and Bernstein and Newhouse’s Sections 3.1 and 3.2 use it to construct layerwise duality maps.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: Frobenius geometry recovers the normalized gradient
text:
Frobenius geometry recovers the normalized gradient
For \(N(D)=\lVert D\rVert_F\), Cauchy-Schwarz gives
\[
\langle G,D\rangle_F
\leq\lVert G\rVert_F\lVert D\rVert_F.
\]
For nonzero \(G\), equality is attained by \(D_*=G/\lVert G\rVert_F\). Thus the Frobenius norm is self-dual, and the fixed-radius step is
\[
\Delta W_*=-\epsilon\frac{G}{\lVert G\rVert_F}.
\]
That is a normalized gradient update. Ordinary gradient descent, \(-\eta G\), also uses this direction, but its radius is \(\eta\lVert G\rVert_F\) rather than a fixed \(\epsilon\).
Now change the norm while keeping \(G\) fixed.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: A spectral budget produces a polar direction
text:
A spectral budget produces a polar direction
Let \(N(D)=\lVert D\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\), the largest singular value. Write a compact singular value decomposition using only the positive singular values of \(G\):
\[
G=U\Sigma V^\top
=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i u_i v_i^\top.
\]
For any \(D\) with operator norm at most one,
\[
\langle G,D\rangle_F
=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i u_i^\top Dv_i
\leq\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i.
\]
The bound follows because \(u_i\) and \(v_i\) are unit vectors and \(\lvert u_i^\top Dv_i\rvert\leq1\). It is attained by the partial polar factor
\[
D_*(G)=UV^\top.
\]
This matrix has singular value one on each active singular mode. Consequently,
\[
N^*(G)=\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{nuc}}
=\sum_{i=1}^r\sigma_i,
\qquad
\Delta W_*=-\epsilon UV^\top.
\]
The spectral norm’s dual is the nuclear norm, not the spectral norm again. I use the subscript \(\mathrm{op}\) for the largest singular value and \(\mathrm{nuc}\) for their sum. The asterisk on \(N^*\) means duality.
If \(G\) is rank deficient, the compact polar factor is one maximizer. Additional components on unused subspaces can also be optimal if they stay feasible. If \(G=0\), choose the zero update. These cases should not be implemented by dividing blindly by a zero norm or singular value.
This operation changes the singular values of the update direction. It does not impose a norm constraint on the current weight matrix \(W\).

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: The same derivative, three different unit balls
text:
The same derivative, three different unit balls
Take \(G=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\) and a budget radius \(\epsilon=0.1\).
Under a Frobenius budget,
\[
\Delta W_F=-\frac{0.1}{\sqrt{10}}\operatorname{diag}(3,1),
\qquad \langle G,\Delta W_F\rangle_F=-0.1\sqrt{10}\approx-0.316228.
\]
Under a spectral budget,
\[
\Delta W_{\mathrm{op}}=-0.1 I,
\qquad \langle G,\Delta W_{\mathrm{op}}\rangle_F=-0.4.
\]
For comparison, a nuclear-norm budget has dual value \(\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=3\). One optimal update spends the whole budget on the leading singular mode:
\[
\Delta W_{\mathrm{nuc}}=-0.1\operatorname{diag}(1,0),
\qquad \langle G,\Delta W_{\mathrm{nuc}}\rangle_F=-0.3.
\]



Diagonal slices of the Frobenius, spectral, and nuclear unit balls. For the same derivative with diagonal entries three and one, their maximizing directions lie on a circle, a square, and a diamond respectively.


The figure shows positive support directions \(D_*\). The actual descent update is \(-\epsilon D_*\). Restricting the picture to diagonal matrices is enough to display maximizers for this diagonal \(G\).
The larger decrease under the spectral budget is not an optimizer victory. It is a comparison of different feasible sets. The spectral step has Frobenius norm \(0.1\sqrt2\), so it would not fit inside the Frobenius budget of radius \(0.1\).
There is another useful comparison inside the spectral ball. Simply dividing the gradient by its spectral norm gives
\[
\frac{G}{\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}}=\operatorname{diag}(1,1/3).
\]
It is feasible, but its support value is \(10/3\), below the optimum four. Normalization alone does not solve a general support problem.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: Carry the RMS ruler through the dual calculation
text:
Carry the RMS ruler through the dual calculation
Part 5 measured a dense-layer perturbation with
\[
N(D)=k\lVert D\rVert_{\mathrm{op}},
\qquad k=\sqrt{n/m}.
\]
Its unit ball allows operator norm \(1/k\). Scaling the support problem therefore gives
\[
N^*(G)=\frac1k\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{nuc}},
\qquad
D_*(G)=\frac1k UV^\top
=\sqrt{m/n}\,UV^\top.
\]
The width factor reverses because a larger primal norm makes the feasible unit ball smaller. For a nine-input, four-output layer, the polar factor is multiplied by \(2/3\) to have unit RMS-to-RMS norm.
This is the dense-layer duality map in Bernstein and Newhouse’s Example 3. The activation ruler, its induced matrix norm, and its support direction are three connected parts of one construction.


What changes for an embedding lookup?

For Euclidean output measurements, Part 5’s lookup budget was \(N(D)=\max_j\lVert D[:,j]\rVert_2\). Each column can use its unit budget independently, so
\[
N^*(G)=\sum_j\lVert G[:,j]\rVert_2,
\qquad
D_*[:,j]=\frac{G[:,j]}{\lVert G[:,j]\rVert_2}
\]
for nonzero columns. Choose zero for a zero gradient column. With an RMS output ruler, multiply both the dual value and the direction by \(\sqrt m\).
The largest-column update norm is paired with a sum of gradient-column norms. It does not mean spending the entire update on only one column. This is the Embed duality map in the paper’s Example 4.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: A direction and a step-size model are separate choices
text:
A direction and a step-size model are separate choices
The fixed-radius support problem is not the only way to choose a step. Consider instead
\[
\min_\Delta\left\{\langle G,\Delta\rangle_F
+\frac1{2\eta}N(\Delta)^2\right\},\qquad \eta>0.
\]
At radius \(r\), the best linear term is \(-rN^*(G)\). Minimizing \(-rN^*(G)+r^2/(2\eta)\) gives \(r=\eta N^*(G)\), hence one minimizer is
\[
\Delta_*=-\eta N^*(G)D_*(G).
\]
For the Frobenius norm, this recovers \(-\eta G\). For the spectral norm, it gives \(-\eta\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{nuc}}UV^\top\). A fixed-radius polar update omits that dual-magnitude factor because it solves a different optimization problem.
Neither linear model automatically controls a large finite loss change. A useful quadratic upper bound, a line search, or an appropriately chosen small step needs its own justification. The norm describes which perturbations are allowed. Curvature describes what the loss does along them.
The same care applies to momentum. If we replace \(G\) by a buffer \(M\), dualization solves the support problem for the linear functional represented by \(M\). The actual current derivative is still \(G\). A norm-feasible buffer step need not be a descent direction for the current loss.
We now know how to choose a direction for one module’s geometry. The next post asks how those local budgets fit together across the network, and why Modula uses a weighted maximum to combine them.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: Try solving the support problem
text:
Try solving the support problem

For \(G=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\), compare the spectral-budget support values of \(G/\lVert G\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\) and \(UV^\top\).
For \(G=\operatorname{diag}(3,0)\), give a compact polar maximizer and a different spectral-unit-ball maximizer with the same support value.
Under a Euclidean lookup budget with gradient columns \((3,4)\) and \((0,2)\), find the dual value and one maximizing matrix.
Let \(L(W)=\lVert W\rVert_F^2/2\) at \(W=\operatorname{diag}(3,1)\). A spectral-budget step is \(\Delta=-\epsilon I\). Compute the exact loss change at \(\epsilon=5\), and compare it with the linear prediction.



Answer sketches


They are \(10/3\) and four. Both proposals have spectral norm one, but only the polar factor attains the support maximum here.
The compact polar factor is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\). The matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1)\) also has operator norm one and support value three. The unused second mode does not affect the linear objective.
The dual value is \(5+2=7\). Normalize each column separately, giving columns \((3/5,4/5)\) and \((0,1)\).
The exact change is \(-4\epsilon+\epsilon^2\), so it equals five. The linear prediction is \(-20\). A direction that is steepest for the linear model can still overshoot badly.

title: Choosing an update with a dual norm
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, Section 9.4 and Appendix A.1.6, explains normed steepest descent, dual norms, and the spectral-nuclear pairing. Keep the normalized direction separate from its dual-norm-scaled version.
Jeremy Bernstein and Laker Newhouse, Modular Duality in Deep Learning (ICML 2025), Sections 3.1 through 3.3, Proposition 1, and Section 4.1, derives the layerwise constructions used here. Section 5 discusses efficient matrix iterations. The exact SVD support calculation above does not by itself specify a complete practical optimizer, its momentum convention, or an approximation algorithm.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: Choose a buffer convention we can actually analyze
text:
Choose a buffer convention we can actually analyze
Use the following momentum update with decoupled decay:
\[
m_t=\beta m_{t-1}+g_t,
\qquad g_t=\nabla L_t(w_t),
\]
\[
w_{t+1}=a_t w_t-\eta_t m_t,
\qquad a_t=1-\eta_t\lambda_t>0.
\]
Here \(0\leq\beta<1\), \(m_{-1}=0\), \(\eta_t>0\), and \(\lambda_t\geq0\). The buffer stores gradients before multiplication by the learning rate. There is no \((1-\beta)\) factor, dampening, Nesterov lookahead, or decay term inside this buffer.
That last choice matters. A coupled quadratic penalty would instead give
\[
m_t^{\mathrm{coupled}}
=\beta m_{t-1}^{\mathrm{coupled}}+g_t+\lambda_t w_t,
\qquad
w_{t+1}=w_t-\eta_t m_t^{\mathrm{coupled}}.
\]
The penalty then persists in the buffer. With zero initial buffers, the first weight update agrees with our decoupled version, but the stored states differ and later weight updates generally diverge. With \(\beta=0\) the distinction disappears for these equations.
Loshchilov and Hutter’s decoupled-weight-decay paper, Section 2 and Algorithm 1, is a useful reference for keeping these choices separate. Its buffer stores a learning-rate-scaled contribution. Our displayed convention stores the unscaled gradient, so a changing learning rate requires its own bookkeeping.
For the geometry below, assume the same blockwise forward invariance as before. Then \(g_t\perp w_t\). The statement is about the data gradient, not automatically about \(m_t\).

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: Split the proposed update at the current weight
text:
Split the proposed update at the current weight
Write \(w_t=R_t e_t\) with unit \(e_t\). Decompose the buffer into
\[
p_t=\langle e_t,m_t\rangle,
\qquad v_t=m_t-p_t e_t,
\qquad v_t\perp e_t.
\]
The scalar \(p_t\) is the radial component of the buffer. The vector \(v_t\) is its tangent component. The weight update becomes
\[
w_{t+1}
=(a_tR_t-\eta_t p_t)e_t-\eta_t v_t.
\]
Everything about this one step is now a right triangle. Its new radius is
\[
R_{t+1}^2
=(a_tR_t-\eta_t p_t)^2+\eta_t^2\|v_t\|_2^2.
\]
If \(a_tR_t-\eta_t p_t>0\), the rotation satisfies
\[
\tan\theta_t
=\frac{\eta_t\|v_t\|_2}{a_tR_t-\eta_t p_t}.
\]
The denominator contains information that \(\eta_t\|m_t\|_2/R_t\) loses. If the denominator is zero or negative, use
\[
\theta_t=\operatorname{atan2}
\left(\eta_t\|v_t\|_2,\ a_tR_t-\eta_t p_t\right),
\]
with an angle in \([0,\pi]\) and a nonzero resulting weight. A negative denominator can mean a rotation beyond \(90^\circ\). Ordinary arctangent of the ratio would choose the wrong quadrant. If both arguments vanish, the next weight is zero and its direction is undefined.
These are exact finite-step identities. No assumption about random gradients or equilibrium is needed.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: A two-step example exposes the radial memory
text:
A two-step example exposes the radial memory
Use the same normalized predictor and squared loss as Parts 1 and 3. Turn decay off for this example, set \(\eta=1/2\) and \(\beta=0.9\), and begin at \(w_0=(1,0)\).
The first gradient and buffer are \(g_0=m_0=(0,-1)\), so \(w_1=(1,1/2)\). The old gradient is no longer perpendicular to the new weight:
\[
\langle w_1,m_0\rangle=-1/2.
\]
The new gradient is still tangent. Direct differentiation gives
\[
g_1\approx(0.197771,-0.395542),
\qquad
m_1\approx(0.197771,-1.295542).
\]
Since \(R_1=\sqrt5/2\), the radial component is
\[
p_1=\frac{\langle w_1,m_1\rangle}{R_1}
=-\frac{\beta\eta\|m_0\|_2^2}{R_1}
\approx-0.402492.
\]
The equality uses \(m_0\perp w_0\) and \(g_1\perp w_1\). It is a statement about this second step with a zero initial buffer, not a formula for every later \(p_t\).
The tangent component has norm \(\|v_1\|_2\approx1.247214\). The exact geometric formula gives a rotation of approximately \(25.30^\circ\), and the next weight is
\[
w_2\approx(0.901115,1.147771).
\]
Pretending that the whole buffer were tangent would instead give \(\arctan(\eta\|m_1\|_2/R_1)\approx30.37^\circ\).



The second momentum step in the worked example. The current gradient step is tangent, but the contribution from the previous gradient has a radial component. The same total step splits exactly into radial and tangent displacements.


The negative \(p_1\) has a useful interpretation. We subtract the buffer, so its negative radial component adds an outward displacement. The step contains more radial growth than we would infer from a tangent-gradient picture alone.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: A unit update does not fix a rotation
text:
A unit update does not fix a rotation
Suppose we normalize a nonzero proposed update \(u\) to length one and apply \(w^+=aw-\eta u\). Set
\[
r=\langle e,u\rangle,
\qquad \|u-r e\|_2=\sqrt{1-r^2}.
\]
When \(aR-\eta r>0\),
\[
\tan\theta
=\frac{\eta\sqrt{1-r^2}}{aR-\eta r}.
\]
For a tangent unit update, \(r=0\) and the familiar ratio is \(\eta/(aR)\). If the update is not tangent, that ratio does not determine the angle.
Take \(w=(1,0)\), \(a=1\), and \(\eta=1/2\). Both \(u=(0,-1)\) and \(\widetilde u=(-0.8,-0.6)\) have unit norm. They produce
\[
w^+=(1,0.5),\qquad
\widetilde w^+=(1.4,0.3),
\]
with rotations \(26.57^\circ\) and \(12.09^\circ\). Both relative displacement lengths are \(1/2\).



Two unit-length update proposals at the same weight and learning rate. Their displacement lengths match, but one rotates the weight by 26.57 degrees and the other by 12.09 degrees.


Normalizing an update controls its length. Removing its radial component is a separate operation. Renormalizing the resulting weight is another: multiplying a nonzero \(w^+\) by a positive scalar does not undo the angle it already acquired.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: A rescaled checkpoint also needs a rescaled buffer
text:
A rescaled checkpoint also needs a rescaled buffer
Momentum makes the optimizer state part of any trajectory comparison.
For a constant \(c>0\), an exactly corresponding run under our convention uses
\[
\widetilde w_t=cw_t,
\qquad
\widetilde m_{t-1}=m_{t-1}/c,
\qquad
\widetilde\eta_t=c^2\eta_t.
\]
Keep \(\beta\) and \(a_t\) the same in both runs. The gradients scale as \(1/c\), so the buffer recurrence preserves \(\widetilde m_t=m_t/c\). The weight recurrence then preserves \(\widetilde w_{t+1}=cw_{t+1}\).
If decay is parameterized by \(a_t=1-\eta_t\lambda_t\), matching \(a_t\) requires \(\widetilde\lambda_t=\lambda_t/c^2\). Rescaling the learning rate while leaving \(\lambda_t\) fixed would change the shrinkage too.
At a checkpoint, keeping the old buffer unchanged, or resetting it to zero, breaks this correspondence in general. A resulting transient cannot automatically be attributed to the geometry of the represented function.


What becomes of Part 3’s exact clock change?

Keep the cumulative shrinkage \(c_{t+1}=a_tc_t\) and the coordinates \(z_t=w_t/c_t\). For the decoupled convention used here, define \(q_t=c_tm_t\). For \(t\geq1\),
\[
q_t=\beta a_{t-1}q_{t-1}+\nabla L_t(z_t),
\]
and
\[
z_{t+1}=z_t-\frac{\eta_t}{c_tc_{t+1}}q_t.
\]
With the zero initial buffer, \(q_0=\nabla L_0(z_0)\). This is again an exact no-decay representation, but the effective momentum coefficient has changed as well as the learning rate. For constant \(a\), it is \(\beta a\).
The transformation is a direct calculation for our explicitly chosen buffer. It is not the momentum formula from Li and Arora’s coupled-penalty convention. Their Section 2.2 treats that convention with a different full-state transformation.
Copying only the schedule from Part 3 while retaining \(\beta\) would generally compare different trajectories.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: One angle cannot summarize the whole learning process
text:
One angle cannot summarize the whole learning process
Even an exact angle only describes the present directional displacement. Momentum also changes correlations between updates over time. A long sequence of similarly directed rotations can travel differently from a sequence whose rotations cancel, even if their per-step angle magnitudes agree.
Kosson, Messmer, and Jaggi distinguish instantaneous update sizes from longer-term contributions in their rotational-equilibrium analysis. Their predictions use a simplified random-walk model. We have used exact local identities here, rather than importing its equilibrium assumptions.
We now have three quantities to keep track of: the radius, the tangent displacement, and the radial component of the optimizer’s proposal. We also need its memory when comparing trajectories. None of these alone says whether a learned feature became more useful.
The next part of the series turns toward that missing functional measurement: what should count as a small change to a layer when its job is to transform activations?

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: Try moving the memory
text:
Try moving the memory

At \(w=(1,0)\), let \(u=(0,-1)\), \(a=0.8\), and \(\eta=0.2\). Compute the new weight and its angle.
With \(w=(1,0)\), \(u=(1,0)\), and \(a=1\), what happens at \(\eta=1\) and \(\eta=2\)? Why is the tangent-ratio formula insufficient?
Double a weight and compare the same represented predictor. How should the unscaled buffer, learning rate, and decay coefficient change under our constant-\(c\) correspondence?
In the expandable clock calculation, use \(a=0.9\) and \(\beta=0.9\). What momentum coefficient does the no-decay \(q\) recurrence use after the first step?



Answer sketches


\(w^+=(0.8,0.2)\) and \(\theta=\arctan(1/4)\approx14.04^\circ\).
At \(\eta=1\), the new weight is zero and its direction is undefined. At \(\eta=2\), it is \((-1,0)\) and the angle is \(180^\circ\). The tangent numerator is zero in both cases, but the radial part distinguishes them.
Divide the buffer by two, multiply the learning rate by four, and divide \(\lambda\) by four, preserving the same shrinkage factor and \(\beta\). Resetting the buffer is a different intervention.
It is \(\beta a=0.81\). This answer depends on the decoupled, unscaled-buffer convention displayed in this post.

title: Momentum, rotation, and normalized updates
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Ilya Loshchilov and Frank Hutter, Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (ICLR 2019), Section 2 and Algorithm 1, distinguishes coupled regularization from decoupled shrinkage. Check both decay placement and whether the buffer stores a gradient or a learning-rate-scaled displacement.
Zhiyuan Li and Sanjeev Arora, An Exponential Learning Rate Schedule for Deep Learning (ICLR 2020), Definition 1.2 and Sections 2.2 and 2.3, treats trajectory equivalence with momentum and the required state transformations. Its coupled-penalty convention differs from the decoupled example derived here.
Atli Kosson, Bettina Messmer, and Martin Jaggi, Rotational Equilibrium: How Weight Decay Balances Learning Across Neural Networks (ICML 2024), Sections 2 and 3.1 and Appendices C and L, connects angular updates, momentum, and total update contributions. The equilibrium estimates require their modeling assumptions. Our worked examples and radial-tangent identities are direct finite-step calculations, not evidence for an optimizer ranking.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: Fix the convention before interpreting the penalty
text:
Fix the convention before interpreting the penalty
Let \(L_t\) be the data loss on the minibatch used at step \(t\). Assume a positive rescaling of the block \(w\) preserves the model’s predictions, so that
\[
L_t(cw)=L_t(w),\qquad c>0.
\]
All other parameters are fixed in this calculation. The identity must hold for every minibatch used, and we stay away from \(w=0\).
Our update is raw SGD without momentum:
\[
w_{t+1}=a_t w_t-\eta_t\nabla L_t(w_t),
\qquad a_t=1-\eta_t\lambda_t>0.
\]
Take \(\eta_t>0\) and \(\lambda_t\geq0\). For this algorithm, adding the penalty \(\lambda_t\|w\|_2^2/2\) to the current loss produces exactly the displayed update. With an adaptive preconditioner or a momentum buffer, we must inspect the actual equations before making that identification.
For the data loss, all radii on a positive ray are equivalent. Along that ray, the penalty can be made arbitrarily small by shrinking \(w\). It therefore does not directly distinguish a simpler predictor from a more complicated one within this equivalence class. That does not make the training dynamics, or their eventual effect on generalization, irrelevant.
This distinction is the starting point of van Laarhoven’s normalization analysis, Sections 2 through 4. It concerns a specified symmetry, not every weight in a normalized network.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: The radius records what decay and gradients do together
text:
The radius records what decay and gradients do together
Write \(w_t=R_t e_t\) with \(R_t>0\) and \(\|e_t\|_2=1\). Define \(h_t=\nabla L_t(e_t)\). The scale identities from Part 1 give
\[
\nabla L_t(w_t)=\frac{h_t}{R_t},
\qquad \langle e_t,h_t\rangle=0.
\]
The radial and tangent parts of the update are perpendicular. Squaring its norm gives the exact recurrence
\[
R_{t+1}^2
=a_t^2R_t^2+\frac{\eta_t^2}{R_t^2}\|h_t\|_2^2.
\]
Decay contributes the first term. The finite gradient displacement contributes the second. A tangent step can increase a radius even though its first-order radial derivative is zero.
The corresponding direction is
\[
e_{t+1}
=\frac{e_t-\alpha_t h_t}{\|e_t-\alpha_t h_t\|_2},
\qquad
\alpha_t=\frac{\eta_t}{a_tR_t^2}.
\]
Here \(\alpha_t\) is the coefficient in the exact normalized update. The actual rotation obeys \(\tan\theta_t=\alpha_t\|h_t\|_2\). An effective learning rate, a displacement length, and an angle are related quantities, but they are not interchangeable.
At the same current weight and gradient, decreasing \(a_t\) increases the rotation. Across different training runs, however, the weights and gradients soon differ. This one-step comparison is not a theorem that stronger decay always helps or always produces faster progress.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: Replace decay with a different learning-rate schedule
text:
Replace decay with a different learning-rate schedule
There is a stronger statement than the local observation about \(R_t\).
Define the cumulative shrinkage
\[
c_0=1,\qquad c_{t+1}=a_t c_t,
\]
and introduce coordinates \(z_t=w_t/c_t\). Since every \(c_t\) is positive, \(z_t\) and \(w_t\) represent the same predictor. Their gradients satisfy
\[
\nabla L_t(w_t)=\frac1{c_t}\nabla L_t(z_t).
\]
Substitute \(w_t=c_tz_t\) into the SGD update and divide by \(c_{t+1}\):
\[
z_{t+1}
=z_t-\widetilde\eta_t\nabla L_t(z_t),
\qquad
\widetilde\eta_t=\frac{\eta_t}{c_t c_{t+1}}.
\]
There is no decay in the \(z\) update. Its learning rate has changed instead. Starting both runs from the same weight, using the same minibatches, and using this transformed schedule makes their predictions agree at every step, under the stated symmetry.
No equilibrium, averaging, or small-step approximation entered this derivation. If the minibatches are random, it is an identity for the same realized sequence of minibatches. The exact prediction agreement also uses the assumed forward symmetry, rather than merely an equality of scalar losses.
For constant \(\eta\) and \(a=1-\eta\lambda\), the formula simplifies to
\[
c_t=a^t,\qquad
\widetilde\eta_t=\eta a^{-(2t+1)}.
\]
The first transformed learning rate is \(\eta/a\). Each subsequent one is larger by the factor \(a^{-2}\). This is the momentum-free equivalence studied in Li and Arora’s Section 2.1. The initialization and first-step factor matter.
The word clock is shorthand for this change in step coefficients. It does not mean that an arbitrary finite-step training run is the same trajectory played back faster.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: One toy run in two coordinate systems
text:
One toy run in two coordinate systems
Return to our predictor \(f_w(x)=w^\top x/\|w\|_2\), input \(x=(0,1)\), and target \(1\):
\[
L(w)=\frac12\left(\frac{w_2}{\|w\|_2}-1\right)^2.
\]
Use \(w_0=(1,0)\), \(\eta=0.1\), and \(\lambda=1\), so \(a=0.9\). These deliberately simple numbers illustrate the identity, not a recommended training configuration.
The decayed first step is \(w_1=(0.9,0.1)\). The matched run has no decay and starts with learning rate \(0.1/0.9\), giving \(z_1=(1,1/9)\). Since \(w_1=0.9z_1\), their predictions agree exactly. Both rotate by approximately \(6.34^\circ\).
The first three transformed learning rates are approximately \(0.111111\), \(0.137174\), and \(0.169351\). Keeping the no-decay learning rate fixed at \(0.1\) would not give the same run.



A 24-step toy calculation. Decayed SGD shrinks the weight radius while the equivalent no-decay coordinates keep a radius close to one. Their prediction curves overlap.


The figure computes both recurrences independently. Their prediction discrepancy stays below \(10^{-12}\) in this calculation. This verifies the example numerically. The algebra above is what establishes the equivalence.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: An equilibrium estimate needs one more assumption
text:
An equilibrium estimate needs one more assumption
The radius recurrence is exact, but \(\|h_t\|_2^2\) changes with direction and minibatch. To get a simple scalar model, freeze that quantity at a positive constant \(Q\), and also hold \(\eta>0\) and \(\lambda>0\) fixed with \(0<a<1\).
If this simplified recurrence has a fixed radius \(R_*\), then
\[
R_*^4=\frac{\eta^2Q}{1-a^2}
\approx\frac{\eta Q}{2\lambda},
\qquad \eta\lambda\ll1.
\]
The approximation uses \(1-(1-\eta\lambda)^2\approx2\eta\lambda\). It does not follow from scale invariance alone. In our deterministic toy problem, the directional gradient becomes small as the prediction approaches its target, so holding \(Q\) fixed would miss part of the dynamics.
For stochastic gradients, replacing \(Q\) by an average also requires care: the radius and gradient magnitude may be correlated, and an expectation of an inverse radius is not the inverse of an expected radius. A stationary-radius heuristic is not the same result as the pathwise schedule identity.
This is where the distinctions in the Intrinsic Learning Rate paper become useful. Its direction-and-radius SDE and its Fast Equilibrium Conjecture have their own assumptions. Neither licenses a universal statement that every optimizer on every architecture depends only on \(\eta\lambda\).

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: What a decay comparison must hold fixed
text:
What a decay comparison must hold fixed
On a truly invariant block, decay can change the optimization path without directly changing the predictor when applied alone. Those are compatible facts.
To understand a comparison, I want the actual shrinkage factor \(a_t\), the nominal learning rate, the radius, and the angular displacement. Matching only the nominal learning rate can leave the directional dynamics unmatched. Matching one angle still does not establish matching useful feature changes.
We also cannot transfer the derivation unchanged to epsilon-sensitive normalization, scale-sensitive gains, or a block that is only invariant under a joint transformation with another parameter. Part 2 explains why those distinctions matter.
Next comes a complication that is present even under perfect forward invariance: the optimizer remembers. The current gradient is tangent, but its memory need not be.

title: Weight decay changes the clock
section: Try changing the clock
text:
Try changing the clock

Set \(\lambda=0\). What happens to \(c_t\) and the transformed schedule?
With constant \(a=0.9\), what is the ratio \(\widetilde\eta_{t+1}/\widetilde\eta_t\)? Why is it not \(1/a\)?
In the frozen-\(Q\) model, take \(\eta=0.1\), \(\lambda=1\), and \(Q=1\). Compute the exact fixed radius and its angular step.



Answer sketches


Every \(a_t=1\), so \(c_t=1\) and \(\widetilde\eta_t=\eta_t\). The change of coordinates becomes the identity.
The ratio is \(1/0.9^2\approx1.234568\). Both \(c_t\) and \(c_{t+1}\) appear in the denominator of the transformed learning rate.
\(R_*=(0.01/0.19)^{1/4}\approx0.4790\). At that fixed point, \(\tan\theta=\sqrt{1-a^2}/a\), so \(\cos\theta=a\) and \(\theta\approx25.84^\circ\). These are predictions of the frozen-\(Q\) model, not of the earlier fitting trajectory.

title: What the edge of stability actually says
section: Start with one excited quadratic mode
text:
Start with one excited quadratic mode
Consider
\[
L(x)=\tfrac12 a(x-x_\star)^2,
\qquad a>0,
\qquad x^+=x-\eta L'(x).
\]
Writing \(e=x-x_\star\) gives the exact recurrence
\[
e_{t+1}=(1-\eta a)e_t,
\qquad e_t=(1-\eta a)^t e_0.
\]
For a nonzero initial error, the cases are:



Dimensionless curvature
Behavior of the error




\(0<\eta a<1\)
Decay without changing sign


\(\eta a=1\)
Reach the minimizer in one step


\(1<\eta a<2\)
Alternating decay


\(\eta a=2\)
A constant-amplitude two-cycle


\(\eta a>2\)
Alternating growth



The boundary \(2/\eta\) comes from a multiplier reaching \(-1\). It is a property of this discrete map. At \(e_0=0\), the iterate stays exactly at the minimizer for every rate, including unstable rates. Instability concerns the response to a displacement, not a claim that an unexcited coordinate moves by itself.
For a fixed symmetric quadratic Hessian \(H\), diagonalize into eigenvectors. Each coordinate has its own multiplier \(1-\eta\lambda_j\). Positive modes contract when \(0<\eta\lambda_j<2\). Negative modes have a multiplier above one, and a flat direction may be neutral or have affine drift.
Thus the largest positive eigenvalue supplies the familiar upper boundary only after we specify the relevant modes and objective. Momentum, preconditioning, or normalization of the proposal changes the update map whose stability must be analyzed.

title: What the edge of stability actually says
section: A falling loss can conceal an unstable coordinate
text:
A falling loss can conceal an unstable coordinate
Take the fixed quadratic
\[
L(z,x)=\tfrac12(0.2)z^2+\tfrac12(2.2)x^2,
\qquad \eta=1,
\qquad (z_0,x_0)=(2,10^{-4}).
\]
Then
\[
z_t=2(0.8)^t,
\qquad x_t=10^{-4}(-1.2)^t.
\]
The loss initially falls because the large stable coordinate shrinks. The tiny unstable coordinate grows throughout, eventually dominating. An early downward loss curve is therefore compatible with an unstable fixed quadratic.



A scalar quadratic mode contracts only below the discrete boundary, and a mixed quadratic can initially lose error before its small unstable component dominates.


This figure evaluates the displayed formulas. It contains no neural-network training. It also shows why a meaningful nonlinear experiment needs a long enough observation window: brief progress alone does not demonstrate self-stabilization.

title: What the edge of stability actually says
section: Gradient flow has no corresponding sign flip
text:
Gradient flow has no corresponding sign flip
Use the continuous clock \(\tau=\eta t\). The quadratic gradient-flow equation is
\[
\frac{de}{d\tau}=-ae,
\qquad e(\tau)=e_0e^{-a\tau}.
\]
Over one interval of length \(\eta\), its amplification is \(e^{-\eta a}\), always positive and below one. GD replaces this with the first-order approximation \(1-\eta a\). That approximation has qualitatively different behavior when \(\eta a\) is order one.
For a smooth general loss, exact gradient flow satisfies
\[
\frac{d}{d\tau}L(w(\tau))=-\|\nabla L(w(\tau))\|^2.
\]
Finite GD need not share this monotonicity. Comparing the two requires a common clock and a numerically accurate flow reference. A stable numerical ODE solver can still have appreciable integration error, so step refinement matters before interpreting a trajectory difference.

title: What the edge of stability actually says
section: Curvature at the starting point does not control a whole step
text:
Curvature at the starting point does not control a whole step
Let \(g=\nabla L(w)\) and take \(w^+=w-\eta g\). The integral Taylor formula is
\[
L(w^+)-L(w)
=-\eta\|g\|^2
+\eta^2\int_0^1(1-s)
g^\top H(w-s\eta g)g\,ds.
\]
If \(H\preceq MI\) along the entire segment, this gives
\[
L(w^+)-L(w)
\le-\eta(1-\eta M/2)\|g\|^2.
\]
That is a segment-wide hypothesis. Measuring the Hessian only at \(w\) does not establish it.
For an explicit counterexample, use the smooth, bounded-below polynomial
\[
L(x)=x+\tfrac12x^2+10x^4.
\]
At \(x=0\), the gradient is one and the Hessian is one. With \(\eta=1\), the pointwise product \(\eta L''(0)=1\) is below two, yet the update lands at \(-1\) and raises the loss from zero to \(9.5\). Curvature increases sharply along the step.
Conversely, a large Hessian eigenvalue at one nonlinear iterate does not make every future Hessian equal to that value. The fixed-quadratic prediction can fail because subsequent motion changes the landscape being sampled.

title: What the edge of stability actually says
section: What the neural-network observation adds
text:
What the neural-network observation adds
Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability, Sections 3 and 4, reports full-batch trajectories whose sharpness tends toward the quadratic boundary and remains nearby while loss decreases over longer intervals. Its central contribution is empirical characterization. It does not prove global convergence for arbitrary neural objectives.
The interesting observation is the combination: a frozen local quadratic predicts growing oscillations, while the changing nonlinear objective can avoid that frozen prediction. Explaining the boundary is therefore only the first step. We still need to explain why curvature rises toward it and what opposes further growth.
Here sharpness means the largest algebraic training-loss Hessian eigenvalue, in the stated parameter coordinates. Parts 2 and 23 already explained why coordinate scaling can change such a number. Keep the parameterization, loss normalization, and optimizer fixed when interpreting its relation to \(2/\eta\).

title: What the edge of stability actually says
section: Progressive sharpening has a sign that needs explaining
text:
Progressive sharpening has a sign that needs explaining
Suppose the top eigenvalue \(S(w)\) is simple, with unit eigenvector \(u\). Differentiating \(Hu=Su\) gives
\[
DS(w)[v]=u^\top DH(w)[v]u.
\]
The eigenvector-derivative terms cancel after multiplication by \(u^\top\). Consequently, along gradient flow,
\[
\frac{dS}{d\tau}=-\langle\nabla S,\nabla L\rangle.
\]
This formula contains no universal positive sign. For \(L(x)=x^4/4\) at \(x=1\), it is \(-6\). For the local cubic \(L(x)=-x+x^3/6\) at \(x=1\), it is \(+1/2\). Both follow from direct differentiation.
Progressive sharpening asks why this contraction is positive over substantial parts of particular training trajectories. Repeating the formula is not an explanation of its sign. At repeated top eigenvalues, even this scalar derivative needs replacement by a critical-subspace calculation.

title: What the edge of stability actually says
section: Loss curvature is not just feature geometry
text:
Loss curvature is not just feature geometry
For a scalar predictor \(f(w)\) and scalar loss \(\ell(f)\), the chain rule gives
\[
\nabla^2_w\ell(f(w))
=\ell''(f)\nabla f\nabla f^\top
+\ell'(f)\nabla^2 f.
\]
Both predictor geometry and the loss’s output derivatives matter. In logistic classification, the first coefficient is \(p(1-p)\), which becomes small at confident predictions. Growth of a predictor Jacobian does not by itself imply growth of the loss Hessian.
The paper’s Appendix A records exceptions and qualifications: late cross-entropy sharpness reduction, weak sharpening in some wide or simple settings, early decreases, and complications from normalization and nonsmooth components. These matter when turning a recurring observation into a research hypothesis.

title: What the edge of stability actually says
section: The next question is the feedback
text:
The next question is the feedback
The fixed quadratic has no mechanism that changes its own curvature. A nonlinear objective does. The next post keeps one mixed cubic term and follows its effect on both the oscillating coordinate and the coordinate that controls curvature.
That will give us an explicit case where oscillations feed back on the geometry. It will not settle why an arbitrary neural network progressively sharpens, or turn a full-batch mechanism into an SGD theorem.

title: What the edge of stability actually says
section: Try checking the boundary
text:
Try checking the boundary

Does \(\eta a=1.8\) produce growing or shrinking oscillations on a positive scalar quadratic?
Can an exactly zero unstable coordinate remain zero?
What is missing when a descent argument uses only \(H(w)\) but takes a finite step?
Does the identity \(\dot S=-\nabla S\cdot\nabla L\) establish sharpening?



Answer sketches


Shrinking. The multiplier is \(-0.8\).
Yes, on the exact decoupled quadratic. A perturbation can excite it.
Curvature control along the segment, or another justified remainder bound.
No. Its sign depends on the loss and current state.

title: What the edge of stability actually says
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability, Sections 2 through 4 and Appendices A and B, is the primary source for the observation and quadratic comparison. The examples and figure here are independent low-dimensional evaluations, not reproductions of its neural experiments.
Return to Part 23 for coordinate-sensitive sharpness and Part 27 for why a finite observed contrast needs an explanation that survives stronger controls.

title: When update noise selects a feature
section: Construct a feature family with fixed total energy
text:
Construct a feature family with fixed total energy
Use the two training inputs \(e_1,e_2\in\mathbb R^2\). Let \(Z\) be a trainable two by two residual matrix and define
\[
B(\theta)=\operatorname{Diag}(\sqrt{a_1(\theta)},\sqrt{a_2(\theta)}),
\qquad a_1+a_2=2,
\quad a_j>0.
\]
The prediction matrix on the training inputs is \(M+ZB(\theta)\), where \(M\) is a fixed teacher. At each step, targets are \(M+\Xi\), with fresh independent standard Gaussian entries in \(\Xi\). The sampled loss is
\[
\ell(\theta,Z,\Xi)=\tfrac12\|ZB(\theta)-\Xi\|_F^2.
\]
For uniform sampling over the two input columns, mean feature energy is \((a_1+a_2)/2=1\). This normalizes energy across the training distribution. It does not force every input’s feature to have the same norm.
Choose
\[
a_1(\theta)=\frac{2}{1+100e^{1.05(\theta-0.2)}},
\qquad a_2=2-a_1.
\]
Near \(\theta=0.2\), increasing \(\theta\) makes the already smaller energy \(a_1\) decrease and the larger energy \(a_2\) increase.

title: When update noise selects a feature
section: Keep a functional interpretation explicit
text:
Keep a functional interpretation explicit
The training predictor \(M+ZB(\theta)\) alone does not make \(\theta\) an identifiable feature of the represented function. Changing \(B\) can be absorbed into \(Z\).
The constructed model therefore extends predictions off the training inputs as
\[
f_{\theta,Z}(x)=Mx+\theta v x_1x_2+ZB(\theta)x,
\]
with fixed nonzero output vector \(v\). The quadratic term vanishes on \(e_1,e_2\), but changes predictions on mixed inputs. A linear adjustment to \(Z\) cannot absorb that coefficient.
This deliberately shares the parameter controlling feature energies with a nonlinear extrapolation term. Untying those parameters removes this particular functional conclusion. An ordinary network needs a separate check that the selected feature quantity corresponds to a meaningful learned function.
The clean training loss is
\[
L(\theta,Z)=\tfrac12\sum_j a_j(\theta)\|Z_{:j}\|^2.
\]
Every \(Z=0\) is a zero-loss point. Its full Hessian trace in \((\theta,Z)\) coordinates is \(2(a_1+a_2)=4\). Other spectral quantities, including the largest eigenvalue, can change. Constant trace is a controlled property, not a claim that all sharpness-based explanations have been eliminated.

title: When update noise selects a feature
section: Write the actual coupled update
text:
Write the actual coupled update
Put \(A=B^2\). Differentiation gives
\[
G_Z=ZA-\Xi B,
\]
and
\[
g_\theta=\tfrac12\sum_j a'_j\|Z_{:j}\|^2
-\sum_j\frac{a'_j}{2\sqrt{a_j}}\langle\Xi_{:j},Z_{:j}\rangle.
\]
The current noise is independent of the current parameters, so the second term has conditional mean zero. Update with
\[
Z^+=(1-\eta\lambda)Z-\eta D_\theta(G_Z),
\qquad\theta^+=\theta-\eta g_\theta.
\]
Decay acts on \(Z\), a residual map that changes the function. It does not decay the scalar \(\theta\). This is different from decay acting only on a redundant radius in Parts 3 and 22.

title: When update noise selects a feature
section: Compute columnwise response and noise
text:
Compute columnwise response and noise
At fixed \(\theta\), let \(N=\sigma\Xi B\), with \(\sigma=1\) in the displayed experiments. For the odd, left-orthogonally equivariant maps considered here, row symmetry and independent column sign symmetry give a local expansion
\[
\mathbb E D(ZA-N)=Z\operatorname{Diag}(\kappa_1,\kappa_2)+o(\|Z\|_F).
\]
In square dimension \(d\), the Gaussian score identity yields
\[
\kappa_j=\frac{\mathbb E\langle D(N)_{:j},N_{:j}\rangle}{d\sigma^2},
\qquad
v_j=\frac{\mathbb E\|D(N)_{:j}\|^2}{d}.
\]
The factor \(a_j\) in the Gaussian column variance cancels the factor \(a_j\) in the mean perturbation \(ZA\). The response is with respect to \(Z\), rather than an unscaled perturbation of the gradient input.
For \(D(N)=\operatorname{polar}(N)/\sqrt d\), each column of the proposal has squared norm \(1/d\). Hence \(v_j=1/d^2\). Noise variance is equal across matrix coordinates even when the feature energies differ. The restoring responses \(\kappa_j\) need not be equal.
For a raw linear proposal \(D(G)=cG\) with a common positive scalar \(c\) while \(\theta\) is frozen,
\[
\kappa_j=ca_j,\qquad v_j=c^2\sigma^2a_j.
\]
Changing \(c\) changes the comparison’s scale. It does not reverse the column ordering within a fixed state.

title: When update noise selects a feature
section: Derive the fast variance before averaging the feature
text:
Derive the fast variance before averaging the feature
Linearizing the mean matrix response gives the frozen scalar-coordinate surrogate
\[
z^+=(1-\eta(\kappa_j+\lambda))z-\eta\zeta,
\quad\mathbb E\zeta=0,
\quad\operatorname{Var}(\zeta)=v_j.
\]
With independent innovations and \(0<\eta(\kappa_j+\lambda)<2\), its stationary variance is
\[
\mathbb E z^2
=\frac{\eta v_j}{2(\kappa_j+\lambda)-\eta(\kappa_j+\lambda)^2}
=\frac{\eta v_j}{2(\kappa_j+\lambda)}+O(\eta^2).
\]
Substitute the leading variance into the conditional mean of \(g_\theta\), summing over \(d\) rows. On the slow clock \(\tau=\eta^2t\),
\[
\boxed{\frac{d\theta}{d\tau}
=-\frac d4\sum_j a'_j(\theta)
\frac{v_j(\theta)}{\kappa_j(\theta)+\lambda}.}
\]
The matrix fluctuates on a faster scale, while its squared fluctuations create a systematic feature drift. To justify this substitution for the full coupled recursion, one needs uniform stability, mixing, moment bounds, and control as \(\theta\) changes. We have a checked local calculation and numerical agreement, rather than a proved uniform averaging theorem for this nonlinear recursion.

title: When update noise selects a feature
section: Opposite signs in the two-feature calculation
text:
Opposite signs in the two-feature calculation
Suppose \(a_1<a_2\) and \(a'_1=-s\), \(a'_2=s\), with \(s>0\). Write \(k_j=v_j/(\kappa_j+\lambda)\).
For the raw linear proposal and \(\lambda>0\),
\[
k_j=\frac{c^2\sigma^2a_j}{ca_j+\lambda}
\]
increases strictly with \(a_j\). Thus \(k_2>k_1\), and the averaged \(\dot\theta\) is negative. It favors balancing the two energies. At zero decay, these leading ratios are equal, so this leading drift vanishes when their sum is fixed. Finite-step terms can still produce motion.
For the polar proposal, \(v_1=v_2=1/d^2\). In the two-column Gaussian model, \(\kappa_2>\kappa_1\). One way to see the ordering is to use the symmetric convex function
\[
\mathcal F(b_1,b_2)=\mathbb E\|\sigma\Xi\operatorname{Diag}(b_1,b_2)\|_*,
\qquad b_j=\sqrt{a_j}.
\]
Symmetry and convexity order its partial derivatives when \(b_2>b_1\). They are positive, and the nuclear-norm differential gives \(\mathbb E[(N^\top N)^{1/2}_{jj}]=b_j\partial_j\mathcal F\). The strict ordering transfers to the polar response coefficients.
Consequently \(k_1>k_2\), and the polar averaged drift is positive. The two directions of feature selection cannot be reconciled by a common positive change of time. This is a statement about the displayed averaged equation in this constructed family, not a proof of eventual feature collapse.

section: What the archived coupled calculation measured
text:

The stronger numerical control matched the matrix contribution to the training-output step by imposing \(\|D_\theta(G)B(\theta)\|_F=1\). It compared an output-normalized gradient, exact polar, and five finite quintic stages with a norm graft.

The larger rate used 40,000 steps and 128 independent copies. Halving the rate required four times as many steps to preserve \(\eta^2t=16\), using 64 copies. It does not match the complete network’s finite functional step. A momentum buffer would also require an augmented response and temporal covariance analysis.

title: When update noise selects a feature
section: What survives, and what still needs a network test
text:
What survives, and what still needs a network test
The construction establishes a possible mechanism: nonlinear matrix updates can change the balance between restoring response and stochastic forcing, which can bias a slower learned feature parameter. A flat training family and fixed total feature energy do not erase that mechanism.
It does not say which extrapolation is better. The held-out target determines that. It also does not show the same feature dependence arises without the deliberately shared scalar parameter, or that a predicted anisotropy drift becomes rank collapse in a normal network.
Part 27 follows that next test. Independently trained features did change after angular matching, but a local response baseline explained much of the difference. Keeping both findings is more informative than treating the constructed model as a universal explanation.

The feature step has one factor \(\eta\) from its rate and another from the matrix’s squared fluctuation size.

Muon Under Gradient Noise, Theorem 4.1 and Section 6, supplies the response and frozen-surrogate context. Its theorem is not a uniform theorem for the evolving-feature recursion used here.

title: When the optimizer respects a symmetry
section: Gradients and displacements transform differently
text:
Gradients and displacements transform differently
Suppose an invertible linear map \(T\) acts on parameters and preserves the model’s predictions and every sampled loss. For \(\theta'=T\theta\), the chain rule gives
\[
g'=T^{-\top}g.
\]
A parameter displacement representing the same transformed step instead obeys
\[
d'=Td.
\]
The gradient is a covector, while the displacement is a vector. Euclidean gradient descent identifies them using the chosen inner product. That identification respects orthogonal transformations, but not arbitrary invertible rescalings.
For an update \(d=-Pg\) with a preconditioner mapping covectors to vectors, the required transformation is
\[
P'=TPT^\top.
\]
Then \(-P'g'=T(-Pg)\). This is a transformation rule to check, not a property enjoyed automatically by any matrix called a preconditioner. Nonlinear parameter actions also need their derivative and a finite-step rule compatible with the action.

title: When the optimizer respects a symmetry
section: A scale symmetry gives different raw-rate rules
text:
A scale symmetry gives different raw-rate rules
Take a block with exact positive scale invariance, \(w'=cw\), \(c>0\). Then \(g'=g/c\). For raw SGD with a common decay multiplier \(a\),
\[
w^+=aw-\eta g,
\]
the transformed run requires \(\eta'=c^2\eta\) to give \((w')^+=cw^+\). Copying the same raw rate does not satisfy that equation.
For a degree-zero direction such as a normalized gradient or the partial polar factor of a matrix gradient, positive rescaling leaves the direction unchanged. Its raw rate instead needs \(\eta'=c\eta\).







Proposal multiplied by the raw rate
Required raw rate after \(w\mapsto cw\)




Raw gradient
\(c^2\eta\)

\(c\eta\)

\(c\eta\)



If \(a=1-\eta\lambda\), preserving the same multiplier also requires adjusting \(\lambda\) so that \(\eta'\lambda'=\eta\lambda\). This calculation concerns the stated decoupled update, rather than every implementation’s convention for a penalty inside a momentum buffer.

title: When the optimizer respects a symmetry
section: Momentum and damping belong in the transformed checkpoint
text:
Momentum and damping belong in the transformed checkpoint
For a gradient EMA,
\[
m_t=\beta m_{t-1}+(1-\beta)g_t,
\]
matching a scale transformation requires \(m'_t=m_t/c\), including the buffer at the initial comparison point. That relation follows inductively only if the histories and starting states are coupled correctly.
For coordinatewise Adam-style moments, the corresponding rules are
\[
m'=m/c,\qquad v'=v/c^2.
\]
Consider the explicitly defined direction \(m/(\sqrt v+\epsilon)\), with the square root and division taken coordinatewise. If \(\epsilon'=\epsilon/c\), the transformed direction is unchanged, so \(\eta'=c\eta\) gives the required weight displacement. Bias corrections preserve the relation when their coefficients and step counts match.
Keeping a fixed positive epsilon changes this identity, especially when it competes with \(\sqrt v\). Resetting a buffer at a transformed checkpoint changes it too. A buffer storing velocity rather than raw gradient averages has another transformation rule. The update equation determines the answer.
Exact trajectory transformations with momentum already appear in An Exponential Learning Rate Schedule for Deep Learning. The existence of a forward symmetry alone does not specify the needed state transformation.

title: When the optimizer respects a symmetry
section: A rotation exposes the coordinate axes in a diagonal moment
text:
A rotation exposes the coordinate axes in a diagonal moment
Now consider an orthogonal action \(O\). For a column-vector gradient, \(g'=Og\). An EMA first moment transforms as \(m'=Om\), while a full second moment \(C=\mathbb E[gg^\top]\) transforms as
\[
C'=OCO^\top.
\]
The diagonal vector stores only coordinatewise squares. In general,
\[
\operatorname{diag}(OCO^\top)
\]
cannot be reconstructed from \(\operatorname{diag}C\) alone, because off-diagonal correlations contribute after rotation. Thus even correctly transformed gradient histories can yield different diagonal-preconditioned directions in different bases.
Take
\[
m=(1/2,1)^\top,
\qquad C=\operatorname{Diag}(1,9),
\qquad d=\frac m{\sqrt{\operatorname{diag}C}}=(1/2,1/3)^\top.
\]
After a 45-degree rotation, both rotated diagonal variances equal five. Rotating the resulting direction back gives \((1/2,1)^\top/\sqrt5\), rather than \((1/2,1/3)^\top\). The relative discrepancy is about 0.49746. This is a state-level algebraic example, not a training comparison.



Diagonal moment normalization depends on the chosen basis, while a full-matrix spectral function transforms consistently under the same orthogonal changes.

title: When the optimizer respects a symmetry
section: Full and scalar moments can respect this rotation
text:
Full and scalar moments can respect this rotation
A full-matrix direction
\[
d=(C^{1/2}+\epsilon I)^{-1}m,
\qquad\epsilon>0,
\]
obeys \(d'=Od\) because matrix square roots and inverses commute with orthogonal conjugation. Here epsilon sits outside the matrix square root, matching the stated diagonal convention. At zero damping, require positive definiteness or specify a support convention.
A shared scalar second moment based on \(\|g\|^2\) is also invariant under orthogonal rotations, so dividing an equivariant first moment by that scalar preserves equivariance. It discards directional adaptivity that a full matrix retains. Storage, conditioning, numerical evaluation, and practical loss performance are additional considerations.
This orthogonal argument is not a proof of equivariance under arbitrary nonorthogonal actions. The preconditioner transformation law from the first section still has to hold for the actual symmetry being claimed.

title: When the optimizer respects a symmetry
section: Equivariant does not mean free of redundant motion
text:
Equivariant does not mean free of redundant motion
Let \(z\in\mathbb R^3\) be trainable logits for one example. Softmax and cross-entropy are invariant under \(z\mapsto z+b\mathbf1\). At \(z=0\) with class one as the label,
\[
g=(-2/3,1/3,1/3)^\top,
\qquad\mathbf1^\top g=0.
\]
For an undamped, bias-corrected first Adam step, the descent direction is \(-\operatorname{sign}(g)=(1,-1,-1)^\top\). Its entries sum to \(-1\). Coordinatewise normalization has introduced a component along the common-logit shift direction.
Yet this update is translation equivariant: shifting the starting logits leaves the gradient and a correspondingly coupled moment history unchanged. The updated logits remain shifted by exactly the same \(b\mathbf1\).
Euclidean horizontality means a displacement has zero mean across logits. Projecting this particular direction gives
\[
d_H=d-\frac{\mathbf1^\top d}{3}\mathbf1
=(4/3,-2/3,-2/3)^\top.
\]
The projected and unprojected finite steps have identical probabilities because their difference is a common offset. We have removed redundant parameter motion, without improving the immediate represented function in this example.
Thus equivariance and horizontality are different properties. The first compares updates at symmetry-related states. The second chooses a complement to directions tangent to the symmetry orbit, using a declared metric. A quotient construction needs to state both the action and that choice.

title: When the optimizer respects a symmetry
section: Check the architectural symmetry before conditioning it
text:
Check the architectural symmetry before conditioning it
For unpositioned attention, simultaneous right rotations \(Q\mapsto QO\), \(K\mapsto KO\) preserve \(QK^\top\). Fixed positional operators can restrict that symmetry: an arbitrary rotation need not commute with RoPE’s relative rotations. Shared consumers, tied weights, gains, and normalization epsilon can change other proposed actions as well.
A useful numerical test therefore starts with predictions. Transform all parameters required by the proposed symmetry and verify the same outputs on held-fixed examples. Next transform the optimizer state and compare one actual update. Repeat over a coupled sequence, recording damping, clipping, decay, retractions, and precision. A disagreement should first be traced to the claimed action or update rule.
Dead-Direction Conditioners, Section 3.2, explores architecture-aware optimizer conditioning, including scalar and matrix second moments for rotation actions. That is an existing design direction. Our elementary tests here do not reproduce its optimizer or its training claims, and a generic claim about coordinatewise moments must still distinguish rotation dependence from the translation example above.

title: When the optimizer respects a symmetry
section: What this adds to the scale story
text:
What this adds to the scale story
The previous two posts described particular ways a redundant scale affects noise and finite-step solution selection. This post adds another source of dependence: the optimizer’s stored state and coordinate geometry.
A symmetry can guide a reproducible comparison and suggest an update construction. It does not by itself prove useful learning, better generalization, or superiority to a tuned scalar control. Those claims need the kind of separate evaluation developed in Part 21.

No. The explicit first-step example is translation equivariant while its displacement has a redundant common-offset component.

title: The learning rate hidden in the noise
section: Require the symmetry for every sampled loss
text:
Require the symmetry for every sampled loss
Let \(w=ru\), with \(r>0\) and \(\|u\|_2=1\). Suppose each differentiable sampled loss is invariant under \(w\mapsto cw\) for \(c>0\). Write its unit-radius gradient as
\[
\widehat g(u)=g(u)+\xi(u),
\qquad \mathbb E[\xi(u)\mid u]=0,
\qquad C(u)=\mathbb E[\xi(u)\xi(u)^\top\mid u].
\]
Differentiating the symmetry gives \(u^\top\widehat g(u)=0\) and \(\widehat g(ru)=r^{-1}\widehat g(u)\). Consequently the mean gradient and noise are tangent, and \(C(u)u=0\).
Invariance of the population average alone would not establish tangency of every sampled gradient. Batch construction and normalization statistics belong in that assumption.
For constant \(\eta>0\), \(\lambda\geq0\), and \(a=1-\eta\lambda>0\), the exact update is
\[
w^+=ar u-\frac\eta r\widehat g(u).
\]
Orthogonality gives
\[
(r^+)^2=a^2r^2+\frac{\eta^2}{r^2}\|\widehat g(u)\|_2^2.
\]
Thus the conditional expected kick contains both \(\|g(u)\|^2\) and \(\operatorname{tr}C(u)\). This is a finite-step identity, with no diffusion approximation yet.

title: The learning rate hidden in the noise
section: Declare the continuous stochastic model
text:
Declare the continuous stochastic model
Use iteration time, so one unit represents one update, and model the noise by an Itô stochastic differential equation:
\[
dw=-\delta w\,dt-\eta\nabla L(w)\,dt
+\eta S(w)\,dB_t,
\qquad S(w)S(w)^\top=C(w).
\]
Brownian increments satisfy \(\mathbb E[dB_t\,dB_t^\top]=I\,dt\). Choose the tangent noise factor with \(S(ru)=r^{-1}S(u)\). The sign of the Brownian term is a convention that does not change its law.
This is a model of discrete SGD, rather than an exact representation of its finite steps. Within this model, however, Itô calculus gives exact identities. Define \(G=r^2\) and \(T(u)=\operatorname{tr}C(u)\). Then
\[
dG=\left(-2\delta G+\frac{\eta^2}{G}T(u)\right)dt.
\]
The stochastic linear term vanishes because the noise is tangent. Its quadratic variation still contributes the positive trace term. Ordinary deterministic differentiation would miss it.
For the direction,
\[
du=-\frac\eta G g(u)\,dt
+\frac\eta G S(u)\,dB_t
-\frac{\eta^2T(u)}{2G^2}u\,dt.
\]
The last, normal drift is necessary. Its contribution to \(d\|u\|^2\) cancels the noise’s quadratic variation, preserving unit norm. It is not an additional arbitrary weight penalty.
These are the direction-and-radius equations in The Intrinsic Learning Rate, Theorem 5.1, with an explicit iteration-time convention.

title: The learning rate hidden in the noise
section: Remove the arbitrary scale of the raw rate
text:
Remove the arbitrary scale of the raw rate
Let
\[
\Gamma=\frac{r^4}{\eta^2}=\left(\frac G\eta\right)^2,
\qquad q=\Gamma^{-1/2}=\frac\eta{r^2}.
\]
Since \(G\) has finite variation in this tangent-noise model,
\[
\frac{d\Gamma}{dt}=-4\delta\Gamma+2T(u).
\]
The directional equation becomes
\[
du=-qg(u)\,dt+qS(u)\,dB_t
-\frac{T(u)}{2\Gamma}u\,dt.
\]
The raw \(\eta\) has disappeared from these two equations. Their remaining inputs include \(\delta\), \(g\), \(C\), and \((u_0,\Gamma_0)\). If the raw rate changes, matching \(\Gamma_0\) requires changing the initial radius proportionally to \(\sqrt\eta\).
Thus equal products \(\eta\lambda\) do not give an unconditional equivalence when we keep every initial weight array fixed. Nor do they equate models with different noise covariances, minibatch sizes, or scale-sensitive paths.

title: The learning rate hidden in the noise
section: Solve the radius equation before claiming equilibrium
text:
Solve the radius equation before claiming equilibrium
For general \(T(u_t)\),
\[
\Gamma_t=e^{-4\delta t}\Gamma_0
+2\int_0^t e^{-4\delta(t-s)}T(u_s)\,ds.
\]
It is an exponentially weighted history of the noise trace. If \(T(u_t)=T_0>0\) is constant and \(\delta>0\), then
\[
\Gamma_t=\Gamma_*+(\Gamma_0-\Gamma_*)e^{-4\delta t},
\qquad\Gamma_*=\frac{T_0}{2\delta},
\qquad q_*=\sqrt{\frac{2\delta}{T_0}}.
\]
The equilibrium formula concerns \(q=\eta/r^2\), so taking the reciprocal correctly matters. Larger \(\Gamma\) means a smaller directional coefficient.
For \(T_0=1\) and \(\delta=0.001\), we get \(\Gamma_*=500\), \(q_*\approx0.0447214\), and a half-life of \(\log2/(4\delta)\approx173.287\) iteration-time units. This is the half-life of \(\Gamma_t-\Gamma_*\), not necessarily of the radius or of a loss statistic.



Two constant-trace radius models relax at different iteration speeds but collapse when time is measured in units of the learning-rate and decay product.


There is a legitimate constant-trace example. Take sampled losses \(\ell_\xi(w)=\xi^\top w/\|w\|\), with centered isotropic \(\xi\) of covariance \(\sigma^2I\) in dimension \(d\). Their mean loss is zero, while \(C(u)=\sigma^2(I-uu^\top)\) and \(T_0=(d-1)\sigma^2\). The figure evaluates the resulting radius equation, rather than simulating a trained network.

title: The learning rate hidden in the noise
section: Noise strength and noise shape play different roles
text:
Noise strength and noise shape play different roles
At the constant-trace balance, the trace of directional quadratic variation per unit time is
\[
q_*^2T_0=2\delta.
\]
This scalar does not specify which directions receive noise. Two tangent covariance matrices can have the same trace and different eigenvectors or rank. Their normalized trajectories can behave differently even when their radius equations agree.
For independent averaging over \(B\) samples at a fixed state, covariance scales as \(C_B=C_1/B\). In that idealization \(q_*\propto\sqrt B\) at fixed \(\delta\), while \(q_*^2T_B\) remains \(2\delta\). The mean-gradient drift coefficient changes along with the covariance. This is not a general batch-size transfer rule. Correlations, sampling, and parameter motion can alter its premises.

title: The learning rate hidden in the noise
section: The discrete process retains terms the SDE drops
text:
The discrete process retains terms the SDE drops
Set \(Z=\|\widehat g(u)\|^2\). Squaring the exact finite-step radius identity gives
\[
\Gamma^+=a^4\Gamma+2a^2Z+\frac{Z^2}{\Gamma}.
\]
Its conditional expectation depends on \(\mathbb E Z\) and \(\mathbb E Z^2\), including the mean gradient and a fourth-moment term. It is not the linear ODE above. The ODE is useful in a justified diffusion regime, but a finite step, heavy tails, or changing covariance can make its omitted terms consequential.
The deterministic boundary is especially revealing. If \(C=0\), the SDE radius simply contracts exponentially. Discrete gradient descent still has the \(\eta^2\|g(u)\|^2/r^2\) radius kick. That finite-step effect will be central to the sharpness-bias calculation in Part 23.
If \(\delta=0\) and \(T_0>0\), the modeled \(\Gamma\) grows linearly instead of approaching a finite equilibrium. If the trace itself changes across the visited region, the exponential filter remains valid, while the constant-trace equilibrium does not describe the whole trajectory.

title: The learning rate hidden in the noise
section: Radius relaxation is not function-space mixing
text:
Radius relaxation is not function-space mixing
The Intrinsic Learning Rate separately proposes a Fast Equilibrium Conjecture about function-space distributions. It should remain separate from the proved radial identities. Losing memory of \(\Gamma_0\) in a scalar equation does not prove that two normalized parameter processes explore the same regions, forget their initial directions, or attain the same validation loss.
A practical comparison should therefore record norms, directional steps, covariance information where feasible, initialization conventions, and actual loss trajectories. If two runs with the same \(\eta\lambda\) differ, the first step is to inspect those declared ingredients. A single product is a compact description of a particular model, rather than a replacement for the optimizer equation.

title: The learning rate hidden in the noise
section: Try reading the stochastic clock
text:
Try reading the stochastic clock

With \(T_0=2\) and \(\delta=0.002\), find \(\Gamma_*\) and \(q_*\).
Halve \(\eta\) while preserving \(\delta\) and \(\Gamma_0\). How must \(\lambda\) and the initial radius change?
Why can two equal-trace covariance fields produce different directional behavior?
Does convergence of \(\Gamma_t\) establish the Fast Equilibrium Conjecture?



Answer sketches


\(\Gamma_*=500\) and \(q_*=1/\sqrt{500}\approx0.0447214\).
Double \(\lambda\) and divide the initial radius by \(\sqrt2\).
Trace sums noise energy without recording its allocation across tangent directions.
No. Radius relaxation is one scalar statement, whereas mixing concerns distributions of represented functions.

section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
