Reconciling Modern Deep Learning with Traditional Optimization Analyses: The Intrinsic Learning Rate, Sections 3 and 5, Theorem 5.1, Lemma 5.2, and Conjecture 5.3, supplies the normalized-network SDE and the separate mixing conjecture. The equilibrium and figure here follow from the displayed constant-trace ODE. The exact finite-step fourth-moment identity makes explicit a distinction that the diffusion model does not erase.
The argument assumes exact sampled-loss scale invariance, tangent gradient noise, constant raw hyperparameters for the stated change of variables, and an SDE valid away from zero. It does not assert the same one-product description for arbitrary AdamW or Muon trajectories.

title: Should attention and MLPs use the same constraints?
section: Orthogonal columns can still have free lengths
text:
Orthogonal columns can still have free lengths
For a tall matrix \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(m\geq n\), consider
\[
\mathrm{St}(m,n)=\{W:W^\top W=I_n\},
\]
and the diagonal-Gram set
\[
\mathrm{DG}(m,n)=\{W:\operatorname{Off}(W^\top W)=0\}.
\]
Here \(\operatorname{Off}\) keeps the off-diagonal entries. Stiefel fixes all \(n\) singular values at one. Diagonal Gram, or DGram, requires mutually orthogonal columns while allowing their lengths to vary.
Indeed, if \(W=[w_1,\ldots,w_n]\) is in DGram,
\[
W^\top W=\operatorname{Diag}(\|w_1\|_2^2,\ldots,\|w_n\|_2^2).
\]
Its singular values are the column lengths, as a multiset. Thus \(\|W\|_{\rm op}=\max_j\|w_j\|_2\). If all lengths are positive, write \(W=QD\) with \(Q^\top Q=I\) and positive diagonal \(D\). Zero columns are feasible in the stated set, but require care when discussing a smooth manifold or using \(D^{-1}\).
This is different from unit-column normalization, which fixes lengths while permitting correlations. DGram permits unbounded operator norm. It does not require the norm to grow along any particular training trajectory.

title: Should attention and MLPs use the same constraints?
section: Query and key scales multiply
text:
Query and key scales multiply
Use a bias-free, unnormalized attention head with token-row matrix \(H\in\mathbb R^{T\times D}\) and effective projections \(W_Q,W_K\in\mathbb R^{D\times d}\). Its logits are
\[
Z=\frac{HW_QW_K^\top H^\top}{\sqrt d}.
\]
Submultiplicativity gives
\[
\|Z\|_{\rm op}\leq
\frac{\|H\|_{\rm op}^2\|W_Q\|_{\rm op}\|W_K\|_{\rm op}}{\sqrt d}.
\]
Scaling both projections by \(c\) scales actual logits by \(c^2\) at fixed \(H\). Scaling one by \(c\) and the other by \(c^{-1}\) leaves them unchanged. If the growing directions do not overlap with the features, even the first amplification can disappear.
This formula is not the forward map of a head that separately normalizes queries and keys. Positive projection scales cancel in an ideal unit normalization, while learned temperatures introduce other scales. Use the actual map, including epsilon and gains, before importing the argument. Part 18 treats the normalized projection itself.

title: Should attention and MLPs use the same constraints?
section: Gaps, rather than common offsets, sharpen softmax
text:
Gaps, rather than common offsets, sharpen softmax
For one finite logit row \(z\), let \(p=\operatorname{softmax}(z)\). Adding a common scalar to all logits changes nothing. Suppose there is a unique largest entry \(z_1\) and gap
\[
\Delta=z_1-\max_{j\ne1}z_j.
\]
Dividing numerator and denominator by \(e^{z_1}\) gives
\[
1-p_1\leq(T-1)e^{-\Delta}.
\]
The softmax Jacobian is
\[
J_{\rm sm}=\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^\top.
\]
It is positive semidefinite. Write \(e=1-p_1\). Since
\[
\operatorname{tr}J_{\rm sm}=1-\sum_i p_i^2
\leq1-p_1^2\leq2e,
\]
and a positive semidefinite matrix has Frobenius norm at most its trace,
\[
\|J_{\rm sm}\|_F\leq2(T-1)e^{-\Delta}.
\]
At fixed support size, a diverging unique-winner gap makes every Jacobian singular value small. Large logit magnitude alone does not. The row \((a,a,a,a)\) remains uniform for arbitrarily large \(a\).
For an explicit DGram example, take \(D=d=1\), four token features \((1,0,0,0)^\top\), and \(W_Q=W_K=c\). The first row is \((c^2,0,0,0)\). Its gap grows and its Jacobian shrinks. By contrast, four identical token features give a common-offset row and uniform probabilities at every \(c\).



Growing query and key scale shrinks a softmax Jacobian when it creates a winner gap, while a common-offset control remains uniform.


This is a constructed possibility within the feasible set, not a prediction of optimizer behavior. A causal mask requires applying the argument only to allowed keys. A row with one allowed key has zero Jacobian regardless of the weight geometry.

title: Should attention and MLPs use the same constraints?
section: What a bounded projection can guarantee
text:
What a bounded projection can guarantee
Suppose each token satisfies \(\|h_i\|_2\leq R\) and both projections are contractions. Then every allowed logit has magnitude at most \(M=R^2/\sqrt d\).
For a support of size \(s\geq2\), every probability is at least
\[
a=e^{-2M}/s.
\]
It is also at most \(1-a\), because there is another allowed competitor with probability at least \(a\). Therefore every diagonal Jacobian entry obeys \(p_i(1-p_i)\geq a(1-a)\), giving
\[
\|J_{\rm sm}\|_F\geq\sqrt s\,a(1-a)>0.
\]
This lower bound depends on the feature radius and support. It can be numerically tiny. Every softmax Jacobian still annihilates the constant vector, so a positive Frobenius norm does not ensure response to every upstream derivative. Useful end-to-end gradients additionally involve values, residual paths, and the loss.
Exact Stiefel projections remove one unbounded weight-scale pathway. They do not establish a universal training-stability theorem.

title: Should attention and MLPs use the same constraints?
section: The MLP has a different nonlinearity
text:
The MLP has a different nonlinearity
For a bias-free MLP \(f(x)=W_o\phi(W_ix)\),
\[
Df(x)=W_o\operatorname{Diag}(\phi'(W_ix))W_i.
\]
For exact GELU, \(\phi(t)=t\Phi(t)\) and
\[
\phi'(t)=\Phi(t)+t\varphi(t),
\]
where \(\Phi\) and \(\varphi\) are the standard Gaussian distribution function and density. Its derivative approaches one on the positive tail and zero on the negative tail. There is no probability-sum constraint forcing all coordinates into a shared winner competition.
This supports a structural distinction from attention. It does not bound the product of MLP weight norms. DGram can still amplify MLP outputs and derivatives. In a pre-normalized residual block \(x+\operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{LN}(x))\), normalizing the branch input does not erase arbitrary growth of the branch relative to the skip connection.

These are shared-setting point estimates, with no seed distribution in the table. The unconstrained and manifold-managed weights also use different decay rules. The table motivates a module-specific hypothesis rather than establishing the best separately tuned geometry.
There are implementation details to resolve before attributing the result solely to feasible sets.
Packing changes the constraint. For a stacked projection \(B=[B_Q^\top\ B_K^\top\ B_V^\top]^\top\), exact Stiefel gives \(B_Q^\top B_Q+B_K^\top B_K+B_V^\top B_V=I\). Each component is a contraction, but individual heads need not be isometries. Packed DGram need not diagonalize each head’s own Gram. Wide stored matrices require stating which transpose is constrained.
Feasible restoration need not be a retraction. The paper’s Appendix A uses \(R_{\rm DG}(Y)=(UV^\top)\Sigma\) for a descending-order SVD \(Y=U\Sigma V^\top\). Its output has diagonal Gram. But at the already feasible point \(W=\operatorname{Diag}(1,2)\), the polar factor is \(I\) and sorted singular values are \((2,1)\), so \(R_{\rm DG}(W)=\operatorname{Diag}(2,1)\ne W\). A manifold retraction must fix its base point at zero step. This formula can reassign column scales without a proposed displacement.
Actual update norms matter. If every trial direction has norm at most one and DGram restoration preserves singular values, triangle inequality gives
\[
\|W_N\|_{\rm op}\leq\|W_0\|_{\rm op}+\sum_{t<N}\eta_t.
\]
The stated 50,000-step schedule with peak rate 0.02 permits growth of at most 1000 under those exact premises. Figure 2 displays attention-group norms in the hundreds of thousands. This discrepancy calls for checking actual numerical direction norms, run settings, and logs. It does not identify which premise failed. Finite polar approximations are one reason to audit the unit-budget premise explicitly.
The pinned accompanying implementation matches the stated DGram restoration. Its exact relationship to the plotted runs is not established by the snapshot alone.

title: Should attention and MLPs use the same constraints?
section: What would test the proposed explanation?
text:
What would test the proposed explanation?
At the same checkpoints and on the same examples, measure effective per-head query and key norms, realized row gaps, entropy, Jacobian response, and loss. A maximum over the entire attention parameter group can be driven by values or output projections, so it does not locate the proposed query-key mechanism.
Then intervene on the suspected pathway. Compare controlled query-key scales or temperatures, a zero-step-preserving restoration, and a verified spectral cap. Keep the assignment experiment distinct from these interventions because each changes the algorithm. Report tangent residuals, restoration displacement, learning-rate and decay searches, repeated seeds, and compute.
If scale control improves loss while preventing the predicted gap and derivative changes, that supports the mechanism. If the weight statistic changes but gaps do not, the proposed mediator has not moved. If another restoration changes the outcome, constraint geometry alone is an incomplete explanation.

title: The exact spectral update on a tangent space
section: Specify the local optimization problem
text:
Specify the local optimization problem
Let \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) satisfy \(X^\top X=I_p\), with \(n>p\). Given a cost matrix \(M\) of the same shape, solve
\[
\min_B\langle M,B\rangle_F
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
X^\top B+B^\top X=0,
\quad\|B\|_{\rm op}\leq1.
\]
The cost could be the current gradient or a momentum estimate. The oracle is optimal for that supplied cost. If it is momentum, exact oracle evaluation does not make it the steepest direction for the current loss automatically.
The tangent equation follows by differentiating \(X(t)^\top X(t)=I_p\) at zero. It requires \(X^\top B\) to be skew-symmetric, rather than zero. The direction can rotate columns within the current span as well as move them into its orthogonal complement.

title: The exact spectral update on a tangent space
section: Lift the direction to a skew generator
text:
Lift the direction to a skew generator
For any \(Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) with \(Y^\top=-Y\), set \(B=YX\). Then
\[
X^\top B+B^\top X=X^\top(Y+Y^\top)X=0,
\qquad\|B\|_{\rm op}\leq\|Y\|_{\rm op}.
\]
Thus every skew contraction gives a feasible tangent direction. Define
\[
N=\operatorname{skew}(MX^\top)
=\frac12(MX^\top-XM^\top).
\]
Cyclic trace and orthogonality of symmetric and skew matrices give
\[
\langle M,YX\rangle_F
=\langle MX^\top,Y\rangle_F
=\langle N,Y\rangle_F.
\]
We have transformed the objective. To replace the original feasible set, however, we still need the converse: can every tangent contraction be lifted without increasing its norm?

title: The exact spectral update on a tangent space
section: The converse is a norm-preserving completion problem
text:
The converse is a norm-preserving completion problem
Complete \(X\) to an orthogonal basis \(Q=[X\ X_\perp]\). For a tangent \(B\), write
\[
A=X^\top B,\qquad S=X_\perp^\top B.
\]
In this basis, any skew lift taking \(X\) to \(B\) has the form
\[
Q^\top YQ=
\begin{pmatrix}A&-S^\top\\S&D\end{pmatrix},
\qquad D^\top=-D.
\]
The first block column is prescribed, while \(D\) has no effect on \(YX\). Setting \(D=0\) always gives a lift, but can make its norm too large.
Here is the nontrivial ingredient. The norm-preserving block-completion theorem used in Muon on the Stiefel Manifold Admits an Exact Closed-Form Update, Proposition 3, supplies an unrestricted block \(D_0\) such that
\[
H_0=\begin{pmatrix}A&-S^\top\\S&D_0\end{pmatrix}
\quad\text{has}\quad
\|H_0\|_{\rm op}=\|B\|_{\rm op}.
\]
It applies because the fixed first block row and column have the same norm \(\|B\|_{\rm op}\). We are using this completion theorem, rather than proving it from elementary inequalities here.
Now take \(H=\operatorname{skew}(H_0)\). Since \(A\) is already skew and the off-diagonal blocks already match, this changes only the free block. Moreover,
\[
\|H\|_{\rm op}\leq\|H_0\|_{\rm op}=\|B\|_{\rm op}.
\]
The fixed first block column gives the opposite inequality \(\|H\|_{\rm op}\geq\|B\|_{\rm op}\). Hence equality holds. With \(Y=QHQ^\top\), we get a skew lift satisfying \(YX=B\) and exactly the same norm.
Together, the two directions prove
\[
\{YX:Y^\top=-Y,\ \|Y\|_{\rm op}\leq1\}
=\{B:X^\top B+B^\top X=0,\ \|B\|_{\rm op}\leq1\}.
\]
This is equality of feasible images, not a one-to-one correspondence. Several generators can act identically on \(X\).

title: The exact spectral update on a tangent space
section: Why the apparently unused block matters
text:
Why the apparently unused block matters
Take \(n=4\), \(p=2\), and
\[
X=\begin{pmatrix}I_2\\0\end{pmatrix},
\quad J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},
\quad B=\begin{pmatrix}J\\I_2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Here \(\|B\|_{\rm op}=\sqrt2\). The zero-block lift and a completed lift are
\[
H_z=\begin{pmatrix}J&-I_2\\I_2&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
H_c=\begin{pmatrix}J&-I_2\\I_2&-J\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both have the same action on the first two coordinate vectors. But
\[
\|H_z\|_{\rm op}=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},
\qquad\|H_c\|_{\rm op}=\sqrt2.
\]
The first identity follows from the eigenvalues \((3\pm\sqrt5)/2\) of \(H_z^\top H_z\). The second follows from \(H_c^\top H_c=2I_4\). Divide all three matrices by \(\sqrt2\): the tangent direction and completed lift are contractions, while the zero-block lift is not.



A zero-block lift exceeds the unit spectral budget even though another lift of the same tangent direction fits it exactly.


The free block matters because the constraint controls the whole generator, including directions outside the current frame.

title: The exact spectral update on a tangent space
section: Solve the lifted problem with a support polar factor
text:
Solve the lifted problem with a support polar factor
For a square skew cost \(N\), the spectral-ball lower bound is
\[
\langle N,Y\rangle_F\geq-\|N\|_*,
\qquad\|Y\|_{\rm op}\leq1,
\]
where \(\|N\|_*\) is nuclear norm. Retain only positive singular values in a compact SVD \(N=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^\top\) and define \(P_N=U_rV_r^\top\). Set \(P_0=0\).
A real skew matrix has an orthogonal block decomposition into positive multiples of \(J\) and a zero block. Its support polar factor replaces each positive multiple by \(J\) and leaves the zero block at zero. Thus \(P_N\) is itself skew, has norm at most one, and
\[
\langle N,-P_N\rangle_F=-\|N\|_*.
\]
Feasibility and equality to the lower bound certify the solution
\[
\boxed{B_*=-P_NX,
\qquad\langle M,B_*\rangle_F=-\|N\|_*.}
\]
The feasible-image theorem is what makes this a certificate for the original tangent problem.

title: The exact spectral update on a tangent space
section: Specify what happens at zero singular values
text:
Specify what happens at zero singular values
Rank deficiency is routine here: \(\operatorname{rank}(N)\leq2p\), so \(n>2p\) forces a kernel. A real skew matrix of odd dimension is singular too.
The support convention gives a canonical selection, with no action on the kernel. A full square SVD product \(UV^\top\) can add an orthogonal action there and need not be skew. The safe alternative \(-\operatorname{skew}(UV^\top)X\) is also optimal in exact arithmetic, but can choose a different tangent direction at the same cost.
In particular, a purely normal cost \(M=XS\) with \(S=S^\top\) gives \(N=0\). Every feasible direction then has zero cost. Returning zero is a deliberate, reproducible choice.
Floating-point evaluation needs a rank threshold. Treating a genuinely positive singular value as zero changes the exact support value. Keeping roundoff-sized modes can instead select a large direction from a nearly zero cost. State the convention and measure the resulting support defect.

title: The exact spectral update on a tangent space
section: Compress before evaluating the polar factor
text:
Compress before evaluating the polar factor
When \(2p\leq n\), form the thin QR factorization
\[
F=[-X\ M]=Q_cR,
\qquad
J_p=\begin{pmatrix}0&I_p\\-I_p&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Block multiplication gives \(FJ_pF^\top=2N\). Therefore
\[
K=\tfrac12RJ_pR^\top,
\quad N=Q_cKQ_c^\top,
\quad B_*=-Q_cP_K(Q_c^\top X).
\]
The polar evaluation now uses a \(2p\times2p\) matrix. QR and reconstruction cost order \(np^2\), with a dense small factorization costing order \(p^3\). These are arithmetic estimates, excluding cost-matrix construction, rather than measured training speedups. A rank-deficient \(F\) makes \(R\) singular without invalidating the factorization or requiring its inverse.
For example, \(n=1024\), \(p=32\) gives a 64 by 64 compressed cost. If \(2p>n\), this declared QR shape is unavailable. Use the dense formulation or justify another reduction.

title: The exact spectral update on a tangent space
section: A direction still needs a finite step
text:
A direction still needs a finite step
For a tangent \(B\), polar retraction gives
\[
X^+=(X+\eta B)(I_p+\eta^2B^\top B)^{-1/2}.
\]
Its columns are orthonormal in exact arithmetic, and
\[
X^+=X+\eta B-\tfrac12\eta^2XB^\top B+O(\eta^3).
\]
The correction is not part of the tangent direction. An exact oracle does not make an arbitrary finite step decrease a nonlinear loss. A polynomial approximation to \(P_N\) adds another issue: skewing its output enforces skewness but does not prove unit norm or optimal support. Part 13 explains those numerical distinctions.

title: The exact spectral update on a tangent space
section: Try checking the certificate
text:
Try checking the certificate

For \(p=1\), let \(x\) be unit and \(g=m-x(x^\top m)\ne0\). What direction solves the tangent problem?
What should the canonical oracle return for \(M=XS\) with symmetric \(S\)?
Why does \(D=0\) fail as a general proof of norm-preserving lifting?
Does identical oracle objective imply identical directions under different kernel conventions?



Answer sketches


\(-g/\|g\|_2\), the unit descent direction orthogonal to \(x\). The lifted nuclear norm equals \(\|g\|_2\).
Zero. The cost vanishes on every tangent direction.
The explicit lift above has norm \((1+\sqrt5)/2>\sqrt2\), exceeding the norm of its prescribed action.
No. A zero-cost kernel action can change the selected direction while preserving feasibility and optimal value.

section: Yo twin, go read…
text:

Muon on the Stiefel Manifold Admits an Exact Closed-Form Update, Sections 2 to 4 and Appendix A.3, supplies the skew formulation, norm-preserving completion argument, rank discussion, and compressed algorithm. Proposition 3 is the imported completion result. Section 5 adds assumptions for convergence of a sequence of retracted steps. The explicit lift comparison above checks the algebra and is not a reproduction of the paper’s runtime experiments.

title: Why a learning rate can transfer across widths
section: Start with the units of a layer change
text:
Start with the units of a layer change
For \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), measure incoming and outgoing features in RMS norm. Part 5 derived
\[
\|\Delta Wh\|_{\rm RMS}
\leq\sqrt{\frac nm}\|\Delta W\|_{\rm op}\|h\|_{\rm RMS}.
\]
A matrix budget that gives a width-independent upper bound on RMS motion is therefore
\[
N(\Delta W)=\sqrt{\frac nm}\|\Delta W\|_{\rm op}.
\]
Write the raw optimizer step as \(\Delta W=-\eta_{\rm raw}\Psi\). If the proposal has nonzero spectral norm \(q(m,n)\), then setting
\[
\eta_{\rm raw}
=\bar\eta\frac{\sqrt{m/n}}{q(m,n)}
\]
gives \(N(\Delta W)=\bar\eta\). If we know only an asymptotic scale for \(q\), the resulting statement is an asymptotic scale too, not this exact equality.
This quotient is useful because it makes the dependency visible: initialization and optimizer details determine proposal scales, while \(\bar\eta\) specifies the common budget. In practical parametrizations, one normally derives fixed shape factors rather than measuring and cancelling the exact proposal norm at every step. Those are distinct algorithms.

title: Why a learning rate can transfer across widths
section: A spectral upper bound does not force feature motion
text:
A spectral upper bound does not force feature motion
Let \(u,v,z\) be unit vectors, with \(z\perp v\), and let \(h=\sqrt n\,v\). The matrices
\[
D_1=uv^\top,\qquad D_2=uz^\top
\]
both have spectral norm one. Yet
\[
D_1h=\sqrt n\,u,\qquad D_2h=0.
\]
The budget allows a maximal change and a zero change. To get a lower bound on feature motion, we also need overlap with the actual incoming feature.
A single-example gradient supplies a clear form of alignment. If the derivative with respect to the layer output is \(\delta\), then
\[
G=\delta h^\top,
\qquad
Gh=\delta\|h\|_2^2,
\qquad
\|Gh\|_2=\|G\|_{\rm op}\|h\|_2.
\]
The same example that created the update saturates the operator bound. A different example need not. A minibatch sum or a history-dependent optimizer changes the geometry again.
In a moving network,
\[
\Delta(Wh)=\Delta Wh+W\Delta h+\Delta W\Delta h.
\]
Even a large first term can be cancelled by the other terms. A sufficient lower-bound condition is
\[
\|\Delta(Wh)\|_2\geq c\|\Delta Wh\|_2
\]
for a width-independent \(c>0\). An upper bound alone cannot supply this condition. This distinction is central to reading A Spectral Condition for Feature Learning, especially its single-example argument and extensions in Section 3.

title: Why a learning rate can transfer across widths
section: Three update maps on the same exact example
text:
Three update maps on the same exact example
Use a square width-\(d\) layer. Let the incoming feature be \(h=\mathbf1_d\), and choose an output derivative \(\delta=\mathbf1_d/d\). This derivative arises, for example, from the mean readout \(\ell(z)=d^{-1}\sum_i z_i\). Then
\[
G=\frac1d\mathbf1_d\mathbf1_d^\top.
\]
This rank-one matrix has a single nonzero singular value equal to one. Its partial polar factor is itself. Its entrywise sign is the all-ones matrix.
Keeping the input fixed, the resulting output RMS changes are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{proposal }\Psi&\|\Psi\|_{\rm op}&\|\Delta Wh\|_{\rm RMS}\\
\hline
G&1&\eta_{\rm raw}\\
\operatorname{polar}(G)&1&\eta_{\rm raw}\\
\operatorname{sign}(G)&d&d\eta_{\rm raw}
\end{array}
\]
Thus gradient and polar steps use \(\eta_{\rm raw}=\bar\eta\) in this example, while sign steps use \(\eta_{\rm raw}=\bar\eta/d\). For \(\bar\eta=0.01\):

Every entry is an exact one-step feature change. The example has no optimizer history, no training trajectory, and no validation loss. It isolates the shape factor that a raw rate must compensate.



Copying a raw sign rate makes the toy feature change grow with width, while scaling the rate keeps it fixed. A second panel shows how a fixed stabilizer can undo that scaling.


The rectangular version is also instructive. With \(h=\mathbf1_n\) and \(\delta=\mathbf1_m/m\), the gradient spectral norm is \(\sqrt{n/m}\). Rates producing the same RMS change \(\bar\eta\) are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\eta_{\rm gradient}&=\bar\eta\,m/n,\\
\eta_{\rm polar}&=\bar\eta\sqrt{m/n},\\
\eta_{\rm sign}&=\bar\eta/n.
\end{aligned}
\]
These formulas follow from this particular mean-readout example. They are not a table for every layer of every optimizer. Input, hidden, and readout layers can have different dimensional roles, and an implementation may already include a shape factor inside its proposal.

title: Why a learning rate can transfer across widths
section: A small stabilizer can change the width regime
text:
A small stabilizer can change the width regime
Replace the sign by the elementwise map
\[
\Psi_{ij}=\frac{G_{ij}}{|G_{ij}|+\epsilon},\qquad\epsilon\geq0.
\]
This is a stabilized sign map, not a complete Adam update. In our square example, each entry equals \(1/(1+d\epsilon)\). Even with the sign rate \(\bar\eta/d\), the RMS feature change becomes
\[
\frac{\bar\eta}{1+d\epsilon}.
\]
For fixed positive \(\epsilon\), it vanishes as width grows. If instead \(\epsilon=c/d\), the change is \(\bar\eta/(1+c)\), independent of width.
The figure uses \(\epsilon=0.01\) and the matched scaled choice \(0.16/d\), which agree at width 16. The large stabilizer makes the effect visible. These values are illustrative, not recommended Adam settings. Actual moment estimates, bias corrections, and placement before or after a square root require their own formula.
Tensor Programs V, Appendix B.3, explicitly discusses when a non-negligible Adam epsilon needs width scaling. The broader lesson is that the asymptotic regime belongs to the entire denominator. A constant called tiny can become dominant relative to a shrinking gradient.

title: Why a learning rate can transfer across widths
section: Initialization is a separate calculation
text:
Initialization is a separate calculation
The update quotient assumes features and proposals have the scales used in its derivation. Initialization helps establish those conditions, but it does not determine the learning-rate rule by itself.
For a square Gaussian hidden matrix, entry standard deviation proportional to \(d^{-1/2}\) gives spectral scale of order one. A rectangular matrix needs its aspect ratio considered. A readout with a fixed output dimension is different again. Even at the same initial weight scale, changing the loss reduction from a mean to a sum changes the gradient in our example by a factor \(d\).
This is why a width-transfer recipe needs to declare parameter multipliers, initialization, forward scaling, loss reduction, and optimizer equations together. Extending \(\mu\)P, Section 4.1, uses the proposal-norm quotient as a generic organizing calculation. Applying it to a new optimizer still requires its proposal norm and the assumptions behind any claimed lower bounds. A history buffer can change rank and alignment. Damping can change the active scale.
Width and depth are also different questions. Part 16 used a specific \(1/L\) averaged residual construction with sensitivity assumptions. It did not derive a general depth-transfer rule for ordinary Transformers. Changing depth, batch size, or training duration alongside width introduces more variables than a width-only argument controls.

title: Why a learning rate can transfer across widths
section: What would successful transfer actually measure?
text:
What would successful transfer actually measure?
Let \(V_d(\bar\eta)\) be validation loss at width \(d\), after a declared training budget, using all layerwise conversions of the master rate. Tune \(\bar\eta_0\) at a source width. For a target width, define grid transfer regret
\[
R(d)=V_d(\bar\eta_0)-\min_{\bar\eta\in\mathcal G}V_d(\bar\eta),
\]
where the comparison grid \(\mathcal G\) includes \(\bar\eta_0\). This quantity is nonnegative. A small value means the transferred rate performs near the best rate on that tested grid and budget.
A convincing study reports the whole target curve, repeated seeds, uncertainty, and whether the optimum hits a grid boundary. It holds data, schedule conventions, token budgets, and tuning opportunities to a declared comparison. If a boundary wins, expand the grid before treating it as an optimum. A grid minimum is not the unknown optimum over all positive rates.
Stable activation RMS and width-independent one-step motion are useful diagnostics. Neither guarantees low transfer regret or useful learned representations. Tensor Programs V studies actual hyperparameter transfer, beyond the algebraic example here. We have not run a new training sweep for this post.

title: Why a learning rate can transfer across widths
section: Try changing width without changing the budget
text:
Try changing width without changing the budget

title: Weight decay as a norm budget
section: Separate the direction budget from the parameter update
text:
Separate the direction budget from the parameter update
Let \(N\) be a norm, and suppose every proposal obeys
\[
N(v_t)\leq\rho.
\]
For a norm oracle, \(v_t\) could be the descent output \(-\rho D(m_t)\) from Part 14. It could also be another bounded proposal. The norm argument below only needs its bound.
Without decay, the update is
\[
w_{t+1}=w_t+\eta_t v_t,
\qquad\eta_t\geq0.
\]
Telescoping and the triangle inequality give
\[
N(w_t)\leq N(w_0)+\rho\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\eta_j.
\]
The right side can grow without bound. A unit direction budget is a limit on each displacement, not a fixed feasible region for the weights.
Now use decoupled decay with coefficient \(\lambda>0\):
\[
w_{t+1}=(1-\eta_t\lambda)w_t+\eta_t v_t.
\]
This convention ties the decay multiplier to the same learning rate as the proposal. Other conventions need their own calculation.

title: Weight decay as a norm budget
section: The update is a convex combination
text:
The update is a convex combination
Define
\[
a_t=\eta_t\lambda,
\qquad R=\frac\rho\lambda,
\qquad z_t=\frac{v_t}{\lambda}.
\]
Then \(N(z_t)\leq R\), and
\[
w_{t+1}=(1-a_t)w_t+a_tz_t.
\]
If \(0\leq a_t\leq1\) and \(N(w_t)\leq R\), both points in this convex combination lie in the radius-\(R\) ball. Therefore
\[
N(w_{t+1})\leq(1-a_t)R+a_tR=R.
\]
Induction proves an invariant ball whenever the initialization is feasible. The argument works for Euclidean, spectral, Frobenius, or any other genuine norm on the specified block.
For an exact linear minimization oracle, \(z_t=v_t/\lambda\) is an oracle output over the enlarged ball of radius \(\rho/\lambda\), with a consistent choice among ties. The parameter recurrence is then the conditional-gradient update with coefficient \(a_t\). This is the SCG/uSCG connection developed in Training Deep Learning Models with Norm-Constrained LMOs.
The connection concerns a ball and an update rule. It does not force every weight to have norm exactly \(R\). For example, starting at zero with \(a_t<1\) generally places the first iterate strictly inside the ball.

title: Weight decay as a norm budget
section: Initialization leaves a decaying memory
text:
Initialization leaves a decaying memory
What if \(N(w_0)>R\)? The same one-step estimate remains valid, but it no longer proves immediate feasibility.
Write
\[
P_t=\prod_{j=0}^{t-1}(1-a_j),\qquad P_0=1.
\]
Unrolling the scalar inequality gives
\[
N(w_t)\leq P_tN(w_0)+R(1-P_t)
\leq\max\{N(w_0),R\}.
\]
This includes the initial radius instead of silently assuming it away. An initially infeasible trajectory can approach the ball from outside at every finite step.
The coefficient \(P_t\) is the surviving weight of the initialization. If it tends to zero, the upper envelope approaches \(R\). If a schedule leaves a positive product, some of that initial contribution survives in the bound.

title: Weight decay as a norm budget
section: A scalar example saturates the bound
text:
A scalar example saturates the bound
Choose \(v_t=1\), \(\rho=1\), \(\lambda=1/2\), and \(\eta_t=0.1\). Then \(R=2\), \(a_t=0.05\), and
\[
w_{t+1}=0.95w_t+0.1.
\]
The exact solution is
\[
w_t=2+(w_0-2)(0.95)^t.
\]
Starting at zero approaches two from below. Starting at five approaches from above and remains above two for every finite \(t\). Both exactly attain the scalar envelope while they remain positive.
With zero initialization, the no-decay trajectory is \(w_t=0.1t\).



A constant unit proposal accumulates without bound when decay is absent. With learning rate 0.1 and decay coefficient one half, the radius-two bound is approached from below for a zero initialization and from above for an initialization of five.


At twenty updates, decay gives approximately \(1.283028\) from an initialization of zero and \(3.075458\) from an initialization of five. The no-decay value is two at that particular step and continues increasing.
These are exact recurrence calculations. They illustrate the envelope, rather than demonstrate improved generalization or a training advantage.

title: Weight decay as a norm budget
section: The learning rate changes the memory time
text:
The learning rate changes the memory time
For constant \(a\in(0,1)\), \(P_t=(1-a)^t\). The number of updates needed to halve the initial coefficient is
\[
t_{1/2}=\frac{\log(1/2)}{\log(1-a)}.
\]
At \(a=0.05\), this is about \(13.51\) updates. When \(a\) is small, the approximation is \(t_{1/2}\approx\log2/a\).
For a varying schedule,
\[
P_t\leq\exp\left(-\lambda\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}\eta_j\right),
\]
using \(1-a\leq e^{-a}\). Cumulative learning-rate exposure controls this initial-memory bound. If the nonnegative exposure diverges, the product vanishes. A finite exposure does not force it to vanish.
Keeping \(\rho\) and \(\lambda\) fixed preserves the radius \(\rho/\lambda\) in this convention, while changing \(\eta_t\) changes how quickly the recurrence forgets its starting point. It also changes the weights given to successive proposals. Matching one of these quantities is not automatically matching the whole trajectory.

title: Weight decay as a norm budget
section: Read the decay convention before inferring a radius
text:
Read the decay convention before inferring a radius
Suppose an implementation instead uses a separate shrinkage \(d_t\):
\[
w_{t+1}=(1-d_t)w_t+\eta_t v_t.
\]
For \(0<d_t\leq1\), this is a convex combination with the point \((\eta_t/d_t)v_t\). Its possible radius at that step is
\[
R_t=\frac{\eta_t\rho}{d_t}.
\]
A common invariant radius needs a common upper bound on those ratios. Setting \(d_t=\eta_t\lambda\) recovers the earlier constant radius. A decay multiplier independent of the learning rate produces a different relation.
The distinction matters when reading hyperparameters, changing accumulation conventions, or transferring schedules. A parameter called weight decay does not specify its numerical action without the update equation.

title: Weight decay as a norm budget
section: The conditions have consequences
text:
The conditions have consequences
Large coefficients can overshoot. The convex-combination proof uses \(a_t\leq1\). With \(w_0=0\), \(z_t=R\), and \(a_t=1.5\), the next weight is \(1.5R\), already outside the ball. Larger coefficients can even make the constant-proposal recurrence diverge. This does not mean every coefficient above one diverges.
An approximate oracle needs a measured bound. If numerical evaluation only guarantees \(N(v_t)\leq\rho(1+\delta)\) for a uniform \(\delta\geq0\), the same calculation gives radius \(\rho(1+\delta)/\lambda\). If no useful uniform proposal bound is available, the claimed fixed radius has lost a premise. Part 13 showed how a polynomial filter can overshoot its intended spectral budget.
A bounded proposal can still be unhelpful. Part 14’s averaged normalized proposal stays bounded even in its uphill example. The parameter bound says where the iterates may go. Descent alignment, task progress, and stationarity require additional arguments.
The bound belongs to the chosen block. It does not automatically bound an effective map involving a moving gain, or control the full network while other parameter groups evolve freely. Parts 10 and 11 explain those dependencies.

title: Weight decay as a norm budget
section: A penalty inside the oracle changes another part of the rule
text:
A penalty inside the oracle changes another part of the rule
Decoupled decay acts after the oracle has selected a direction. Adding an L2 penalty to the gradient before a nonlinear oracle changes that selection instead.
For a Euclidean unit oracle, take \(w=(1,0)\), \(g=(0,1)\), \(\lambda=1/2\), and \(\eta=0.1\). The decoupled update is
\[
w^+_{\rm dec}=(0.95,-0.1).
\]
Putting the penalty inside the normalized gradient, with no separate shrinkage, gives
\[
w^+_{\rm coupled}
=(1,0)-0.1\frac{(1/2,1)}{\sqrt{5/4}}
\approx(0.955279,-0.089443).
\]
The two formulas have different directions and radial effects. Raw Euclidean gradient descent has a linear update map that makes the familiar equivalence possible. A nonlinear norm oracle changes that algebra.
We now have three distinct ingredients to keep track of: how accurately a numerical method evaluates the direction, how a stochastic estimator supplies its input, and how accumulation with decay limits parameter motion. Together they turn a norm choice into a much more complete optimizer description.

text:
Try setting a norm budget

Let \(\rho=3\), \(\lambda=1/2\), and \(\eta=0.2\). What radius and convex-combination coefficient follow?
Under those values, take \(N(w_0)=9\). What upper bound follows after two updates?
In the plotted example, an approximate proposal has norm at most \(1.2\). What radius replaces two?
Why does an invariant norm ball fail to establish that every proposed update decreases the current loss?



Answer sketches


\(R=\rho/\lambda=6\) and \(a=\eta\lambda=0.1\).
\(P_2=0.9^2=0.81\), giving \(0.81(9)+0.19(6)=8.43\). An initially infeasible point need not enter the ball immediately.
The bound becomes \(1.2/(1/2)=2.4\), under the same coefficient and initialization qualifications.
The argument only uses proposal size. A bounded direction may point uphill, be based on stale gradients, or overshoot because of curvature.

title: What a finite polar iteration actually does
section: Keep the target and its zero modes visible
text:
Keep the target and its zero modes visible
Let \(M\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be the matrix we want to dualize. It might be the current gradient or a momentum buffer. Using only its positive singular values, write
\[
M=U_r\Sigma_rV_r^\top,
\qquad P(M)=U_rV_r^\top.
\]
This compact polar factor has operator norm one when \(M\ne0\), and it attains
\[
\langle M,P(M)\rangle_F=\lVert M\rVert_{\mathrm{nuc}}.
\]
At \(M=0\), choose \(P(0)=0\). This fixes a convention rather than dividing by a zero norm.
Rank matters. If \(M\) has a nullspace, then \(P(M)^\top P(M)=V_rV_r^\top\) is a projector. It need not equal the identity. A numerical test that demands full orthogonality from this rank-deficient target is asking for a different object.
Part 6 allowed other support maximizers on unused subspaces. Here the compact convention gives us a definite target for checking an iteration.

title: What a finite polar iteration actually does
section: A matrix polynomial acts separately on singular modes
text:
A matrix polynomial acts separately on singular modes
Consider an odd scalar polynomial
\[
p(s)=a s+b s^3+c s^5.
\]
Its rectangular matrix implementation is
\[
\mathcal P(X)=aX+bX(X^\top X)+cX(X^\top X)^2.
\]
If \(X=U\operatorname{diag}(s_i)V^\top\), direct multiplication gives
\[
\mathcal P(X)=U\operatorname{diag}(p(s_i))V^\top.
\]
The large matrix calculation therefore reduces to a scalar transformation applied to every mode. Repeating polynomials composes their scalar maps.
The formula also explains why ordinary \(X^3\) is the wrong notation for the rectangular calculation. It may not be defined, and even for a square nonsymmetric matrix it generally differs from \(XX^\top X\).
If an intermediate amplitude becomes negative, its orientation has flipped relative to the original polar target. Its singular value is the absolute amplitude. Plotting only absolute values would hide that error.

title: What a finite polar iteration actually does
section: Derive the classical cubic
text:
Derive the classical cubic
For \(M\ne0\), initialize
\[
X_0=\frac{M}{\lVert M\rVert_F}.
\]
Every singular value starts in \([0,1]\). Seek a cubic \(p(s)=as+bs^3\) that fixes one and is flat there:
\[
a+b=1,\qquad a+3b=0.
\]
Solving gives
\[
p_3(s)=\frac32s-\frac12s^3,
\qquad
X_{k+1}=\frac32X_k-\frac12X_kX_k^\top X_k.
\]
For \(0<s<1\),
\[
p_3(s)-s=\frac12s(1-s^2)>0,
\qquad p_3'(s)=\frac32(1-s^2)>0.
\]
Thus a positive amplitude grows while remaining at most one, and its limit is one. A zero amplitude stays zero. In exact arithmetic, this initialization and iteration approach the compact polar factor.
Writing \(s=1-e\) gives the error recurrence
\[
e_{k+1}=\frac32e_k^2-\frac12e_k^3.
\]
The convergence is quadratic near the target. Near zero, however, \(p_3(s)\approx1.5s\). A tiny mode needs many constant-factor increases before it reaches that fast-convergence region.
Local convergence order does not describe the whole journey.

title: What a finite polar iteration actually does
section: Look at the endpoint after a fixed number of products
text:
Look at the endpoint after a fixed number of products
Take
\[
M=\operatorname{diag}(1,\,0.1,\,0.001,\,0).
\]
Its compact polar factor is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,0)\). The initial amplitudes are the displayed entries divided by \(\sqrt{1.010001}\).
The numerical example below uses the classical cubic in float64. The curves are scalar evaluations of the exact recurrence. They are not a training benchmark or a low-precision kernel comparison.



Classical cubic polar iterations rapidly flatten the large singular modes while the mode starting near one thousandth spends many iterations growing. The exact zero remains zero.

The table reports the poorest active-mode error and the fraction of the momentum’s optimal spectral-ball support value. They measure different things. A small singular value can be poorly resolved while contributing little to the momentum-weighted sum.
For an exact illustration, set \(M=\operatorname{diag}(1,\varepsilon)\) with \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Compare \(P=I\) with \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\). Then
\[
\lVert P-D\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=1,
\qquad
\langle M,P-D\rangle_F=\varepsilon.
\]
The worst-mode error stays one while the lost support tends to zero. This does not establish that the missing mode is unimportant to the current loss. If its gradient is \(G=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\), that mode carries all of the displayed current slope. A momentum buffer and a current gradient can disagree.

title: What a finite polar iteration actually does
section: Higher-degree filters choose a different compromise
text:
Higher-degree filters choose a different compromise
A classical quintic can fix one while setting its first two derivatives there to zero. Solving those three conditions gives
\[
p_5(s)=\frac{15s-10s^3+3s^5}{8}.
\]
Its error is cubic near one, but a tiny amplitude initially grows by only about \(15/8\). Faster local convergence still leaves an early-stage problem.
The Polar Express designs stage-dependent odd polynomials for a whole singular-value interval. Its exact minimax result concerns a specified composition class and positive spectral interval. The practical recipe adds numerical safeguards, so that ideal theorem and the finite-precision implementation have separate qualifications.
Our figure uses the elementary cubic, making its assumptions and arithmetic easy to inspect. It does not reproduce the Polar Express coefficient schedule.
An arbitrary coefficient change can also alter feasibility. The illustrative polynomial \(q(s)=2s-s^3\) sends \(0.8\) to \(1.088\). Applying it to a matrix of operator norm \(0.8\) can produce a direction outside the operator-unit ball. A direction’s approximate similarity to a polar factor does not by itself certify the update budget.

title: What a finite polar iteration actually does
section: Rectangular shape changes how to evaluate the same formula
text:
Rectangular shape changes how to evaluate the same formula
Associativity gives
\[
X(X^\top X)=(XX^\top)X.
\]
For a wide matrix, the left Gram matrix is smaller. For a tall matrix, the right one is smaller. A \(512\times2048\) input offers a \(512\times512\) Gram matrix instead of a \(2048\times2048\) one, reducing the number of Gram entries by a factor of sixteen.
This is an arithmetic and storage observation, not a measured speedup. Product ordering, precision, hardware, and kernel implementation affect actual runtime. Equivalent exact formulas can also round differently.
The initial normalization deserves the same attention. Changing its scale changes the finite scalar starting points. Adding a fixed denominator stabilizer also changes exact rescaling properties. A zero-input convention, a known safe initial interval, and a consistent rank policy belong in the algorithm description.

title: What a finite polar iteration actually does
section: What should count as a useful approximation?
text:
What should count as a useful approximation?
For a proposed step \(-\eta\widehat P\), the first-order loss change uses
\[
-\eta\langle G,\widehat P\rangle_F,
\]
where \(G\) is the current gradient. Polar error, support for \(M\), actual update norm, and alignment with \(G\) are distinct diagnostics. Curvature and finite step size enter the actual loss change too.
A practical comparison should record the numerical work, the returned update’s scale, and the training outcome. Correcting a tiny singular mode more accurately may be worthwhile, irrelevant at the tested budget, or harmful through a changed step. The approximation error alone does not choose among those possibilities.
The next post adds another finite-computation question. Before we apply this nonlinear map, how should we combine noisy gradients?

title: What a finite polar iteration actually does
section: Try following the singular values
text:
Try following the singular values

Start a cubic iteration at \(s=1/2\). Compute the next amplitude and its error from one.
For a rank-three matrix in four dimensions, why can \(\lVert P^\top P-I\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\) equal one even at the exact compact polar factor?
A matrix is \(128\times1024\). How many entries do the smaller and larger Gram matrices contain?
In the two-mode example, find the support lost by dropping the weak mode when \(\varepsilon=10^{-3}\).



Answer sketches


\(p_3(1/2)=11/16\). The remaining error is \(5/16\), also obtained from \(3e^2/2-e^3/2\) at \(e=1/2\).
The compact polar factor has a zero direction. Its Gram matrix is a rank-three projector, so subtracting the full identity leaves eigenvalue minus one on that direction.
The counts are \(128^2=16{,}384\) and \(1024^2=1{,}048{,}576\). The larger has sixty-four times as many entries.
The lost momentum support is \(10^{-3}\), while the operator-norm approximation error remains one.
