title: One gain, several constraints
section: Specify what must be preserved
text:
Specify what must be preserved
Let \(z(x)\in\mathbb R^d\) be fixed features, and let several branches compute
\[
f_i(x)=A_i z(x),\qquad
A_i=W_i\operatorname{diag}(\gamma).
\]
We prescribe the target matrices \(A_i\in\mathbb R^{m_i\times d}\) and require
\[
\lVert W_i\rVert_F=R_i>0
\]
for every branch. Every gain entry must be finite and nonzero. The question is whether one shared gain vector can represent all those target maps while meeting all the radii.
Preserving each branch map is stronger than preserving the final network function. We keep the stronger requirement visible rather than quietly switching between them.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: The compatibility problem becomes linear
text:
The compatibility problem becomes linear
Define a nonnegative matrix of target column energies and a vector of squared radii:
\[
C_{ij}=\lVert A_i[:,j]\rVert_2^2,
\qquad r_i=R_i^2.
\]
Then the representation exists if and only if
\[
Cq=r\quad\text{for some }q\in(0,\infty)^d.
\]
For necessity, the target identity forces \(W_i[:,j]=A_i[:,j]/\gamma_j\), so
\[
R_i^2=\sum_j\frac{\lVert A_i[:,j]\rVert_2^2}{\gamma_j^2}.
\]
Set \(q_j=\gamma_j^{-2}\). This gives the positive linear system.
For sufficiency, given such a \(q\), choose \(\gamma_j=q_j^{-1/2}\) and \(W_i[:,j]=q_j^{1/2}A_i[:,j]\). The effective maps and every required radius then follow directly.
The criterion uses squared Frobenius lengths. It is not automatically a criterion for spectral or Stiefel constraints. It also excludes zero gain entries, which can hide nonzero weight columns when their target columns vanish.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Two branches make the geometry visible
text:
Two branches make the geometry visible
Assume the first branch has positive column energies \(C_{1j}>0\). For any feasible \(q>0\),
\[
\frac{r_2}{r_1}
=\sum_j\omega_j\frac{C_{2j}}{C_{1j}},
\qquad
\omega_j=\frac{C_{1j}q_j}{\sum_s C_{1s}q_s}>0,
\quad\sum_j\omega_j=1.
\]
The required squared-radius ratio must be a positive weighted average of the column-energy ratios. If those ratios are not all equal, feasibility is equivalent to
\[
\min_j\frac{C_{2j}}{C_{1j}}
<\frac{r_2}{r_1}
<\max_j\frac{C_{2j}}{C_{1j}}.
\]
Conversely, choose strictly positive averaging weights with the required mean and set \(q_j=r_1\omega_j/C_{1j}\). If all energy ratios equal a constant, the required radius ratio must equal that constant too.
Take target rows \(A_1=(1,1)\) and \(A_2=(1,2)\). Then
\[
C=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&4\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The squared-radius vector \(r=(2,4)\) is feasible, with \(q=(4/3,2/3)\). The gain magnitudes are approximately \((0.866025,1.224745)\).
The boundary target \(r=(2,2)\) would require \(q_2=0\). It is not feasible with a finite nonzero second gain. Allowing nonnegative coefficients can therefore admit limits that the original parameterization does not attain.



Positive combinations of the column-energy vectors one-one and one-four fill the open wedge between their rays. The target squared radii two-four lies inside. Two-two is on the excluded boundary, and two-ten lies outside.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Finite gain bounds impose more than formal feasibility
text:
Finite gain bounds impose more than formal feasibility
If \(0<g_{\min}\leq|\gamma_j|\leq g_{\max}<\infty\), then the exact condition becomes
\[
Cq=r,\qquad
g_{\max}^{-2}\leq q_j\leq g_{\min}^{-2}.
\]
This is a box-constrained linear feasibility problem. A representation can exist in principle while requiring gain magnitudes outside a chosen stable range.
In the example above, restricting both gain magnitudes to \([1,2]\) forces \(q_j\in[1/4,1]\). The first equation \(q_1+q_2=2\) then forces both coefficients to one, making the second equation equal five rather than four. The formally feasible target is no longer feasible under these gain bounds.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: A proportional pair is incompatible at equal radii
text:
A proportional pair is incompatible at equal radii
If \(A_2=2A_1\ne0\), then \(C_{2j}=4C_{1j}\) for every column. Any shared-gain representation must satisfy \(r_2=4r_1\).
Equal imposed radii contradict that requirement. Increasing the number of columns does not repair this particular obstruction while the target relation \(A_2=2A_1\) is preserved.
That is an exact local statement. Learned upstream features, independent branch multipliers, or other function-preserving transformations can change the question. They are not included in this prescribed-map criterion.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: A scalar gain gives an exact fitting floor
text:
A scalar gain gives an exact fitting floor
Now use one shared scalar \(g\geq0\) instead of a channelwise vector. Assume fixed features satisfy \(\mathbb E[zz^\top]=I\), and supervise all branch outputs with targets \(A_i z\). The population loss is
\[
\mathcal L(g,W)=\frac12\sum_i\lVert gW_i-A_i\rVert_F^2,
\qquad \lVert W_i\rVert_F=R_i.
\]
Write \(b_i=\lVert A_i\rVert_F>0\). For a fixed positive \(g\), Cauchy-Schwarz shows that an optimal \(W_i\) aligns with its target, giving
\[
\min_W\mathcal L(g,W)=\frac12\sum_i(gR_i-b_i)^2.
\]
Minimizing this scalar quadratic yields
\[
g_* =\frac{\sum_iR_ib_i}{\sum_iR_i^2},
\]
\[
\mathcal L_* =\frac12\left(\sum_i b_i^2
-\frac{(\sum_iR_ib_i)^2}{\sum_iR_i^2}\right).
\]
The floor vanishes exactly when the target norm vector is proportional to the radius vector. For \(R=(1,1)\) and \(b=(1,2)\), the optimal gain is \(3/2\) and the minimum loss is \(1/4\).
No learning-rate correction can remove a global fitting floor inside this model. The formula does not say that every optimizer reaches the optimum, or that an end-to-end attention task has this same floor.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Grouping changes the feasible set
text:
Grouping changes the feasible set
Replace the individual radii with a joint constraint
\[
\sum_i\lVert W_i\rVert_F^2=R^2.
\]
For any nonzero target tuple, choose
\[
g=\frac{\sqrt{\sum_i\lVert A_i\rVert_F^2}}{R},
\qquad W_i=A_i/g.
\]
All target maps are preserved and the joint constraint holds. Independent learned branch multipliers provide another way to restore the missing amplitude freedom.
The distinction is which scales the constraint fixes. Individual radii fix relative branch norms as well as total scale. A group radius leaves those relative norms available.
The next post asks whether this local obstruction predicts a failure in a real module. Before making that claim, we need to let attention use its own factorization freedoms and run controls that could overturn the proposed explanation.

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Try the compatibility test
text:
Try the compatibility test

Verify \(Cq=(2,4)\) for the example’s \(q=(4/3,2/3)\).
If \(A_2=3A_1\ne0\), what ratio \(R_2/R_1\) is necessary under a shared gain?
In the scalar-gain model, take \(R=(1,1)\) and \(b=(1,3)\). Find the optimum and fitting floor.



Answer sketches


The row sums are \(4/3+2/3=2\) and \(4/3+4(2/3)=4\).
Squared energies scale by nine, so \(R_2/R_1=3\).
\(g_*=2\) and \(\mathcal L_*=[(2-1)^2+(2-3)^2]/2=1\).

title: One gain, several constraints
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
The cone criterion and scalar fitting-floor calculation are elementary derivations from the displayed model. They are not claims of publication priority or a theorem about a full trainable Transformer.
Hyperball Optimization, Section 4.1, gives the matrix-and-gain rescaling that motivates asking whether several constraints are compatible. Learnable Multipliers, Sections 2 and 4.1 and Appendix C, supplies established multiplier and symmetry baselines. Neither citation substitutes for checking the exact consumers and constraints in a proposed application.

title: The same network, a different step
section: A predictor that forgets its radius
text:
A predictor that forgets its radius
Let \(w\in\mathbb R^2\) be nonzero and define
\[
f_w(x)=\frac{w^\top x}{\|w\|_2}.
\]
For every positive \(c\), \(f_{cw}(x)=f_w(x)\). The predictor remembers the direction of \(w\) and forgets its length. The restriction \(c>0\) matters: a negative multiplier reverses the prediction.
Write \(w=Re\), where \(R=\|w\|_2>0\) and \(\|e\|_2=1\). All points on the positive ray through \(e\) describe the same function. The parameter vector has two coordinates, but this predictor has only one directional degree of freedom.
For a fixed dataset, any differentiable loss built only from these predictions satisfies
\[
L(cw)=L(w).
\]
This is an assumption about a particular parameter block with everything else fixed. We will spend the next post checking when normalization actually gives us this assumption.

title: The same network, a different step
section: Two derivatives tell us what SGD sees
text:
Two derivatives tell us what SGD sees
Differentiate \(L(cw)=L(w)\) with respect to \(c\) at \(c=1\):
\[
\langle w,\nabla L(w)\rangle=0.
\]
The gradient is perpendicular to the weight. Moving directly along the ray has zero first-order effect on the loss, so the gradient has no radial component.
Next differentiate the same identity with respect to \(w\), holding \(c\) fixed. The chain rule gives
\[
c\nabla L(cw)=\nabla L(w).
\]
Doubling the weight therefore halves its gradient. These are standard scale-invariance identities. Their implication for effective learning rates is developed in van Laarhoven’s analysis of regularization and normalization, especially Section 3.1.
Let \(g(e)=\nabla L(e)\). Since \(\nabla L(Re)=g(e)/R\), one raw SGD step is
\[
w^+=Re-\frac{\eta}{R}g(e)
=R\left(e-\frac{\eta}{R^2}g(e)\right).
\]
The outside factor \(R\) does not affect our predictor. The directional change is governed by \(\eta/R^2\), rather than \(\eta\) alone.
One factor of \(1/R\) comes from the smaller gradient. The other comes from comparing that displacement with a longer weight vector.

title: The same network, a different step
section: One exact step, with numbers
text:
One exact step, with numbers
Use the single input \(x=(0,1)\), target \(1\), and squared loss
\[
L(w)=\frac12\left(\frac{w_2}{\sqrt{w_1^2+w_2^2}}-1\right)^2.
\]
Start one copy at \(w=(1,0)\) and another at \(\widetilde w=(2,0)\). Both predict zero and have loss \(1/2\). Their gradients are
\[
\nabla L(1,0)=(0,-1),
\qquad
\nabla L(2,0)=(0,-1/2).
\]
With the same learning rate \(\eta=1/2\), the updated weights are
\[
w^+=(1,1/2),\qquad
\widetilde w^+=(2,1/4).
\]
Their slopes are \(1/2\) and \(1/8\). The rotation angles are approximately \(26.57^\circ\) and \(7.13^\circ\). Their new predictions are \(1/\sqrt5\approx0.4472\) and \(1/\sqrt{65}\approx0.1240\).



Two SGD steps from equivalent predictors. At radius one the tangent step is one half and the rotation is 26.57 degrees. At radius two the tangent step is one quarter and the rotation is 7.13 degrees.


The second copy moved less in parameter space and started farther from the origin. Both effects reduced its rotation. The initial function was identical, but the optimizer did not treat the two representations identically.
To recover the first copy’s new direction, the second copy would need learning rate \(2\), four times as large. That statement concerns this corresponding step. Maintaining equivalence through a whole run requires tracking how radii and optimizer states evolve.

title: The same network, a different step
section: The angle is exact, the effective step is local
text:
The angle is exact, the effective step is local
Because \(g(e)\) is perpendicular to \(e\), the angle \(\theta\) between \(w\) and \(w^+\) obeys
\[
\tan\theta=\frac{\eta\|g(e)\|_2}{R^2}.
\]
This is an exact finite-step identity for the stated update. Calling \(\eta/R^2\) an effective learning rate describes the coefficient in the normalized directional update. It is not a claim that the angle equals that coefficient for a large step.
The next radius also changes:
\[
\|w^+\|_2^2
=R^2+\frac{\eta^2}{R^2}\|g(e)\|_2^2.
\]
A tangent displacement leaves the radius unchanged to first order, but a finite tangent step ends outside the original circle. Repeated SGD steps can grow the radius and thereby change subsequent directional steps. We do not need an equilibrium approximation to see this feedback.

title: The same network, a different step
section: Where weight decay will enter
text:
Where weight decay will enter
For the update convention
\[
w^+=(1-\eta\lambda)w-\eta\nabla L(w),
\]
assume \(1-\eta\lambda>0\). The decay term shortens the radial part while the gradient remains tangent. The same right triangle now gives
\[
\tan\theta
=\frac{\eta\|g(e)\|_2}{(1-\eta\lambda)R^2}.
\]
Decay alone preserves the predictor in this model, but decay inside a training update can alter the direction learned next. This is the first reason to be suspicious of the phrase “scale does not matter.”
The equation is for raw SGD with this decay convention. With momentum, the accumulated update need not remain tangent to the current weight. With a normalized update, the displacement need not shrink as \(1/R\). We will derive those cases separately rather than reuse the SGD formula.
An angular change is also not a universal measure of progress. Our example changes one prediction by a known amount. In a large network, a rotation could help, hurt, or barely affect the output.

title: The same network, a different step
section: The coordinates we choose become part of learning
text:
The coordinates we choose become part of learning
The example isolates three different objects: the function, its redundant parameter representation, and the rule that moves that representation. Equality of the first does not imply equality of the third.
That distinction will connect the rest of this series. Weight decay changes radii. Normalization determines which rescalings preserve a function. Layer norms specify which perturbations count as small. Modula combines those local choices into a network geometry. Before choosing any constraint, we need to know which of these scales it controls.
The next post asks where the exact symmetry comes from, and why normalizing the input to a matrix does not usually make that matrix’s own scale disappear.

title: The same network, a different step
section: Try the calculation
text:
Try the calculation

Start a third copy at \((3,0)\). What learning rate makes its first updated direction agree with the radius-one copy using \(\eta=1/2\)?
Use the unit update \(u=\nabla L(w)/\|\nabla L(w)\|_2\) instead of the raw gradient. What is \(\tan\theta\) when the gradient is nonzero?
Why can a tangent step increase the radius even though the directional derivative of the squared radius is zero?



Answer sketches


The coefficient \(\eta/R^2\) must equal \(1/2\), so \(\eta=9/2\).
The displacement has length \(\eta\) and is perpendicular to \(w\), so \(\tan\theta=\eta/R\). The squared-radius law for raw SGD no longer applies to this normalized update.
Expanding the squared norm gives the zero first-order cross term plus the positive second-order term \(\eta^2\|\nabla L(w)\|_2^2\).

title: The same network, a different step
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Twan van Laarhoven, L2 Regularization versus Batch and Weight Normalization (2017) supplies the foundational scale-to-step argument. The two-dimensional numerical example above is a direct calculation under the explicitly defined predictor and squared loss.
Zhiyuan Li and Sanjeev Arora, An Exponential Learning Rate Schedule for Deep Learning (ICLR 2020) develops stronger trajectory equivalences with normalization, decay, and momentum. Matching a whole trajectory involves more than matching the one scalar learning rate in our example.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: Put the product in a positive form
text:
Put the product in a positive form
For positive semidefinite \(A,B\), use \[
P=A^{1/2}BA^{1/2}.
\] It is positive semidefinite because \[
x^*Px=(A^{1/2}x)^*B(A^{1/2}x)\geq0.
\] Cyclicity gives \[
\operatorname{Tr}(P^k)=\operatorname{Tr}((AB)^k).
\] For invertible \(A\), the matrices are similar: \[
A^{-1/2}(AB)A^{1/2}=A^{1/2}BA^{1/2}.
\] For singular \(A\), the determinant identity \(\det(I-tXY)=\det(I-tYX)\) still gives the same characteristic polynomial, with \(X=A^{1/2}\) and \(Y=A^{1/2}B\). Nevertheless, the positive representative is preferable for spectral analysis and numerical eigensolvers.
For bounded positive free variables \(a,b\) in a tracial operator-algebra setting, the law of \(a^{1/2}ba^{1/2}\) is called multiplicative free convolution, written \[
\mu_a\boxtimes\mu_b.
\] It is determined by the marginal laws and freeness. Our assumptions of positivity and boundedness make the law and square root unambiguous.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: The first two product moments
text:
The first two product moments
Let \(\alpha=\tau(a)\) and \(\beta=\tau(b)\). Freeness gives \[
\tau(ab)=\alpha\beta.
\] Write \(a=\alpha1+a_0\), \(b=\beta1+b_0\), where the subscripted variables are centered. Expanding \(abab\), terms with one centered factor vanish. Terms with two centered factors survive only when they use the same variable. The terms with three centered factors vanish by freeness and cyclicity, and \(\tau(a_0b_0a_0b_0)=0\).
Therefore \[
\begin{aligned}
\tau(abab)
&=\alpha^2\beta^2+\beta^2\tau(a_0^2)+\alpha^2\tau(b_0^2)\\
&=\beta^2m_2(a)+\alpha^2m_2(b)-\alpha^2\beta^2.
\end{aligned}
\] For mean-one variables with variances \(v_a,v_b\), the product has mean one and variance \(v_a+v_b\).
Classically independent positive variables instead give \(\mathbb E[X^2Y^2]=\mathbb E[X^2]\mathbb E[Y^2]\), hence variance \(v_a+v_b+v_av_b\) when both means are one. The same two marginal spectra can produce a different second product moment depending on how their directions interact.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: Build the S-transform
text:
Build the S-transform
Define the moment series without its constant term: \[
\psi_\mu(t)=\int\frac{tx}{1-tx}\,d\mu(x)
=\sum_{k\geq1}m_kt^k.
\] Assume \(m_1\neq0\). Since \(\psi_\mu'(0)=m_1\), it has a local compositional inverse \(\chi_\mu\) near zero. Set \[
\boxed{S_\mu(w)=\frac{1+w}{w}\chi_\mu(w).}
\] The apparent singularity at zero is removable. Because \(\chi(w)=w/m_1+O(w^2)\), \[
S_\mu(0)=\frac1{m_1}.
\] For a positive law, the only zero-mean case is \(\delta_0\), whose product law is trivially \(\delta_0\). A centered sign variable, however, does not have this ordinary S-transform: its moment series has no linear term. We cannot reuse the sign example without changing the setup.
The multiplicative analogue of R-transform additivity is the theorem \[
\boxed{S_{\mu\boxtimes\nu}(w)=S_\mu(w)S_\nu(w).}
\] This is a substantive theorem about free products, not a consequence of the inverse-function definition alone. Its combinatorial proof uses noncrossing partitions and their complements. See Nica and Speicher, Lectures 14 and 18.
A short expansion connects it to our earlier calculation. Inverting \(\psi(t)=m_1t+m_2t^2+\cdots\) gives \[
S(w)=\frac1{m_1}
+\left(\frac1{m_1}-\frac{m_2}{m_1^3}\right)w+O(w^2).
\] For mean-one laws this is \(1-vw+O(w^2)\). Multiplying the two series adds their variances, exactly as the direct mixed-moment calculation predicted.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: Checking the S-transform normalization
text:
Checking the S-transform normalization
For a constant \(c>0\), \[
\psi(t)=\frac{ct}{1-ct},\quad
\chi(w)=\frac{w}{c(1+w)},\quad
S_{\delta_c}(w)=\frac1c.
\] Thus multiplying by a constant rescales the law and divides its S-transform by that constant.
For a projection \(p=p^*=p^2\) with \(\tau(p)=\alpha>0\), every positive-order moment is \(\alpha\). Its law is \((1-\alpha)\delta_0+\alpha\delta_1\), so \[
\psi_p(t)=\frac{\alpha t}{1-t},\quad
\chi_p(w)=\frac{w}{\alpha+w},\quad
\boxed{S_p(w)=\frac{1+w}{\alpha+w}.}
\] If \(q\) is a free projection with trace \(\beta>0\), then \[
S_{pqp}(w)=\frac{(1+w)^2}{(\alpha+w)(\beta+w)}.
\] Although \(p\) and \(q\) are projections, \(pqp\) generally is not. Randomly oriented subspaces produce intermediate eigenvalues between zero and one.
Its first two moments, using the calculation above, are \[
m_1=\alpha\beta,\qquad
m_2=\alpha\beta(\alpha+\beta-\alpha\beta).
\] At \(\alpha=\beta=1/2\), these are \(1/4\) and \(3/16\). An intersection indicator for independent commuting scalar events would instead have both moments equal to \(1/4\). This gives a concrete distinction between multiplying free projections and multiplying independent indicator variables.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: Recovering a law from its S-transform
text:
Recovering a law from its S-transform
Use the same Cauchy-transform convention as Part III. Then \[
\psi(1/z)=zG(z)-1.
\] Writing \(w=zG(z)-1\), the inverse relation is \(\chi(w)=1/z\). Substituting into the S-transform definition gives \[
\boxed{zwS(w)=1+w,\qquad G(z)=\frac{1+w}{z}.}
\] Choose the solution with \(w\to0\) as \(z\to\infty\) and the correct upper-half-plane behavior for \(G\). This is the computational route we will use for covariance products in the final post.

title: Multiplying positive matrices
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

What is \(S_{\delta_1}\), and why is that necessary?
Show directly that \(S_{ca}(w)=S_a(w)/c\) for \(c>0\).
If two free positive mean-one variables each have second moment two, what is the second moment of their product?



Answer sketches


It is one, the multiplicative identity. Multiplying by the identity operator must preserve the law.
\(\psi_{ca}(t)=\psi_a(ct)\), so the compositional inverse is \(\chi_a(w)/c\).
Each variance is one. The product variance is two and its mean is one, so its second moment is three.

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: The Cauchy transform
text:
The Cauchy transform
For a compactly supported probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R\), define its Cauchy transform by \[
G_\mu(z)=\int\frac{1}{z-x}\,d\mu(x),\qquad \operatorname{Im}z>0.
\] Our sign convention matters. With \(1/(z-x)\), the imaginary part of \(G\) is negative in the upper half-plane. Some references use the negative of this transform.
For sufficiently large \(|z|\), expand the geometric series: \[
G_\mu(z)=\frac1z+\frac{m_1}{z^2}+\frac{m_2}{z^3}+\cdots.
\] Thus \(G\) encodes every moment, and its leading behavior must be \(1/z\).
It also recovers the density. Indeed, \[
-\frac1\pi\operatorname{Im}G_\mu(x+i\eta)
=\int\frac{\eta}{\pi((x-t)^2+\eta^2)}\,d\mu(t).
\] The right side smooths the measure with a Cauchy kernel. At continuity points of a density \(\rho\), letting \(\eta\downarrow0\) gives \(\rho(x)\). More generally, Stieltjes inversion recovers masses of intervals. An atom at \(x_0\) can be checked separately through \[
\mu(\{x_0\})=\lim_{\eta\downarrow0}i\eta G_\mu(x_0+i\eta).
\]

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: From the moment formula to a functional equation
text:
From the moment formula to a functional equation
Introduce the two generating series \[
M(t)=1+\sum_{n\geq1}m_nt^n,
\qquad R(w)=\sum_{n\geq1}\kappa_nw^{n-1}.
\] Look at the block containing position 1 in a noncrossing partition. If that block has size \(k\), it leaves \(k\) ordered gaps, each carrying an independent noncrossing partition. This decomposes the moment formula into \[
M(t)=1+\sum_{k\geq1}\kappa_k t^kM(t)^k
=1+tM(t)R(tM(t)).
\] Since \(G(z)=z^{-1}M(z^{-1})\), substitution gives \[
zG(z)=1+G(z)R(G(z)),
\] or \[
\boxed{z=\frac1{G(z)}+R(G(z)).}
\] Initially this identity holds near infinity, or as a formal Laurent-series identity. We should not assume that the power series for \(R\) converges at every value of \(G\).
Equivalently, let \(K\) denote the local compositional inverse of \(G\) near infinity, so \(K(w)\sim1/w\) near zero. Then \[
R(w)=K(w)-\frac1w.
\] This is the R-transform. Cumulant additivity becomes \[
\boxed{R_{\mu\boxplus\nu}(w)=R_\mu(w)+R_\nu(w).}
\] The local inverse and analytic extension are developed rigorously in Speicher, Theorem 4.12.

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: Warm-up: adding semicircles
text:
Warm-up: adding semicircles
A centered semicircular variable of variance \(v\) has only one nonzero cumulant, \(\kappa_2=v\). Therefore \(R(w)=vw\) and \[
vG(z)^2-zG(z)+1=0.
\] For \(v>0\), choose the solution \[
G(z)=\frac{z-\sqrt{z^2-4v}}{2v},
\] where the square root is the branch asymptotic to \(z\) at infinity. The other solution grows like \(z/v\), which cannot be the transform of a probability measure.
Taking the boundary value in the upper half-plane recovers the semicircle density. Adding free semicircles of variances \(v_1,v_2\) simply replaces \(vw\) by \((v_1+v_2)w\). Their sum is semicircular with variance \(v_1+v_2\).

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: Adding two free sign variables
text:
Adding two free sign variables
Let \(\mu=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_1\). Its transform is immediate: \[
G_\mu(z)=\frac12\left(\frac1{z-1}+\frac1{z+1}\right)
=\frac{z}{z^2-1}.
\] Solve \(w=z/(z^2-1)\) for \(z\): \[
z=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1+4w^2}}{2w}.
\] The inverse with a \(1/w\) pole uses the plus sign, with the square root analytic and equal to one at \(w=0\). Hence \[
R_\mu(w)=\frac{\sqrt{1+4w^2}-1}{2w}.
\] Expanding gives \(R_\mu(w)=w-w^3+2w^5-\cdots\), consistent with \(\kappa_2=1\) and \(\kappa_4=-1\).
For \(\nu=\mu\boxplus\mu\), add the two R-transforms. The equation for \(G_\nu\) becomes \[
z=\frac1{G_\nu(z)}+
\frac{\sqrt{1+4G_\nu(z)^2}-1}{G_\nu(z)}
=\frac{\sqrt{1+4G_\nu(z)^2}}{G_\nu(z)}.
\] Squaring yields \((z^2-4)G_\nu(z)^2=1\). Choose the branch matching \(G_\nu(z)\sim1/z\): \[
\boxed{G_\nu(z)=\frac1{\sqrt{z^2-4}}.}
\] Here \(\sqrt{z^2-4}\) means the analytic branch on \(\mathbb C\setminus[-2,2]\) asymptotic to \(z\). It is not the pointwise principal square root of \(z^2-4\) everywhere. The formula agrees with the transform near infinity and continues analytically to the upper half-plane.
For \(-2<x<2\), its boundary value is \[
G_\nu(x+i0)=-\frac{i}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}.
\] Therefore the answer is the arcsine law: \[
\boxed{d\nu(x)=\frac{\mathbf1_{(-2,2)}(x)}{\pi\sqrt{4-x^2}}\,dx.}
\] The density diverges at the endpoints, but its integral is one. These integrable divergences are not atoms: multiplying the transform by \(i\eta\) at either endpoint gives zero in the limit.

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: Checking the moments
text:
Checking the moments
Set \(x=2\cos\theta\). The arcsine measure becomes uniform \(d\theta/\pi\) on \([0,\pi]\), so \[
\int x^2\,d\nu(x)=2,\qquad
\int x^4\,d\nu(x)=6.
\] More generally, its odd moments vanish and its \(2k\)th moment is \(\binom{2k}{k}\). This agrees with our mixed-word calculations.
Two free sign variables produce an arcsine law. Many free sign variables, summed and divided by the square root of their number, approach a semicircle. These are different questions, so there is no conflict between the two answers.

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Find \(R_{\delta_c}\).
Derive the transform rule for \(ca\) from cumulant scaling.
Why is solving a polynomial equation for \(G\) insufficient without a branch condition?



Answer sketches


\(G(z)=1/(z-c)\), so \(K(w)=c+1/w\) and \(R(w)=c\). Free addition of a constant translates the law.
\(R_{ca}(w)=cR_a(cw)\), since the \(n\)th cumulant scales by \(c^n\).
A polynomial may have several solutions. A probability Cauchy transform must be analytic in the upper half-plane, have negative imaginary part there, and behave like \(1/z\) at infinity. Squaring can introduce extraneous branches.

title: Calculating the law of a sum
section: Further reading
text:
Further reading
Speicher’s lecture notes, Section 4 contain the analytic R-transform theory and the symmetric two-point example. Tao’s free probability notes give another route from transforms to free convolution. Check the sign convention when moving between references.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Eigenvalues are not enough
text:
Eigenvalues are not enough
Take \[
A=B_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad B_2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\] Both choices of \(B\) have spectrum \(\{-1,1\}\). Nevertheless, \[
\operatorname{spec}(A+B_1)=\{-2,2\},\qquad
\operatorname{spec}(A+B_2)=\{0,0\}.
\] The individual spectra have lost the information about which directions line up.
Writing \(A=U\Lambda U^*\) and \(B=V\Gamma V^*\) makes the missing ingredient explicit: the spectrum of their sum depends on the relative basis \(U^*V\).
Here is a useful replacement for choosing an alignment. Keep deterministic diagonal matrices \(D_n,E_n\), draw a Haar unitary \(U_n\), and study \[
D_n+U_nE_nU_n^*.
\] Haar measure is the uniform probability measure on the unitary group, in the precise sense of invariance under multiplication by any fixed unitary. Conjugation preserves the spectrum of \(E_n\) and randomizes its eigenbasis.
Under suitable hypotheses, this produces a limiting rule for mixed moments. That rule is freeness.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: The trace turns a matrix into a distribution
text:
The trace turns a matrix into a distribution
Define the empirical spectral measure and normalized trace by \[
\mu_A=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{\lambda_j(A)},
\qquad \tau_n(A)=\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}(A).
\] Then \[
\boxed{\tau_n(A^k)=\int x^k\,d\mu_A(x).}
\] A normalized trace of a power is exactly a spectral moment. The normalization gives total mass one, so moments remain comparable as the dimension changes.
To study the sum, expand \(\tau_n((A+B)^k)\). Now words such as \(AABB\) and \(ABAB\) appear. They cannot generally be rearranged into each other. Trace is cyclic, so \(\tau(ABBA)=\tau(AABB)\), but it does not permit arbitrary permutations.
For a random matrix, \(\tau_n(A^k)\) is itself random. Its ensemble average is \(\mathbb E[\tau_n(A^k)]\). We will distinguish these when discussing experiments and convergence.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Noncommutative probability
text:
Noncommutative probability
Our setting is a unital algebra \(\mathcal A\) with an adjoint operation and a normalized positive trace \(\tau\). Thus \(\tau\) is linear and satisfies \[
\tau(1)=1,\qquad \tau(x^*x)\geq0,\qquad \tau(xy)=\tau(yx).
\] Matrices with normalized trace are the finite-dimensional example. For bounded self-adjoint operators, the spectral theorem gives a probability law whose moments are \(\tau(a^k)\). We use compactly supported laws throughout the series, so their moments determine them uniquely.
Think of a self-adjoint element \(a=a^*\) as a real random variable and \(\tau\) as expectation. Multiplication may fail to commute, but positivity and spectral measures remain available.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Freeness is a rule for centered, alternating products
text:
Freeness is a rule for centered, alternating products
Unital subalgebras \(\mathcal A_1,\mathcal A_2,\ldots\) are free if \[
\tau(x_1x_2\cdots x_m)=0
\] whenever each \(x_i\) belongs to \(\mathcal A_{j_i}\), consecutive indices differ, and every factor is centered: \[
j_i\neq j_{i+1},\qquad \tau(x_i)=0.
\] We call \(a\) and \(b\) free when the unital algebras they generate are free. The condition therefore applies to centered polynomials in \(a\) and \(b\), not merely to the original variables.
Why center? Because every factor can be split into its mean and its fluctuation. Expanding these splits reduces mixed moments to simpler ones until the alternating-centered rule applies. This recursively determines the joint moments from the two marginal moment sequences.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: A fourth-moment calculation
text:
A fourth-moment calculation
Suppose \(a,b\) are centered and free, with \[
\tau(a^2)=\alpha,\qquad \tau(b^2)=\beta.
\] The definition immediately gives \[
\tau(ab)=0,\qquad \tau(abab)=0.
\] But \(a^2b^2\) is different. Center the squares: \[
0=\tau\bigl((a^2-\alpha1)(b^2-\beta1)\bigr)
  =\tau(a^2b^2)-\alpha\beta.
\] Consequently, \[
\boxed{\tau(a^2b^2)=\alpha\beta,\qquad \tau(abab)=0.}
\] For centered, classically independent scalar variables \(X,Y\) with those variances, both corresponding expressions equal \(\alpha\beta\), since \(XYXY=X^2Y^2\).
At second order, both theories give variance addition. At fourth order, the distinction becomes visible: \[
\tau((a+b)^4)=\tau(a^4)+\tau(b^4)+4\alpha\beta.
\] To see the coefficient four, list the six words containing two of each letter. The words \(aabb,abba,baab,bbaa\) each contribute \(\alpha\beta\). The alternating words \(abab,baba\) vanish. Words with three of one letter and one of the other also vanish, by centering and cyclicity.
Classical independence instead gives a coefficient of six.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Adding two free sign variables
text:
Adding two free sign variables
Let both marginal laws be \[
\mu=\tfrac12\delta_{-1}+\tfrac12\delta_1.
\] Each variable is centered, with second and fourth moments equal to one. The free sum therefore has \[
m_2=2,\qquad m_4=6.
\] The classical sum has masses \(1/4,1/2,1/4\) at \(-2,0,2\), and fourth moment eight. Perfect alignment, where \(b=a\), gives fourth moment sixteen.
We write the law of a free sum as \(\mu\boxplus\nu\), the additive free convolution. Part III will calculate the entire law in this example. Part IV will compare all three eigenbasis choices numerically.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Asymptotic freeness of random matrices
text:
Asymptotic freeness of random matrices
One sufficient setting is that \(D_n,E_n\) are deterministic Hermitian matrices with uniformly bounded operator norms and convergent empirical spectral measures. If \(U_n\) is Haar unitary, then the pair \((D_n,U_nE_nU_n^*)\) converges in joint normalized-trace moments to a free pair, in probability. This is a standard asymptotic-freeness theorem, not something implied just by our definition. Speicher, Section 7.
At each finite dimension, the pair generally fails exact freeness. The theorem describes the limit for each fixed word. Independent random diagonal sign matrices illustrate why ordinary independence alone is insufficient: they commute, and their alternating fourth moment is identically one.

title: Adding large random matrices
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Compute \(\tau((a+b)^2)\) for centered free variables of variances \(\alpha,\beta\).
For the symmetric two-point laws above, compute \(\tau((a+b)^3)\).
Explain why the identity \(a^2=b^2=1\) is compatible with \(\tau(abab)=0\).



Answer sketches


The cross terms vanish, leaving \(\alpha+\beta\).
It is zero. The pure cubic moments vanish by symmetry, and the mixed terms vanish by freeness and cyclicity.
The squares only simplify adjacent equal factors. Simplifying \(abab\) to \(a^2b^2\) would require commutativity.

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Crossing and noncrossing partitions
text:
Crossing and noncrossing partitions
A partition divides \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) into disjoint nonempty blocks. It is noncrossing if there are no indices \(i<j<k<\ell\) with \(i,k\) in one block and \(j,\ell\) in a different block.
For four positions, the three pairings are \[
\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\},\quad
\{\{1,4\},\{2,3\}\},\quad
\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\}.
\] Only the last one crosses when the positions are placed around a circle.



Two noncrossing pairings and the crossing pairing on four cyclically ordered positions.


For \(abab\), pairing equal letters requires precisely the crossing pairing. For \(aabb\), it requires the first noncrossing pairing. This is the diagrammatic trace of our earlier calculation. To make it a general method, we introduce cumulants.

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Cumulants are defined recursively from moments
text:
Cumulants are defined recursively from moments
Write \(NC(n)\) for the set of noncrossing partitions of \(n\) positions. The free cumulants \(\kappa_n\) are the multilinear functionals defined by \[
\tau(x_1\cdots x_n)
=\sum_{\pi\in NC(n)}\kappa_\pi(x_1,\ldots,x_n),
\] where \[
\kappa_\pi(x_1,\ldots,x_n)
=\prod_{V\in\pi}\kappa_{|V|}(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_{|V|}}),
\qquad V=\{i_1<\cdots<i_{|V|}\}.
\] The factors on the right are scalars, so their product commutes. Within each cumulant, the original order of the arguments is retained.
This is a recursive definition: the one-block partition contributes \(\kappa_n\), and all other blocks have smaller size. Once cumulants of lower orders are known, solve for \(\kappa_n\).
For one variable, abbreviate \(m_n=\tau(a^n)\) and \(\kappa_n=\kappa_n(a,\ldots,a)\). The first relations are \[
\begin{aligned}
m_1&=\kappa_1,\\
m_2&=\kappa_2+\kappa_1^2,\\
m_3&=\kappa_3+3\kappa_2\kappa_1+\kappa_1^3,\\
m_4&=\kappa_4+4\kappa_3\kappa_1+2\kappa_2^2
       +6\kappa_2\kappa_1^2+\kappa_1^4.
\end{aligned}
\] That coefficient two counts the noncrossing pairings on four positions. Classical cumulants use all set partitions, so the corresponding coefficient is three.
For a centered variable, \[
\kappa_2=m_2,\qquad \kappa_3=m_3,\qquad
\boxed{\kappa_4=m_4-2m_2^2.}
\] For a symmetric sign variable, \(m_2=m_4=1\), giving \(\kappa_4=-1\). A negative fourth free cumulant is entirely possible.

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Mixed free cumulants vanish
text:
Mixed free cumulants vanish
The crucial result is the mixed-cumulant characterization of freeness: unital subalgebras are free exactly when every mixed free cumulant vanishes. Here mixed means that its arguments come from more than one of the subalgebras. Speicher, Section 3.
This theorem connects the combinatorial definition to the alternating-centered definition. We use it here without reproducing its full induction proof.
For centered free \(a,b\), apply the moment formula to \(abab\). Singleton blocks vanish by centering. Blocks containing both letters vanish by the theorem. Pairing equal letters would cross. Every contribution is therefore zero.
Now expand a cumulant of \(a+b\) by multilinearity. Every mixed choice of arguments vanishes, leaving only the all-\(a\) and all-\(b\) terms: \[
\boxed{\kappa_n(a+b)=\kappa_n(a)+\kappa_n(b).}
\] The full moment sequence does not add. The cumulant sequence does.
For the sum of two free symmetric sign variables, the second cumulant is two and the fourth is minus two. Hence \[
m_4=-2+2(2)^2=6,
\] recovering Part I without listing sixteen words.

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Semicircle moments count noncrossing pairings
text:
Semicircle moments count noncrossing pairings
Suppose \(s\) has cumulants \[
\kappa_1(s)=0,\quad \kappa_2(s)=v,\quad
\kappa_n(s)=0\quad(n\geq3).
\] Only partitions into pairs survive. Odd moments vanish, and \[
\tau(s^{2k})=C_kv^k,
\qquad C_k=\frac1{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}.
\] Why Catalan numbers? Pair the first position with position \(2j+2\). Noncrossing forces the \(2j\) positions inside that pair and the remaining positions outside it to pair separately. If \(C_0=1\), this gives \[
C_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}C_jC_{k-1-j}.
\] Thus the even moments begin \(1,v,2v^2,5v^3,14v^4\) when the initial one is the zeroth moment.
For \(v>0\), these are the moments of the semicircle density \[
\rho_v(x)=\frac{\sqrt{4v-x^2}}{2\pi v}
\,\mathbf1_{\{|x|\leq2\sqrt v\}}.
\] The substitution \(x=2\sqrt v\cos\theta\) verifies the moments by a beta integral. In particular, its variance is \(v\), and its fourth moment is \(2v^2\). When \(v=0\), the law is \(\delta_0\).

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Why a free central limit theorem follows
text:
Why a free central limit theorem follows
Let \(a_1,a_2,\ldots\) be freely independent, identically distributed, bounded self-adjoint variables, centered with variance \(v\). Set \[
s_N=\frac{a_1+\cdots+a_N}{\sqrt N}.
\] Multilinearity gives \(\kappa_k(ca)=c^k\kappa_k(a)\). Additivity then yields \[
\kappa_k(s_N)=N^{1-k/2}\kappa_k(a_1).
\] The first cumulant is zero, the second remains \(v\), and every fixed higher cumulant tends to zero. Since each fixed moment is a finite polynomial in cumulants, the moments converge to those of the semicircle law.
This also gives weak convergence of the laws. The common second moment ensures tightness. Convergence of higher even moments controls the tails needed to pass moments to any weak subsequential limit. The compactly supported semicircle law is moment-determinate, so every such limit is the same.
The normal and semicircle laws play parallel roles: classical independent sums retain all pairings in their limiting moments, while free sums retain the noncrossing pairings.

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Find the fourth cumulant of the variance-one semicircle law.
Find the sixth moment of a centered semicircular variable with variance two.
If \(b\) is another free copy of a centered variance-one \(a\), express \(\tau((a+b)^4)\) in terms of \(m_4(a)\).



Answer sketches


\(2-2(1)^2=0\).
\(C_3\,2^3=5\cdot8=40\).
It is \(2m_4(a)+4\). Equivalently, add the fourth cumulants and use the new variance two.

title: Why crossings disappear
section: Further reading
text:
Further reading
Speicher’s survey on noncrossing partitions explains the combinatorial foundations. Nica and Speicher’s book, Lectures 8 through 12, develops the free central limit theorem and cumulant machinery in detail.

title: Rotate the eigenvectors
section: Three ways to use exactly the same eigenvalues
text:
Three ways to use exactly the same eigenvalues
For even \(n\), set \[
D_n=\operatorname{diag}(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{n/2},
\underbrace{-1,\ldots,-1}_{n/2}).
\] Compare these choices:








Second matrix
Relative eigenbasis
Prediction for the sum




\(D_n\)
Perfectly aligned
Half the eigenvalues at each of \(-2,2\)


\(P_nD_nP_n^*\)
A uniform random permutation
Limiting masses \(1/4,1/2,1/4\) at \(-2,0,2\)


\(U_nD_nU_n^*\)
A Haar-random unitary rotation
Limiting arcsine density on \([-2,2]\)



A permutation randomizes which signs match, but both matrices remain diagonal. Its empirical matching frequencies approach the product of the two sign distributions. A Haar unitary also mixes the coordinate directions themselves.



Identical marginal spectra produce a two-point sum, a three-point sum, or an approximately arcsine sum, depending on the relative eigenbasis.


The Haar panel pools six independent draws at \(n=384\). The other two panels each show one matrix pair at that dimension. The vertical axes distinguish discrete probability mass from continuous density. The density’s endpoint singularity also makes the outer histogram bars sensitive to bin width.

title: Rotate the eigenvectors
section: Sampling a Haar unitary correctly
text:
Sampling a Haar unitary correctly
Start with a complex Gaussian matrix \(Z\) and compute a QR decomposition. Correct the phases on the diagonal of \(R\) so that the resulting triangular factor has positive real diagonal. The corresponding unitary factor has Haar distribution. This is the QR construction described by Mezzadri.
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1729)

def haar_unitary(n):
    z = (rng.normal(size=(n, n))
         + 1j * rng.normal(size=(n, n))) / np.sqrt(2)
    q, r = np.linalg.qr(z)
    d = np.diag(r)
    return q * (d / np.abs(d))[None, :]

n = 384
signs = np.r_[np.ones(n // 2), -np.ones(n // 2)]
a = np.diag(signs)
u = haar_unitary(n)
b = (u * signs) @ u.conj().T
spectrum = np.linalg.eigvalsh(a + b)
The zero-diagonal event has probability zero for an exact Gaussian draw. Column multiplication by signs implements \(UD_n\), and the conjugate transpose is essential for complex matrices.
The phase correction makes this a general Haar sampler. In this particular conjugation experiment, those column phases cancel against the diagonal \(D_n\), but that cancellation would not justify calling an arbitrary uncorrected QR output Haar.

title: Rotate the eigenvectors
section: Test a mixed moment, not just a histogram
text:
Test a mixed moment, not just a histogram
The one-variable spectrum of \(A+B\) checks one consequence of freeness. We can also check a word that appears directly in the definition: \[
T_n=\frac1n\operatorname{Tr}(ABAB).
\] Both \(A=D_n\) and \(B=U_nD_nU_n^*\) are exactly centered. Freeness predicts \(T_n\to0\).
For the aligned and permuted cases, \(A\) and \(B\) commute and square to the identity, so \(ABAB=I\) and \(T_n=1\) exactly. This is a particularly clear distinction.
For ten independent Haar draws at each size, the recorded results are:

The observed root mean square alternating moment becomes smaller across the three tested matrix dimensions.


These observations agree with the theorem. Three dimensions and ten draws do not establish a convergence rate, and the displayed trend need not be monotone for a different random seed.

title: Rotate the eigenvectors
section: Large matrices and finite-size errors
text:
Large matrices and finite-size errors
For deterministic bounded Hermitian sequences with convergent marginal laws, the Haar-rotation theorem controls joint normalized-trace moments for each fixed noncommutative polynomial. The uniformly bounded spectra in this example then let us turn moment convergence for the sum into weak convergence of its empirical spectral measure. Speicher, Section 7.
This does not say that a finite pair is exactly free. It also does not, by itself, provide a finite-size error bound, eigenvalue-spacing statistics, or convergence of the largest eigenvalue.
A simple example explains the last distinction. The matrices \(\operatorname{diag}(10,0,\ldots,0)\) have all fixed positive normalized-trace moments tending to zero, but their largest eigenvalue remains ten. A vanishing fraction of outliers can disappear from a limiting spectral measure. Stronger random-matrix results address such questions, but they require stronger conclusions than ordinary moment convergence.

title: Rotate the eigenvectors
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

Replace the Haar unitary by the identity. What happens to \(T_n\)?
Why would subtracting only the ensemble mean be insufficient for a general finite-sample centered-moment diagnostic?
Would a good histogram of \(A+B\) prove that \(A\) and \(B\) are asymptotically free?



Answer sketches


\(A=B=D_n\), so \(ABAB=I\) and \(T_n=1\).
A particular matrix may still have nonzero normalized trace. If the diagnostic requires centered factors, use \(A-\tau_n(A)I\) and similarly for \(B\), or account for those fluctuations. Our balanced signs are exactly centered already.
No. Freeness constrains all alternating products of centered polynomials. One spectral histogram tests only a small part of that joint structure.

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: Aspect ratio and the Marchenko-Pastur law
text:
Aspect ratio and the Marchenko-Pastur law
Take independent standard complex Gaussian entries, with \(\mathbb E X_{ij}=0\) and \(\mathbb E|X_{ij}|^2=1\). Let \(n,m\to\infty\) with \[
\frac nm\longrightarrow\gamma\in(0,\infty).
\] We normalize the spectral measure by \(1/n\), over all \(n\) eigenvalues of \(C\). Its limiting mean is one.
The Marchenko-Pastur theorem identifies the limit. One moment formulation for this Gaussian model is \[
m_k=\sum_{\pi\in NC(k)}\gamma^{k-|\pi|}.
\] This result comes from Gaussian moment expansion and counting the index sums that survive at leading order. We use that random-matrix theorem as input, rather than proving it from the transform identities. Nica and Speicher, Lecture 22 develop Gaussian moment methods and their connection to Wishart matrices.
Comparing with the free moment-cumulant formula gives \[
\kappa_k=\gamma^{k-1},\qquad
R(w)=\frac1{1-\gamma w}.
\] In particular, \(m_1=1\), \(m_2=1+\gamma\), and the limiting spectral variance is \(\gamma\).
Different references use different parameters for the free Poisson or Marchenko-Pastur law. In the free-Poisson convention with rate \(\lambda\) and jump size \(c\), cumulants are \(\lambda c^k\). Our convention has \(\lambda=1/\gamma\) and \(c=\gamma\).

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: The density and the atom at zero
text:
The density and the atom at zero
Insert the R-transform into the Cauchy-transform equation: \[
z=\frac1G+\frac1{1-\gamma G}.
\] After rearranging, \[
\gamma zG^2-(z+\gamma-1)G+1=0.
\] Let \[
a=(1-\sqrt\gamma)^2,\qquad b=(1+\sqrt\gamma)^2.
\] The branch satisfying \(G(z)\sim1/z\) is \[
G(z)=\frac{z+\gamma-1-\sqrt{(z-a)(z-b)}}{2\gamma z},
\] where the square root is asymptotic to \(z\) at infinity. Stieltjes inversion gives the law \[
\boxed{
\mu_\gamma=
\left(1-\frac1\gamma\right)_+\delta_0
+\frac{\sqrt{(b-x)(x-a)}}{2\pi\gamma x}
\mathbf1_{(a,b)}(x)\,dx.
}
\] Here \((r)_+=\max(r,0)\). The continuous density has mass \(\min(1,1/\gamma)\), with the rest at zero.
The atom is also visible before taking a limit. When \(n>m\), a Gaussian \(n\times m\) matrix has rank \(m\) almost surely. Thus \(C\) has exactly \(n-m\) zero eigenvalues, a fraction approaching \(1-1/\gamma\). Keeping only the nonzero eigenvalues and renormalizing them would produce a different probability measure.



Sample covariance spectra for aspect ratios one half, one, and two, with the predicted continuous densities. The final panel has an additional zero atom of mass one half.


Each panel uses one matrix with \(n=320\). In the final panel, the zero eigenvalues are omitted from the density bars, but their probability mass is retained in the normalization and annotated separately.

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: Find the S-transform without another integral
text:
Find the S-transform without another integral
Let \(w=\psi(t)\) and \(M(t)=1+w\). The moment-cumulant equation from Part III gives \[
w=t(1+w)R(t(1+w))
=\frac{t(1+w)}{1-\gamma t(1+w)}.
\] Solve for \(t\): \[
\chi(w)=\frac{w}{(1+w)(1+\gamma w)}.
\] Consequently, \[
\boxed{S_{\mu_\gamma}(w)=\frac1{1+\gamma w}.}
\] For two free covariance laws with aspect ratios \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\), multiplication gives \[
S(w)=\frac1{(1+\gamma_1w)(1+\gamma_2w)}.
\] The first derivative at zero confirms that the mean-one product has variance \(\gamma_1+\gamma_2\).

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: Multiplying square covariance matrices
text:
Multiplying square covariance matrices
Set \(\gamma_1=\gamma_2=1\). Consider independent square Gaussian covariance matrices \(A_n,B_n\), each normalized by \(1/n\), and the positive product \[
P_n=A_n^{1/2}B_nA_n^{1/2}.
\] These independent Gaussian covariance ensembles are unitarily invariant and asymptotically free. Their norm control and marginal convergence justify using the positive product law. The limiting S-transform is \[
S(w)=\frac1{(1+w)^2}.
\] With \(t=\chi(w)\), this gives the exceptionally simple equation \[
\boxed{w=t(1+w)^3.}
\] Because \(w=\sum_{k\geq1}m_kt^k\), its coefficients are the desired moments. The first terms follow by substitution: \[
w=t+3t^2+12t^3+55t^4+\cdots.
\] For all orders, the Lagrange inversion identity for \(w=t\phi(w)\) states \[
[t^k]w=\frac1k[u^{k-1}]\phi(u)^k.
\] Using \(\phi(u)=(1+u)^3\) yields \[
m_k=\frac1k\binom{3k}{k-1}
=\boxed{\frac1{2k+1}\binom{3k}{k}}.
\] These are the order-two Fuss-Catalan numbers. The terminology is useful, but the equation \(w=t(1+w)^3\) already gives a direct way to compute them.
The same equation locates the positive right edge. With \(t=1/z\), \[
z=\frac{(1+w)^3}{w}.
\] Starting at large positive \(z\), the physical solution has small positive \(w\). Its first positive turning point satisfies \[
\frac{d}{dw}\frac{(1+w)^3}{w}
=\frac{(1+w)^2(2w-1)}{w^2}=0.
\] Thus \(w=1/2\) and the right endpoint is \(z=27/4\). The resulting law has support \([0,27/4]\). A detailed analysis of this branch and its density appears in Młotkowski, Nowak, Penson, and Życzkowski, Section IV.2.1.

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: Assumptions to check on a new problem
text:
Assumptions to check on a new problem
The calculations depend on more than knowing the marginal eigenvalue histograms. First specify the normalized matrix and the aspect ratio. Then justify the joint asymptotic-freeness statement. For a product, choose the positive representative and check that the mean permits the ordinary S-transform. Finally, retain the correct Cauchy-transform branch and any atoms when recovering the law.
These checks prevent several tempting mistakes: multiplying eigenvalues coordinate by coordinate, discarding zero eigenvalues, or choosing a convenient root of an algebraic equation without checking its asymptotics.
The series began with the observation that individual eigenvalues leave out relative geometry. Freeness supplies one precise limiting description of that geometry. Cumulants, the R-transform, and the S-transform then turn it into calculations we can test.

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: Exercises
text:
Exercises

What are the limiting mean, variance, and zero mass for \(\gamma=2\)?
Compute the second moment of a free product with \(\gamma_1=1/2\) and \(\gamma_2=2\).
What moment equation would a product of \(r\) free square covariance variables satisfy?



Answer sketches


Mean one, variance two, zero mass one half. The mean is averaged over all eigenvalues, including the zeros.
The variance is \(1/2+2=5/2\), so the second moment is \(1+5/2=7/2\).
Its S-transform is \((1+w)^{-r}\), so \(w=t(1+w)^{r+1}\). Lagrange inversion gives \(m_k=\binom{(r+1)k}{k}/(rk+1)\).

title: Covariance matrices and their products
section: Further reading
text:
Further reading
Mingo and Speicher, Free Probability and Random Matrices develops the random-matrix foundations. Penson and Życzkowski study the Fuss-Catalan laws arising from squared singular values of products. Młotkowski and collaborators explain the S-transform calculations and explicit densities. Their normalization conventions should be checked against the mean-one convention used here.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: One effective matrix, two parameter blocks
text:
One effective matrix, two parameter blocks
Write a layer as
\[
y=A z,\qquad A=gW,
\]
where \(z\) is fixed for this local calculation and \(g\) is a scalar multiplier. If \(W\) is constrained to Frobenius radius \(R\), then
\[
\lVert A\rVert_F=|g|R.
\]
Fixing \(W\)’s radius has not fixed the forward amplitude when \(g\) remains learnable. For any nonzero target matrix \(A\), choose \(g=\lVert A\rVert_F/R\) and \(W=A/g\). Every such target still has a representative.
This is a single-matrix representation argument. It does not establish that a shared gain can absorb independently chosen scales for many matrices.
With row and column multipliers, the effective map is
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(r)W\operatorname{diag}(c).
\]
These scales can change the distribution of amplification across output and input channels. They are not just another name for one global radius.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Follow the differential through the multiplier
text:
Follow the differential through the multiplier
Let \(G=\partial L/\partial A\) in the usual matrix pairing. For the scalar form \(A=gW\), the chain rule gives
\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=gG,
\qquad
\frac{\partial L}{\partial g}=\langle G,W\rangle_F.
\]
The effective differential is
\[
\delta A=g\,\delta W+W\,\delta g.
\]
Controlling the matrix update alone therefore does not control the whole forward perturbation if the multiplier or its update can grow without bound.
For a normalization gain vector, the corresponding formula is
\[
A=W\operatorname{diag}(\gamma),
\qquad
\delta A=\delta W\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)
+W\operatorname{diag}(\delta\gamma).
\]
In operator norm this implies
\[
\lVert\delta A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
\leq\lVert\gamma\rVert_\infty\lVert\delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
+\lVert W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lVert\delta\gamma\rVert_\infty.
\]
A modular ruler for the effective map needs to account for both contributions. Bounds on matrix motion and bounds on represented-function motion become different when a gain moves too.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Equivalent representations can still learn differently
text:
Equivalent representations can still learn differently
If both factors are free, the transformation \(W\mapsto cW\), \(g\mapsto g/c\) preserves \(A\) for \(c>0\). It can also change ordinary coordinate-based training.
For scalar weights, take \(L(w,g)=(wg)^2/2\). The pairs \((1,1)\) and \((2,1/2)\) represent the same product, one. Use raw SGD with learning rate \(0.1\) for both coordinates.
At \((1,1)\), both gradients equal one. The next pair is \((0.9,0.9)\), with effective product \(0.81\).
At \((2,1/2)\), the gradients are \(1/2\) and two. The next pair is \((1.95,0.3)\), with product \(0.585\).
Both runs began with the same represented function. Their coordinate scales changed the effective update. To first order, separate learning rates give
\[
\delta A=-\eta_W g^2G-\eta_g\langle G,W\rangle_FW.
\]
The finite scalar calculation also includes the product of the two parameter increments. The example is another instance of Part 1’s distinction between a function and the optimizer coordinates used to move it.



Along a function-preserving scalar rescaling, the matrix factor increases and the gain decreases while their product remains fixed. The two equivalent starting pairs in the worked example nevertheless produce different effective products after one coordinate SGD step.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: A shared gain cannot make every branch independent
text:
A shared gain cannot make every branch independent
Suppose two branches use
\[
A_1=W_1\operatorname{diag}(\gamma),
\qquad A_2=W_2\operatorname{diag}(\gamma).
\]
A common rescaling of both matrices can be absorbed by the gain. Rescaling just one matrix and changing the shared gain to compensate also changes the other branch.
Independent branch multipliers \(s_1\) and \(s_2\) can restore a relative-amplitude freedom that a single shared scalar does not provide. Whether those amplitudes matter depends on where the branches meet. Addition makes relative branch strength visible. A product introduces a different compensation symmetry.
For example, scalar query and key multipliers appear in attention scores through their product. Changing one up and the other down can preserve those scores. Scaling both in the same direction generally changes the score scale before softmax. A value multiplier can also interact with the output projection instead of controlling an independent final amplitude.
The architecture determines the redundant directions. A list of tensor norms does not determine them by itself.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Learnable scales do not remove the need for scale management
text:
Learnable scales do not remove the need for scale management
Learnable Multipliers studies scalar and row/column forward multipliers while leaving the underlying matrices subject to decay. Its Section 4.1 discusses redundant parameter symmetries and the numerical drift they can permit. The authors use light decay on multipliers to control that drift in their experiments.
The general distinction matters more than copying a decay coefficient. A scale can be useful for the forward function, redundant in a joint parameterization, or involved in both a useful relative scale and an unstable coordinate direction.
Positive log-parameterizations can make multiplicative changes easy to express, but they change the optimizer coordinates and exclude negative gains unless signs are handled separately. Removing a redundant factor can improve identifiability, but removing an independent branch multiplier may remove a useful degree of freedom.
These are different interventions. They should be compared through the effective map, not only through whether the parameter norms look tidy.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: A joint effective ruler has a kernel
text:
A joint effective ruler has a kernel
There is a natural temptation to measure the tuple \((\delta W,\delta\gamma)\) by the size of \(\delta A\). That does measure the represented linear-map change. But it is generally a seminorm on the redundant parameters.
For example, the infinitesimal transformation
\[
\delta W=tW,\qquad\delta\gamma=-t\gamma
\]
has nonzero parameter motion and zero effective differential. A genuine norm cannot vanish on that nonzero direction.
One can remove the redundancy by a coordinate convention, or work with equivalence classes of parameters that represent the same function. Calling a pulled-back measurement a norm without addressing its kernel skips a mathematical step.
The practical question is whether such a joint construction makes an affordable optimizer with a useful consequence. The existence of a symmetry alone does not establish that result.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Which quantities should remain available?
text:
Which quantities should remain available?
Before fixing a forward scale, identify the function it controls, every consumer that shares it, and the transformations that can compensate it. Then ask whether the complete collection of constraints still admits the intended functions.
This gives us a more precise goal than either freeing every multiplier or fixing every tensor norm. Control redundant coordinate drift while preserving useful relative scales. The next post turns that goal into an exact compatibility calculation for several matrices sharing one gain.

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Try tracking the effective map
text:
Try tracking the effective map

A target matrix has Frobenius norm three and the underlying matrix radius is two. Give a scalar gain and matrix representative.
In the scalar SGD example, verify the effective products \(0.81\) and \(0.585\) after one step.
Show directly that the infinitesimal common rescaling of \(W\) and \(\gamma\) has zero \(\delta A\).



Answer sketches


Choose \(g=3/2\) and \(W=2A/3\). Then \(gW=A\) and \(\lVert W\rVert_F=2\).
The gradients of \((wg)^2/2\) are \(g(wg)\) and \(w(wg)\). Substitute each starting pair, apply the two coordinate updates, and multiply the new factors.
Substitute into the differential: \(tW\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)-tW\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)=0\).

title: Which scales should stay learnable?
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Maksim Velikanov and collaborators, Learnable Multipliers: Freeing the Scale of Language Model Matrix Layers, Sections 2 and 4.1 and Appendix C, studies multiplier placement, redundant symmetries, and their practical management.
Twan van Laarhoven, L2 Regularization versus Batch and Weight Normalization, and Li and Arora’s trajectory analysis, give the earlier scale-to-dynamics context. The parameter-pair examples and effective differential here follow directly from the displayed maps.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: First reproduce the claim in a setting it actually covers
text:
First reproduce the claim in a setting it actually covers
Use fixed isotropic features and two target maps whose Frobenius norms are one and \(b>0\). Impose individual radii \(R_1=R_2=1\) and a shared scalar gain. Part 11 gives
\[
g_*=(1+b)/2,\qquad
\mathcal L_*=(b-1)^2/4.
\]
This is a prediction over a whole family of target imbalances, rather than a single failed training curve.
For a small reproducible check, I used four-dimensional features taking the eight values \(z=\pm2e_j\) with equal weight. Their second moment is exactly \(I\). A fixed matrix \(A_1\) has Frobenius norm one, and \(A_2=bA_1\). The code evaluates the actual branch-output squared loss at the constrained optimum.
Across 45 ratios from \(0.25\) to three, this evaluated loss matches the formula within \(10^{-12}\). A joint group radius and independent branch multipliers both give zero fitting loss to numerical precision in the same calculation.



The minimum branch-fitting loss rises quadratically as the target norm ratio moves away from one under individual radii and a shared scalar gain. A joint radius and independent branch multipliers preserve the prescribed target maps and give zero loss in the same frozen-feature experiment.


These are direct finite-design evaluations, not neural-network training results. They check the algebra and the proposed intervention’s feasible set. Optimizer convergence is a separate experiment.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: Attention can preserve products while changing branches
text:
Attention can preserve products while changing branches
For a bias-free attention head, using column-vector inputs, write
\[
q=W_Qx,\quad k=W_Kx',\quad v=W_Vx.
\]
Without positional rotations, the score depends on \(W_Q^\top W_K\). The value-output composition depends on \(W_OW_V\). For invertible matrices \(S\) and \(T\) of the appropriate head dimensions, the transformations
\[
W_Q\mapsto SW_Q,\qquad W_K\mapsto S^{-\top}W_K
\]
and
\[
W_V\mapsto TW_V,\qquad W_O\mapsto W_OT^{-1}
\]
preserve those products. The individual branch maps and their Frobenius norms may change.
Thus failure to preserve each \(W_i\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)\) is not enough to establish failure to preserve the attention function. Even equality of score matrices is sufficient rather than necessary for equality of softmax weights, since rowwise additive constants cancel.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: An explicit escape from the branch obstruction
text:
An explicit escape from the branch obstruction
Consider a scalar head with no positional rotations. The unconstrained teacher uses the shared gain \(g=1\) and
\[
W_Q=1,\quad W_K=2,\quad W_V=1,\quad W_O=1.
\]
Its query, key, and value maps are respectively \(x\), \(2x\), and \(x\). Part 11’s shared-gain reasoning rules out preserving all three maps while setting \(|W_Q|=|W_K|=|W_V|=1\).
Now require those three unit radii but leave \(W_O\) unconstrained. Choose
\[
g'=\sqrt2,\quad W_Q'=W_K'=W_V'=1,
\quad W_O'=1/\sqrt2.
\]
The new query and key maps are both \(\sqrt2x\). Their product is still \(2xx'\), so the softmax attention weights are unchanged for every input sequence. The values scale by \(\sqrt2\), which the output projection cancels. The final attention output is identical.
The code verifies this directly on a small token sequence. More importantly, the displayed product identities prove it for arbitrary scalar token inputs in this specified architecture.
This is a negative control with teeth. The branch-map obstruction is real, yet it does not imply an output-function obstruction under these constraints. Fixing the output projection too would be a different question and would require another analysis.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: Positional operations restrict the available transformations
text:
Positional operations restrict the available transformations
With rotary position matrices \(R_p\), a query-key score contains
\[
x^\top W_Q^\top R_p^\top R_q W_Kx'.
\]
After the general factor transformation above, the middle expression becomes
\[
W_Q^\top S^\top R_p^\top R_q S^{-\top}W_K.
\]
An arbitrary \(S\) no longer cancels. Scalar rebalancing \(S=cI\) still does. Other surviving transformations depend on the positional operators and the rest of the architecture.
Query/key normalization, shared heads, biases, masks, and nonlinear gates can alter the analysis again. The correct equivalence class belongs to the actual computation graph, not to a convenient isolated matrix identity.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: Measure the mechanism before running a leaderboard
text:
Measure the mechanism before running a leaderboard
A useful progression has several stages.

Frozen branch teachers. Vary target imbalance and gain bounds. Compare measured fitting losses with the exact floor and channelwise feasibility criterion.
Frozen attention teachers. Supervise score and final-output behavior. Optimize over the remaining factorization freedoms before declaring a capacity restriction. Include the scalar escape above as a control the analysis must get right.
Learned features. Let upstream representations adapt. Determine whether they remove the predicted restriction or merely hide it behind extreme gain conditioning.
Completed training comparisons. Only after a mechanism survives the earlier tests, compare tuned decay, fixed norms, grouped constraints, and existing multiplier baselines at matched data and tuning budgets.

The observable should follow the claim. A branch reconstruction error measures a different target from final task loss. Parameter norms, angular displacement, effective map changes, and gain trajectories diagnose different parts of the mechanism.
When intervening at a checkpoint, preserve the represented function and transport optimizer state according to the convention being tested. Resetting moments changes the intervention. If an exact state transport is unavailable, measure and report that limitation.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: What would strengthen or weaken the direction?
text:
What would strengthen or weaken the direction?
The explanation strengthens if compatibility or bounded-gain conditioning predicts a failure on new targets, survives the correct attention symmetries, and predicts a repair that transfers to learned-feature tasks. An effect that survives angular-schedule controls is more informative than an early curve at one nominal learning rate.
It weakens if alternative factorizations remove the restriction, upstream features absorb it, or existing multipliers and scheduling explain all practically relevant differences. Those outcomes should change the research direction rather than be relabeled as optimizer improvements.
The mathematical burden also includes prior work. A positive-feasibility criterion is an elementary matrix-scaling calculation. A publishable novelty claim needs a broader comparison with existing scaling, invariant optimization, and normalization results, not just an unfamiliar notation.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: Return to the question about scale
text:
Return to the question about scale
The series began with identical predictors taking different gradient steps. That forced us to distinguish functions from coordinates. Weight decay, momentum, layer norms, support directions, and manifold constraints each exposed another part of that distinction.
The final question is sharper than fixing all norms or freeing all gains: which redundant scales can be controlled while preserving useful module behavior, and what measurable consequence follows?
We have exact toy calculations and controls that can reject an overly broad interpretation. We do not yet have evidence of a new optimizer advantage on a trainable Transformer. That is the research program to carry into the next stage of the series.

title: From a counterexample to a research claim
section: Try to break the explanation
text:
Try to break the explanation

At \(b=2\), what fitting loss does the independent-radius frozen-branch model predict? What do the two scale-restoring controls achieve?
Verify the query-key and value-output products in the scalar attention escape.
Why would evaluating feasibility only at a checkpoint that already satisfies the constraints be a weak test?



Answer sketches


The floor is \(1/4\). A joint radius and independent branch multipliers can each achieve zero under the stated frozen-feature setup.
The original query-key product is \(1\times2=2\), and the new one is \(\sqrt2\times\sqrt2=2\). The value-output product is one in both cases.
Its own branch maps are feasible by construction. Use prescribed teachers, unconstrained target maps, or alternative representatives that test a prediction beyond that tautology.

section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…

Hyperball May Not Be a Free Lunch, Section 4, motivates schedule controls, and Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them, Sections 3 and 4, motivates completed-budget and tuning comparisons. The frozen-teacher evaluations and scalar attention escape here are self-contained synthetic controls. No literature training claim is reproduced.

title: Why average before choosing an update?
section: Put the averaging operation in the update rule
text:
Put the averaging operation in the update rule
For a norm \(N\), choose a positive support direction
\[
D(s)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{N(D)\leq1}\langle s,D\rangle.
\]
Use \(D(0)=0\) as a zero-slope convention. A descent proposal of radius \(\rho\) is \(-\rho D(s)\). For the Euclidean norm, \(D(s)=s/\lVert s\rVert_2\) when \(s\ne0\). For a spectral matrix budget, one choice is the compact polar factor.
One way to incorporate stochastic gradients is
\[
m_t=(1-\alpha)m_{t-1}+\alpha g_t,
\qquad \Delta w_t=-\eta\rho D(m_t),
\]
where \(0<\alpha\leq1\) is the weight given to the fresh gradient. The more usual old-buffer coefficient is \(\beta=1-\alpha\).
Another rule first applies the oracle:
\[
p_t=(1-\alpha)p_{t-1}+\alpha D(g_t),
\qquad \Delta w_t=-\eta\rho p_t.
\]
Both rules can obey the same norm budget. If \(N(p_0)\leq1\), convexity gives \(N(p_t)\leq1\). But they combine different information, so their directions can differ even under identical samples and coefficients.
The placement of averaging is part of the optimizer, just as the choice of norm is.

title: Why average before choosing an update?
section: An unbiased gradient can become an uphill normalized update
text:
An unbiased gradient can become an uphill normalized update
At one evaluation point, suppose the scalar sampled gradient is
\[
g=\begin{cases}
4,&\text{with probability }1/4,\\
-1,&\text{with probability }3/4.
\end{cases}
\]
Its expectation is \(\mathbb E[g]=1/4\). The unit-ball support direction in one dimension is the sign. Therefore
\[
\mathbb E[-D(g)]
=-\frac14+\frac34=\frac12.
\]
The expected normalized proposal points in the positive direction, while descent for the mean derivative points in the negative direction. Its expected first-order loss change is \(\eta\rho/8>0\).
This distribution can occur at \(w=1/4\) for \(L(w)=w^2/2\), using sample gradients \(g=w+\epsilon\) with \(\epsilon=15/4\) or \(-5/4\) at the stated probabilities. The noise has mean zero. With \(\rho=1\), the exact expected one-step loss increase is
\[
\mathbb E[L(w-\eta D(g))-L(w)]
=\frac\eta8+\frac{\eta^2}{2}.
\]
The rare large gradient mattered to the mean. Normalizing each sample first erased the magnitude that let it offset the common smaller gradients.

title: Why average before choosing an update?
section: Average samples while that magnitude is still available
text:
Average samples while that magnitude is still available
Freeze this evaluation point and average \(B\) independent copies before applying the sign. If \(K\) samples equal four, then
\[
K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(B,1/4),
\qquad \bar g_B=\frac{5K-B}{B}.
\]
With the zero convention at a tie,
\[
\mathbb E[-D(\bar g_B)]
=\Pr(5K<B)-\Pr(5K>B).
\]
We can evaluate these probabilities exactly by summing binomial probabilities. The following table uses those sums, with no sampling error.



Gradients per average \(B\)
Expected unit descent proposal




1
+0.500000
