-0.933480






The two-point gradient distribution has a positive mean even though most samples are negative. Averaging independent gradients before taking their sign changes the expected descent proposal as batch size grows. Small-batch values need not improve monotonically because of the discrete distribution and ties.


As \(B\) grows, \(\bar g_B\) concentrates around \(1/4\), and the expected unit proposal approaches minus one. The small-batch values need not change monotonically. In particular, exact ties change which probability mass contributes zero.
This calculation concerns a frozen evaluation point. A moving optimizer also changes the gradient it is trying to estimate.

title: Why average before choosing an update?
section: What an exponential average does to stationary noise
text:
What an exponential average does to stationary noise
For a fixed mean \(\mu\) and independent scalar noise, write \(g_t=\mu+\epsilon_t\), with variance \(\sigma^2\). Start \(m_0=0\). Expanding the average gives
\[
m_t=\alpha\sum_{j=1}^t(1-\alpha)^{t-j}g_j.
\]
Independence lets us add variances:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(m_t)
=\frac{\alpha\sigma^2}{2-\alpha}
\left[1-(1-\alpha)^{2t}\right].
\]
The limiting variance is \(\alpha\sigma^2/(2-\alpha)\). With \(\alpha=0.1\), this equals the variance of an average of nineteen independent samples. With \(\alpha=0.01\), the corresponding variance-equivalent count is 199.
Those are variance comparisons under this stationary model. They are not literal buffer lengths or assurances that the estimator tracks a changing gradient equally well.
The startup mean is \(\mu[1-(1-\alpha)^t]\). Dividing by that positive scalar removes this mean bias. For an exact support oracle and a consistent choice among ties, a positive scalar correction does not change the selected direction. It still does not remove sampling uncertainty.

title: Why average before choosing an update?
section: Averaging also creates lag
text:
Averaging also creates lag
Let the mean instead follow the simple trend \(\mu_t=\nu t\). If the expected tracking error settles to a constant, its recurrence gives
\[
e=(1-\alpha)(e-\nu),
\qquad e=-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\nu.
\]
Reducing \(\alpha\) suppresses independent noise while increasing this trend lag. At \(\nu=0.01\), the limiting lag is \(-0.09\) for \(\alpha=0.1\) and \(-0.99\) for \(\alpha=0.01\).



For a scalar mean increasing by 0.01 per step with independent noise variance one, smaller fresh-sample weights reduce stationary noise variance but increase squared tracking lag. Their sum has an intermediate minimum in this specified trend model.


This is an exact calculation for the displayed trend model. It is not a model of every training trajectory or a rule for choosing a universal momentum coefficient.
For an actual moving parameter, write \(h_t=\nabla L(w_t)\), \(g_t=h_t+\epsilon_t\), and \(e_t=m_t-h_t\). Then
\[
e_t=(1-\alpha)
\left[e_{t-1}+h_{t-1}-h_t\right]+\alpha\epsilon_t.
\]
Assuming the fresh noise has zero conditional mean given the previous samples and optimizer state, its cross term vanishes in the conditional Euclidean squared-error calculation. The remaining terms contain both noise variance and the drift \(h_{t-1}-h_t\).
The statistical problem is therefore denoising while tracking. Small fresh-sample weights do not solve both parts automatically. The Euclidean variance calculation also needs an appropriate norm conversion before it controls error in a chosen matrix dual norm.

title: Why average before choosing an update?
section: How estimator error reaches the support direction
text:
How estimator error reaches the support direction
Let \(h\) be the current true gradient and \(m\) its estimate. Duality gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle h,D(m)\rangle
&\geq N^*(m)-N^*(h-m)\\
&\geq N^*(h)-2N^*(h-m).
\end{aligned}
\]
The first line uses the oracle’s optimal support for \(m\) and its unit primal norm. The second uses the reverse triangle inequality for \(N^*\).
Thus a sufficiently accurate estimate provides a direction aligned with the current derivative. A large tracking error can consume the entire guarantee. Actual finite loss decrease additionally needs step-size and curvature control.
Part 13 introduces another error. If an approximate direction \(\widehat D\) stays in the unit ball and loses at most \(\delta\) of the estimate’s support, then the same argument yields
\[
\langle h,\widehat D\rangle
\geq N^*(h)-2N^*(h-m)-\delta.
\]
Estimation and numerical approximation appear as separate terms. This bound requires feasibility of the approximate direction, which an arbitrary polynomial filter may fail to preserve.

title: Why average before choosing an update?
section: What remains to specify in a practical optimizer
text:
What remains to specify in a practical optimizer
The new-sample coefficient, buffer initialization, oracle convention, matrix normalization, and update radius all affect the rule. Nesterov variants change the matrix sent to the oracle again.
Training Deep Learning Models with Norm-Constrained LMOs makes gradient averaging before the oracle explicit. Its stochastic analysis also needs assumptions controlling noise, smoothness, and motion. The two operations cannot be exchanged merely because both resulting proposals remain bounded.
The next post uses that boundedness for a different purpose. Once each proposal has a norm bound, decoupled decay can control where the weights themselves are allowed to go.

title: Why average before choosing an update?
section: Try changing the order
text:
Try changing the order

Compute the variance of the two-point sampled gradient.
Average four samples before taking the sign. What is the expected unit descent proposal?
Under the fixed-mean independent-noise model, what variance-equivalent sample count corresponds to \(\alpha=0.2\)?
If \(N^*(h)=1\) and \(N^*(h-m)=0.2\), what lower bound follows for exact unit-ball support alignment? What if the numerical support defect is \(0.1\)?



Answer sketches


\(\mathbb E[g^2]=19/4\) and \((\mathbb E[g])^2=1/16\), giving \(\operatorname{Var}(g)=75/16\).
Only an all-negative block has a negative mean. The expectation is \(2(3/4)^4-1=-47/128\approx-0.367188\).
The count is \((2-\alpha)/\alpha=9\).
Exact alignment is at least \(1-2(0.2)=0.6\). With the stated feasible approximation it is at least \(0.5\).

title: From layer budgets to a residual block
section: First follow both routes through a composition
text:
First follow both routes through a composition
Write a two-module network as
\[
h=F(w_1,x),\qquad y=G(w_2,h).
\]
Hold \(x\) fixed and perturb both parameter groups. The differential is
\[
\delta y
=D_hG[D_{w_1}F[\delta w_1]]
+D_{w_2}G[\delta w_2].
\]
The first change travels through the downstream module. The second is created there directly. If the local parameter bounds are \(N_1,N_2\), and \(\|D_hG\|\leq s_2\) for \(s_2>0\), then
\[
\|\delta y\|\leq s_2N_1(\delta w_1)+N_2(\delta w_2).
\]
For positive shares \(p_1+p_2=1\), define
\[
N(\delta w)=\max\left\{
\frac{s_2N_1(\delta w_1)}{p_1},
\frac{N_2(\delta w_2)}{p_2}\right\}.
\]
Then \(\|\delta y\|\leq N(\delta w)\). This is the budget allocation from Part 7 with the downstream coefficient derived from the chain rule. For more modules, repeat the calculation up the tree. A parallel branch combined by a sum needs a sum bound. A concatenation needs its declared output norm. Architecture alone does not specify that geometry.
Even two scalar multiplications already produce curvature. With \(F(w_1,x)=w_1x\) and \(G(w_2,h)=w_2h\), take \(w_i(t)=w_i+t\Delta w_i\). Although each map is linear in its own weight,
\[
\frac{d^2y(t)}{dt^2}=2\Delta w_1\Delta w_2x.
\]
One weight change alters the feature multiplying the other. Dropping these mixed derivatives would incorrectly predict zero network curvature.

title: From layer budgets to a residual block
section: State the local promises along the whole path
text:
State the local promises along the whole path
Consider independent blocks \(f_l(w_l,h)\), all using the same activation norm \(\|\cdot\|\). Let \(N_l\) be a fixed norm for the parameters of block \(l\). Assume the maps are twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of the states we visit, with
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|D_hf_l[z]\|&\leq\|z\|,\\
\|D_wf_l[v]\|&\leq N_l(v),\\
\|D^2_{ww}f_l[v,v']\|&\leq A N_l(v)N_l(v'),\\
\|D^2_{wh}f_l[v,z]\|&\leq B N_l(v)\|z\|,\\
\|D^2_{hh}f_l[z,z']\|&\leq C\|z\|\|z'\|.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(A,B,C\geq0\) are common upper bounds. Every line must hold along the interpolation \(w_l(t)=w_l+t\Delta w_l\), for \(0\leq t\leq1\), at the resulting moving features. Checking these inequalities only at initialization would not justify the argument.
The three curvature bounds record weight-weight, weight-feature, and feature-feature interactions. Compatible activation spaces matter. So do restrictions such as a bounded incoming feature or a normalization denominator separated from zero.

title: From layer budgets to a residual block
section: A residual stack whose sensitivity stays controlled
text:
A residual stack whose sensitivity stays controlled
Use \(L\) blocks of the form
\[
h_l(t)=\left(1-\frac1L\right)h_{l-1}(t)
+\frac1L f_l(w_l(t),h_{l-1}(t)),
\qquad h_0(t)=x.
\]
The skip and branch coefficients sum to one. Under our input-derivative assumption, each complete block has sensitivity at most one.
Give the joint parameter change the norm
\[
N(\Delta w)=\max_{1\leq l\leq L}N_l(\Delta w_l),
\qquad N(\Delta w)\leq\varepsilon.
\]
For this averaged residual stack, equal allocation of the budget gives precisely this maximum norm: each branch contributes its local change divided by \(L\), and there are \(L\) branches.
Let \(s_l(t)=\|\dot h_l(t)\|\). Differentiating once yields
\[
\dot h_l=
\left[\left(1-\frac1L\right)I+\frac1L D_hf_l\right]\dot h_{l-1}
+\frac1L D_wf_l[\Delta w_l].
\]
Consequently,
\[
s_l\leq s_{l-1}+\frac\varepsilon L,
\qquad s_0=0,
\qquad s_l\leq\frac lL\varepsilon.
\]
In particular, \(\|\dot h_L\|\leq\varepsilon\). Integration gives the finite bound \(\|h_L(1)-h_L(0)\|\leq\varepsilon\) too. This does not yet describe the error of the linear prediction.

title: From layer budgets to a residual block
section: Keep the second derivative
text:
Keep the second derivative
Set \(q_l(t)=\|\ddot h_l(t)\|\). The full chain rule gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ddot h_l={}&
\left[\left(1-\frac1L\right)I+\frac1L D_hf_l\right]\ddot h_{l-1}\\
&+\frac1L\left(
D^2_{ww}f_l[\Delta w_l,\Delta w_l]
+2D^2_{wh}f_l[\Delta w_l,\dot h_{l-1}]
+D^2_{hh}f_l[\dot h_{l-1},\dot h_{l-1}]
\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The factor two is the mixed interaction seen in the scalar example. Applying the local bounds,
\[
q_l\leq q_{l-1}+\frac1L\left(
A\varepsilon^2+2B\varepsilon s_{l-1}+Cs_{l-1}^2\right).
\]
Insert \(s_{l-1}\leq(l-1)\varepsilon/L\) and sum. Since \(q_0=0\),
\[
q_L\leq H_L\varepsilon^2,
\quad
H_L=A+B\frac{L-1}{L}
+C\frac{(L-1)(2L-1)}{6L^2}.
\]
The coefficients come from \(\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}j\) and \(\sum_{j=0}^{L-1}j^2\). In particular,
\[
H_L\leq A+B+\frac C3.
\]
Taylor’s integral remainder now gives
\[
\left\|h_L(1)-h_L(0)-\dot h_L(0)\right\|
\leq\frac12H_L\varepsilon^2.
\]
This is a depth-independent upper bound under the stated assumptions. It is not an exact curvature value. Replacing the averaged residual block by \(h+f_l(w,h)\) changes the sensitivity calculation. Tying parameters across blocks changes the parameter space. Neither alteration inherits this proof automatically.

title: From layer budgets to a residual block
section: A scalar stack we can calculate exactly
text:
A scalar stack we can calculate exactly
Take \(f_l(w,h)=wh\), \(h_0=1\), and keep \(w,h\in[0,1]\). With absolute-value norms, \(A=C=0\) and \(B=1\). Choose every initial weight as \(1/2\) and every change as \(\varepsilon=0.2\). The path stays in the required region, and
\[
y(t)=\left(1-\frac{0.5}{L}+\frac{0.2t}{L}\right)^L,
\qquad
y'(0)=0.2\left(1-\frac{0.5}{L}\right)^{L-1}.
\]
Compute the actual remainder \(y(1)-y(0)-y'(0)\) and compare it with \(0.02(1-1/L)\). At depth two both equal \(0.01\). As depth grows, the actual remainder approaches
\[
e^{-0.3}-1.2e^{-0.5}\approx0.0129814,
\]
while the bound approaches \(0.02\).



The exact scalar residual remainder stays below its finite-depth bound as depth increases.


These are evaluations of a scalar polynomial, not training measurements. Increasing \(L\) also changes the branch multiplier. A comparison with an unscaled network must account for that change and its chosen joint norm.

title: From layer budgets to a residual block
section: From output motion to a loss bound
text:
From output motion to a loss bound
Suppose the scalar loss \(\ell(y)\) has output derivative norm at most \(b\) and Hessian bilinear norm at most \(c\) throughout the output path. Then
\[
\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\ell(h_L(t))
=D^2\ell[\dot h_L,\dot h_L]+D\ell[\ddot h_L],
\]
so its absolute value is at most \((c+bH_L)\varepsilon^2\). Thus, for \(\mathcal L(w)=\ell(h_L(w))\),
\[
\mathcal L(w+\Delta w)
\leq\mathcal L(w)+D\mathcal L[\Delta w]
+\frac12(c+bH_L)N(\Delta w)^2.
\]
A finite empirical average obeys the same bound if its examples share these constants. A population expectation additionally needs justification for exchanging differentiation and expectation.
For a unit support direction \(D(g)\) of the joint norm, a step \(\Delta w=-\varepsilon D(g)\) has linear term \(-\varepsilon N^*(g)\). The quadratic term tells us when that local prediction guarantees descent. Approximate or stochastic directions also carry the alignment errors from Part 14. A budget by itself does not establish descent.

title: From layer budgets to a residual block
section: Where the local promises come from
text:
Where the local promises come from
For a dense map \(Wh\), the mixed derivative is \(\Delta W\Delta h\). The RMS operator norm from Part 5 controls it. For a periodic convolution \(f(C,x)=K^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^K C_sS_sx\), using Euclidean feature norms and norm-preserving spatial shifts, the triangle inequality gives
\[
\|D_Cf[H]\|\leq\max_s\|H_s\|_{\rm op}\|x\|.
\]
Thus a maximum over channel-matrix slices is a natural parameter norm for that explicitly averaged convolution. Input sensitivity at most one additionally needs \(\max_s\|C_s\|_{\rm op}\leq1\). Stride, padding, and different normalization factors need their own estimates.
For attention, split the module into projections, the bilinear score map, softmax, and value aggregation. For scores \(QK^\top\), the differential is \(\Delta QK^\top+Q\Delta K^\top\), and the mixed second derivative contains \(\Delta Q\Delta K^\top\). Bounds therefore need limits on the relevant query and key norms, as well as the chosen sequence norms. A normalized projection introduces an additional denominator. Part 18 will calculate why this can be the fragile part.
The recursive bookkeeping works once those local promises hold. Establishing their region of validity is part of the network argument.

title: From layer budgets to a residual block
section: Try carrying the budget through
text:
Try carrying the budget through

In the two-module bound, take \(s_2=3\), \(p_1=p_2=1/2\), and \(N(\Delta w)\leq0.1\). What local budgets follow?
For \(A=0\), \(B=1\), \(C=0\), \(L=4\), and \(\varepsilon=0.2\), what is the output remainder bound?
Why would retaining only weight-weight curvature miss the scalar residual example?
If \(b=2\), \(c=3\), and \(H_L\leq1\), what quadratic coefficient appears in the loss remainder?



Answer sketches


\(N_1(\Delta w_1)\leq0.1/6\) and \(N_2(\Delta w_2)\leq0.05\). Their transported contributions sum to at most \(0.1\).
\(\tfrac12(3/4)(0.2)^2=0.015\).
Each scalar block has zero weight-weight curvature, but its mixed derivative equals one. Simultaneously moving weights creates a nonzero second-order product.
\(c+bH_L\leq5\), so the remainder is at most \(\tfrac52N(\Delta w)^2\).

title: From layer budgets to a residual block
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm, Sections 3.2 to 3.4, Proposition 4, and Appendices B, C, and E, develops composition, sharpness triples, and the averaged residual construction. Its Proposition 5 connects output error bounds to loss smoothness. The pathwise calculation above spells out the first and second directional derivatives for independent blocks. The scalar example and figure evaluate the displayed polynomial directly.
The result concerns this declared norm, residual multiplier, and region of differentiability. It does not show that an arbitrary trained attention network satisfies the local constants, or that a depth-independent upper bound makes its best learning rate depth independent.

title: Small matrix steps, large normalized rotations
section: Differentiate the normalized projection
text:
Differentiate the normalized projection
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{p\times d}\), \(h\ne0\), and
\[
z=Ah\ne0,\qquad r=\|z\|_2,\qquad u=\frac zr.
\]
Assume \(p\geq2\). Differentiating \(r\) gives \(dr=u^\top dz\). Therefore
\[
du=\frac{dz}{r}-\frac{z\,dr}{r^2}
=\frac{(I-uu^\top)dz}{r}.
\]
Normalization discards the radial component and divides the transverse component by the current output radius. For a frozen input and a weight change,
\[
D_Au[\Delta A]
=\frac{(I-uu^\top)\Delta Ah}{\|Ah\|_2}.
\]
Give the matrix a relative spectral budget
\[
\|\Delta A\|_{\rm op}\leq\eta\|A\|_{\rm op},
\qquad
\kappa(A,h)=\frac{\|A\|_{\rm op}\|h\|_2}{\|Ah\|_2}.
\]
The spectral inequality implies \(\kappa\geq1\) and
\[
\|D_Au[\Delta A]\|_2\leq\eta\kappa(A,h).
\]
This upper bound is attained. Choose a unit vector \(e\perp u\) and set
\[
\Delta A=\eta\|A\|_{\rm op}\,e\frac{h^\top}{\|h\|_2}.
\]
It has exactly the permitted spectral norm, and its action on \(h\) is entirely transverse. Thus
\[
\sup_{\|\Delta A\|_{\rm op}\leq\eta\|A\|_{\rm op}}
\|D_Au[\Delta A]\|_2=\eta\kappa(A,h).
\]
This is a differential statement over the ambient spectral ball. It is not yet a finite angle bound or an oracle restricted to a weight manifold. For \(p=1\), there is no transverse direction: the ideal normalized scalar is locally constant away from zero, so the displayed supremum equality requires \(p\geq2\).

title: Small matrix steps, large normalized rotations
section: Perfect nonzero singular values do not protect a projection
text:
Perfect nonzero singular values do not protect a projection
Consider
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
h=\begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon\\0\\\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2}\end{pmatrix},
\qquad0<\varepsilon\leq1.
\]
The rows of \(A\) are orthonormal. Its two nonzero singular values are both one, and \(\|h\|_2=1\). Nevertheless,
\[
Ah=(\varepsilon,0)^\top,
\qquad\kappa(A,h)=1/\varepsilon.
\]
Most of the feature lies in the projection’s kernel. Perfect row geometry does not give a positive lower bound on \(\|Ah\|\) for all unit inputs of a wide projection.
Nor does changing the global radius fix the relative margin. For any nonzero scalar \(a\),
\[
\kappa(aA,h)=\kappa(A,h).
\]
Positive rescaling also leaves the ideal normalized output unchanged. Part 15 showed how decay can bound a parameter radius. That bound alone does not improve this data-dependent ratio instantly. Decay can still affect future directions, optimizer history, and features.

title: Small matrix steps, large normalized rotations
section: Keep the packed matrix exactly orthogonal
text:
Keep the packed matrix exactly orthogonal
Now use a four-dimensional packed projection \(Q\), and call its first two output coordinates one head. Start from \(Q_0=I_4\) and take
\[
h=(\varepsilon,0,\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2},0)^\top.
\]
Rotate output coordinates two and three:
\[
Q_\alpha=
\begin{pmatrix}
1&0&0&0\\
0&\cos\alpha&\sin\alpha&0\\
0&-\sin\alpha&\cos\alpha&0\\
0&0&0&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
This matrix is exactly orthogonal. Its selected head sees
\[
(Q_\alpha h)_{1:2}
=(\varepsilon,\sin\alpha\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2})^\top.
\]
The normalized head starts along the first coordinate. Its new angle is exactly
\[
\theta_{\rm head}
=\arctan\left(|\sin\alpha|\sqrt{\kappa^2-1}\right),
\qquad\kappa=1/\varepsilon.
\]
The full matrix’s spectral displacement and Frobenius angle are
\[
\|Q_\alpha-I\|_{\rm op}=2|\sin(\alpha/2)|,
\qquad
\cos\theta_{\rm matrix}
=\frac{\langle I,Q_\alpha\rangle_F}{\|I\|_F\|Q_\alpha\|_F}
=\frac{2+2\cos\alpha}{4}.
\]
At \(\alpha=0.01\) radians, the spectral displacement is about \(0.01\) and the whole-matrix angle is about \(0.405\) degrees. A feature with \(\kappa=100\) has a head angle of about \(45.0\) degrees. With \(\kappa=1000\), the angle is about \(84.3\) degrees.



A fixed small orthogonal matrix rotation can produce a large selected-head angle when the projection margin is small.


This example is not an artifact of leaving the manifold. It is also compatible with a spectral support direction. The initial velocity \(J=\left.\frac{d}{d\alpha}Q_\alpha\right|_0\) is skew-symmetric, tangent at the identity, and has spectral norm one. For the cost covector \(G=-J\),
\[
\langle G,J\rangle_F=-2=-\|G\|_*.
\]
Here \(\|\cdot\|_*\) denotes nuclear norm. The tangent direction attains the ambient spectral-ball lower bound, so it also solves the tangent-constrained linear problem for this cost. A polar retraction of \(I+tJ\) yields the same plane rotation with angle \(\arctan t\).
We chose this cost to demonstrate attainability. We have not shown that an ordinary task gradient selects it frequently. The construction establishes a limitation of weight-only control, not a probability of training failure or a prediction of worse loss.

title: Small matrix steps, large normalized rotations
section: Turn the derivative into a finite-step statement
text:
Turn the derivative into a finite-step statement
Write the new projected feature as \(z^+=z+e\). If
\[
\frac{\|e\|_2}{\|z\|_2}\leq q<1,
\]
then
\[
\angle(z,z^+)\leq\arcsin q.
\]
To see the geometry, place a radius-\(q\|z\|\) ball around \(z\). It excludes the origin. The ray from the origin tangent to that ball makes angle \(\arcsin q\) with \(z\), and every possible \(z^+\) is inside that angular cone. The bound is sharp. The corresponding normalized Euclidean displacement is at most \(2\sin(\tfrac12\arcsin q)\).
For frozen \(h\), the relative spectral budget gives \(q\leq\eta\kappa\). If \(\eta\kappa\geq1\), that upper bound provides no useful angular certificate. It does not imply the actual update has a large angle.
The whole-matrix and head angles above are different observables. Controlling the angle between packed matrices does not directly control the angle between every normalized head feature. A head that uses the entire orthogonal output has no projection kernel, so this particular amplification mechanism needs a proper subspace.

title: Small matrix steps, large normalized rotations
section: The incoming feature moves too
text:
The incoming feature moves too
In a complete network, let
\[
\|\Delta A\|_{\rm op}\leq\eta\|A\|_{\rm op},
\qquad
\|\Delta h\|_2\leq\tau\|h\|_2.
\]
The exact raw change is
\[
e=(A+\Delta A)(h+\Delta h)-Ah
=\Delta Ah+A\Delta h+\Delta A\Delta h.
\]
The last term matters for a finite step. Applying the triangle inequality gives
\[
\frac{\|e\|_2}{\|Ah\|_2}
\leq\kappa(A,h)(\eta+\tau+\eta\tau).
\]
Whenever the right side is below one, insert it into the arcsine bound. For example, \(\kappa=5\), \(\eta=0.01\), and \(\tau=0.02\) give \(q=0.151\) and an angle bound of about \(8.69\) degrees.
A bound using the observed post-update \(\tau\) checks an inequality after the event. A pre-update certificate needs an independently valid upstream bound on \(\tau\). Part 16 illustrates what such recursive reasoning can look like under strong local assumptions. It does not establish a cheap, tight certificate for an arbitrary Transformer.
Similarly, if the effective head map is a selector applied to \(QE\) with a learned upstream matrix \(E\), an orthogonality constraint on \(Q\) does not alone constrain that complete map. The module boundary needs to match the actual forward computation.

title: Small matrix steps, large normalized rotations
section: Epsilon changes the Euclidean derivative
text:
Epsilon changes the Euclidean derivative
Real normalization often uses a positive stabilizer. For the explicitly defined map
\[
n_\epsilon(z)=\frac{z}{\sqrt{\|z\|_2^2+\epsilon}},
\qquad\epsilon>0,
\]
write \(s=\sqrt{\|z\|_2^2+\epsilon}\). Its Jacobian is
\[
Dn_\epsilon(z)=\frac Is-\frac{zz^\top}{s^3}.
\]
Transverse eigenvalues are \(1/s\), while the radial eigenvalue is \(\epsilon/s^3\). At zero all directions have derivative \(1/\sqrt\epsilon\). The derivative is globally bounded by that value, but the bound can be large. The radial derivative no longer vanishes, and exact scale invariance is lost.
For nonzero \(z\), this stabilized output points in the same direction as \(z\), so our angular argument still concerns its orientation. Its Euclidean displacement uses the new Jacobian. RMS conventions, epsilon placement, and learned gains change the actual formula and must be included when applying it.

title: Small matrix steps, large normalized rotations
section: What to measure before drawing a training conclusion
text:
What to measure before drawing a training conclusion
The same weights can have small \(\kappa\) on one context and large \(\kappa\) on another. A matrix singular-value plot alone will miss that difference. Inspect the distribution and tails of projection margins on actual features, raw and normalized feature changes, incoming-feature motion, and the task’s actual update directions.
Large internal motion can be useful. Small internal motion can still be badly aligned. To argue for a different geometry, we would need comparisons against tuned scalar step corrections, matched schedules, and completed training budgets, with downstream loss measured. The exact example above supplies a diagnostic question for that study. It does not supply its outcome.

title: Small matrix steps, large normalized rotations
section: Try checking the margin
text:
Try checking the margin

In the row-orthogonal example, take \(\varepsilon=0.01\). What is \(\kappa\)? What happens to it if we multiply \(A\) by ten?
With frozen features, \(\kappa\leq20\), and a target angle of at most five degrees, what relative spectral budget is sufficient?
Why is \(\kappa(\eta+\tau)\) insufficient for the general finite moving-feature bound?
What changes in the ideal differential formula when the normalized output dimension is one?



Answer sketches


\(\kappa=100\), and positive rescaling leaves it at 100.
\(\eta\leq\sin(5\pi/180)/20\approx0.00435779\).
It omits \(\Delta A\Delta h\). Aligned scalar changes already require the additional \(\eta\tau\) term.
Away from zero, \(u=\pm1\) and \(I-uu^\top=0\). There is no nonzero transverse direction, although a finite sign crossing can still occur through zero.

title: Small matrix steps, large normalized rotations
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Return to Part 2 for exact normalization symmetries, Part 8 for tangent constraints and retractions, and Part 16 for pathwise module bounds. The Jacobian, witness, orthogonal construction, and moving-input estimate here follow directly from the displayed maps. They express possible behavior under explicit budgets, with no new benchmark claim.
Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm, Appendix A.3 and the module-design discussion in Appendix B, gives the surrounding normalization and module perspective. A norm’s sensitivity promise belongs to its declared map and admissible region. The packed, headwise normalized construction above should not be read as a description of every attention module using that framework.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: First ask what is being rescaled
text:
First ask what is being rescaled
For a vector \(h\in\mathbb R^d\), define its root mean square by
\[
s(h)=\sqrt{\frac1d\sum_{j=1}^d h_j^2}.
\]
Ignore the stabilizing epsilon for a moment, assume \(h\ne0\), and use the gain-free normalization \(n(h)=h/s(h)\). For \(c>0\),
\[
n(ch)=\frac{ch}{c\,s(h)}=n(h).
\]
Now compare the two compositions:
\[
n(Wx)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
Wn(x).
\]
In the first, replacing \(W\) by \(cW\) disappears inside the normalization, provided \(Wx\ne0\) on the inputs under discussion. In the second, it multiplies the output by \(c\).
If the rest of the computation uses \(W\) only through \(n(Wx)\), the first expression gives blockwise scale invariance. If \(W\) has another consumer, that consumer must be checked too. This is a statement about the computation graph, not just a property of a normalization formula.



Normalization after a matrix cancels a common positive matrix scale in the idealized formula. Normalization before a matrix leaves its output scale visible.


The RMSNorm paper by Zhang and Sennrich studies normalization by root mean square. The cancellation above follows directly from its idealized denominator. It should not be read as permission to rescale arbitrary matrices in a model that uses RMSNorm.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: LayerNorm cancels a particular common scale too
text:
LayerNorm cancels a particular common scale too
Write the mean and variance across channels as
\[
\mu(h)=\frac1d\sum_j h_j,
\qquad
v(h)=\frac1d\sum_j(h_j-\mu(h))^2.
\]
The gain-free, zero-epsilon LayerNorm expression is
\[
\ell(h)=\frac{h-\mu(h)\mathbf1}{\sqrt{v(h)}}.
\]
For \(c>0\) and any scalar \(b\), provided \(v(h)>0\),
\[
\ell(ch+b\mathbf1)=\ell(h).
\]
The common shift cancels in the numerator. The common positive scale cancels between numerator and denominator. This does not say that separately rescaling each channel leaves the result unchanged. Such a transformation usually changes both the centered direction and the relative channel magnitudes.
Ba, Kiros, and Hinton’s Layer Normalization paper defines these per-example statistics and examines the associated invariances in Section 5. The axis used to compute the statistics determines what a common rescaling means. BatchNorm uses different statistics, and frozen inference statistics require their own check.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Epsilon makes the ideal identity approximate
text:
Epsilon makes the ideal identity approximate
With a fixed \(\epsilon>0\), the RMS expression becomes
\[
n_\epsilon(h)=\frac{h}{\sqrt{s(h)^2+\epsilon}}.
\]
For positive \(c\),
\[
n_\epsilon(ch)
=\frac{h}{\sqrt{s(h)^2+\epsilon/c^2}}.
\]
This is generally different from \(n_\epsilon(h)\). The approximation is useful when epsilon is negligible relative to the squared activation scale, but the exact symmetry is gone. LayerNorm has the corresponding change from \(\epsilon\) to \(\epsilon/c^2\) after factoring out a common positive scale.
For example, take \(h=(1,2)\), so \(s(h)^2=5/2\). The denominators for \(n_1(h)\) and \(n_1(2h)\), expressed using the same numerator \(h\), are \(\sqrt{7/2}\) and \(\sqrt{11/4}\). They are visibly unequal. The deliberately large epsilon makes the difference easy to see.
An exact theorem needs the exact identity it assumes. A practical approximation needs a scale regime in which the discrepancy is small.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: A learned gain creates a different symmetry
text:
A learned gain creates a different symmetry
Suppose \(z(x)\) already denotes normalized features and the next operation is
\[
f(x)=W\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)z(x).
\]
The effective linear map is \(A=W\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)\). Replacing only \(W\) by \(cW\) changes \(A\). Replacing both parameters according to
\[
W\mapsto cW,
\qquad
\gamma\mapsto\gamma/c
\]
preserves \(A\) exactly. This cancellation does not depend on neglecting epsilon because the already-computed features \(z(x)\) are unchanged.
There is redundancy in the pair \((W,\gamma)\), but that is not independent scale invariance of \(W\). The elementary loss
\[
L(w,g)=\frac12(wg-1)^2
\]
makes the distinction concrete. At \((w,g)=(1,1)\) the loss is zero. At \((2,1)\) it is \(1/2\). At \((2,1/2)\) it is zero again. The joint transformation preserves the function. Changing one coordinate alone does not.
If a normalized output also includes a learned additive offset, rescaling the entire downstream matrix requires compensating that offset as well. The displayed identity assumes the bias-free form written above.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Sharing a gain couples its consumers
text:
Sharing a gain couples its consumers
Let two branches consume the same gained features:
\[
f_1(x)=W_1\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)z(x),
\qquad
f_2(x)=W_2\operatorname{diag}(\gamma)z(x).
\]
One gain can compensate a common rescaling of both matrices. If we rescale only \(W_1\) and divide the gain to compensate, we also change the second branch. The bookkeeping is no longer local to one matrix.
The scalar version is enough to expose the issue. Take a nonzero scalar feature \(z\) and require branch outputs \(z\) and \(2z\):
\[
g w_1=1,\qquad g w_2=2.
\]
A shared gain allows many representations, for example \((g,w_1,w_2)=(1,1,2)\) and \((2,1/2,1)\). But requiring both \(|w_1|=1\) and \(|w_2|=1\) makes those two target equations incompatible. Their magnitude ratio must remain two, while the constraints force it to one.
That is a claim about prescribed branch outputs with fixed features and one shared scalar gain. It does not prove that a complete trainable attention network loses an entire class of functions. Other factorizations, later layers, or changing features may compensate. The later research posts will ask which of these freedoms matter.
The useful lesson already holds: the existence of one function-preserving rescaling does not prove that every proposed collection of norm constraints is harmless.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Residual paths keep relative scales visible
text:
Residual paths keep relative scales visible
For a residual expression
\[
y=x+Wn(x),
\]
scaling \(W\) changes the branch relative to the skip path. Even a normalization after the addition does not generally erase that change: the sum’s direction can change rather than only its magnitude.
For a direct example, take \(x=(1,0)\) and a branch output \((0,1)\). The sums \((1,1)\) and \((1,2)\) are not positive scalar multiples of one another. RMS normalization preserves their different directions.
This is why a blanket statement about all matrices in a normalized architecture is too coarse. We need to trace where the scale travels and which quantities meet at each addition, product, or shared parameter.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Three questions before imposing a constraint
text:
Three questions before imposing a constraint
When I see a claim that a weight norm can be fixed without changing the model, I now want three things specified:

Which parameters move, and which remain fixed?
Which output or final function is preserved, under what exact assumptions?
Can all the proposed constraints be satisfied simultaneously by a representative of that function?

The first post explains why a redundant radius can still affect learning. This post identifies where that redundancy actually lives. The next step is to put decay back into the dynamics and distinguish its direct penalty from the training path it induces.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Try the symmetries
text:
Try the symmetries

For \(h=(1,2)\), compare zero-epsilon LayerNorm before and after multiplying only the first channel by three.
In the two-branch scalar example, replace the shared gain by independent gains \(g_1,g_2\). Can both weights now have magnitude one?
For nonzero channel gains, find a channelwise transformation of \(\gamma_j\) and every consuming column \(W_i[:,j]\) that preserves all effective maps.



Answer sketches


The normalized first vector is \((-1,1)\). The transformed vector is \((3,2)\), whose normalized form is \((1,-1)\). Both variances are nonzero, but the direction has changed.
Yes. Take \(w_1=w_2=1\), \(g_1=1\), and \(g_2=2\). The missing relative scale is now a learnable parameter.
For any \(d_j>0\), set \(\gamma_j'=d_j\gamma_j\) and \(W_i'[:,j]=W_i[:,j]/d_j\) for every consumer \(i\). A shared gain requires the compensation at every consuming branch.

title: What normalization makes invariant
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Layer Normalization (Ba, Kiros, and Hinton, 2016), especially Section 5, and Root Mean Square Layer Normalization (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019), especially Sections 3 and 4, provide the normalization definitions and invariance context.
L2 Regularization versus Batch and Weight Normalization (van Laarhoven, 2017) explains why the scope of scale invariance matters for optimization. The placement comparisons, epsilon calculation, and scalar shared-gain example above follow directly from their displayed definitions. They do not establish an empirical optimizer ranking or a full-network expressivity result.

title: What our matched-step experiments actually tested
section: First declare the experimental world
text:
First declare the experimental world
The core comparison used two complete Transformer blocks, width 32, and either one or four heads. The task predicted independently masked WikiText-2 bytes in 64-byte bidirectional contexts, with minibatches of 16 sequences. Features, values, output paths, learned temperatures, embeddings, and readout remained trainable.
The two treatments differed in their query-key matrix geometry. One restored the packed matrices to a fixed Frobenius radius, allowing their shape to vary. The other restored them to a Stiefel constraint. The matrix proposals used a custom angular Adam-based rule with its recorded moment and normalization conventions. This was not a reproduction of Modula, ordinary Euclidean Adam, or the exact spectral oracle in Part 19.
Later comparisons added an expanded one-head parametrization with shared width 48. The primary paired seeds were 0, 1, and 2, with 4000 updates as one endpoint. An additional endpoint used 60 seconds of process CPU time spent on training and functional calibration. That clock excluded evaluation and checkpoint serialization. It was neither total wall time nor a GPU throughput measurement.
These details define what the evidence can address. A masked-byte network at fixed width does not directly test learning-rate transfer across model widths or large causal language-model pretraining.

title: What our matched-step experiments actually tested
section: A tiny initialization operation was not innocuous
text:
A tiny initialization operation was not innocuous
The archived hard-constraint branch applied an additional polar restoration to an already orthogonal saved initialization. The norm-only branch did not. This changed entries by at most about \(3\times10^{-8}\), while initial probe logits differed by less than \(2.1\times10^{-7}\).
Faithful replays recovered the archived terminal losses. Replays that instead started the two methods from exactly identical arrays produced a different comparison:

Units are nats per masked byte. Positive means the hard constraint has higher loss. Every mean uses three paired seeds.
For the identical-array one-head replay, the individual differences were \(-0.022846\), \(+0.056520\), and \(+0.015955\). The original single-head penalty became a mixed sign pattern. The four-head replay retained negative differences in all three seeds.
The representational class did not change when we removed a rounding-sized initialization operation. Its effect on a long trajectory therefore cannot, by itself, be evidence of a capacity difference. It also does not identify which later optimizer component amplified the perturbation.

title: What our matched-step experiments actually tested
section: Match predictive motion, rather than matrix angle
text:
Match predictive motion, rather than matrix angle
Equal matrix angles need not mean equal function changes. Parts 9 and 18 explain two reasons: numerical schedules can change the actual angular step, and a normalized head’s sensitivity depends on its feature margin.
The next intervention matched complete-network forward predictive KL:
\[
K(\theta,\theta^+)
=\mathbb E_x D_{\rm KL}\bigl(p_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\|p_{\theta^+}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr).
\]
Each setting received a target sequence frozen from a separate development seed before the main paired runs. At each update, a scalar controller rescaled the entire proposed parameter path. Calibration used eight fresh unlabeled training contexts, independently of the gradient minibatch. Optimizer moments advanced once per minibatch, rather than during controller trials.
At 4000 updates, the recorded test differences were:

The simple head-dependent ordering did not persist. The expanded mean is dominated by one seed. These are heterogeneous paired observations, not a clean winner ranking.



Paired seed loss differences change when the intervention changes from a matrix angular clock to a prescribed predictive-KL clock.


The controller also created new limitations. Some accepted path multipliers exceeded 100, making these steps large extrapolations of the native proposal. Although calibration error was below 0.5 percent, independent contexts did not match the target equally well. One expanded checkpoint had a mean validation KL ratio of about 2.09 for the norm-only method.
Thus the intervention tests a specified predictive clock with an empirical controller. It does not perfectly remove functional speed while leaving all other aspects of training unchanged.

title: What our matched-step experiments actually tested
section: Why matching can remove a real source of benefit
text:
Why matching can remove a real source of benefit
Locally, for direction \(d\) and predictive Fisher matrix \(F\),
\[
K(\theta,\theta+\eta d)
=\tfrac12\eta^2d^\top Fd+O(\eta^3).
\]
For positive target \(k\) and \(d^\top Fd>0\), the quadratic matching rule is
\[
\eta(d)=\sqrt{\frac{2k}{d^\top Fd}}.
\]
If the total direction is multiplied by \(a>0\), then \(\eta(ad)ad=\eta(d)d\). To leading order, this control removes any benefit that operates only through a positive global rescaling of that direction.
It does not remove arbitrary reallocations across layers or heads. Nor does it imply that functional matching is a bad experiment. It tells us which question it asks: does the proposal help beyond an online scalar predictive-step controller? Ordinary training with a practical schedule asks another question. Both comparisons can be informative.

title: What our matched-step experiments actually tested
section: Separate a smaller class from a particular optimizer
text:
Separate a smaller class from a particular optimizer
At a common row-isometric checkpoint, the Stiefel tangent lies inside the fixed-radius sphere tangent. After applying the complete-network Jacobian \(J\),
\[
\operatorname{range}(JT_{\rm hard})
\subseteq\operatorname{range}(JT_{\rm sphere}).
\]
In predictive-Fisher-whitened coordinates, let these accessible linear subspaces be \(\mathcal R\), and let \(r\) be the task’s linear descent covector represented in those coordinates. At radius \(\rho\), the best possible linearized decrease in a subspace is
\[
\max_{u\in\mathcal R,\ \|u\|_2\leq\rho}\langle r,u\rangle
=\rho\|P_{\mathcal R}r\|_2.
\]
Inclusion means the hard model cannot have a better ideal local oracle at the same radius. A particular hard optimizer can still beat a particular sphere optimizer through direction selection, noise, conditioning, or implicit regularization. Neither method necessarily implements this ideal output-space oracle.
The expanded parametrization added a separate control for generic representability under ideal normalization. Its conversion checks preserve complete-network probe logits approximately at finite epsilon and precision. That control weakens global class exclusion as a sufficient explanation there. It does not equate local conditioning, optimizer access, singular boundary cases, or implicit bias.

title: What our matched-step experiments actually tested
section: An exact identity is not a successful forecast
text:
An exact identity is not a successful forecast
Let old logits be \(z\), a finite logit change be \(\Delta z\), old probabilities be \(p=\operatorname{softmax}(z)\), and label distribution be \(q\). Expanding log-sum-exp gives the exact identity
\[
\operatorname{CE}(q,z+\Delta z)-\operatorname{CE}(q,z)
=D_{\rm KL}(p\|p^+)-(q-p)^\top\Delta z.
\]
At equal KL on the scoring examples, immediate loss ordering is determined by signed task alignment. But substituting the observed finite change after updating is an accounting check.
To forecast before updating, use the full-network velocity \(v=J\Delta\theta\) and the quadratic approximation
\[
\widehat{\Delta L}
=\tfrac12\mathbb E[v^\top C_pv]
-\mathbb E[(q-p)^\top v],
\qquad C_p=\operatorname{Diag}(p)-pp^\top.
\]
Estimate this on one set of contexts and score actual finite changes on another. Comparing prediction with observation then tests transfer across samples as well as linearization.

title: What our matched-step experiments actually tested
section: The conservative prediction test exposed that distinction
text:
The conservative prediction test exposed that distinction
A follow-up used 64 calibration contexts and chose a target no larger than either raw proposal’s KL. Accepted path multipliers stayed at most one. A diagnostic split drew 1024 nonoverlapping validation contexts from across the stream, assigning 512 to prediction and 512 to scoring.

Accurate same-example Taylor scores show that local calculus can describe a small step. They do not establish reliable prediction across contexts. Nor does an accurate one-step forecast establish the ordering of losses thousands of steps later.

title: What our matched-step experiments actually tested
section: A broader benchmark is still an open experiment
text:
A broader benchmark is still an open experiment
The later scale audit qualified the negative result. This small, short-horizon, CPU harness with online calibration does not settle whether modular geometry helps ordinary training or width transfer. A changed task, scale, or horizon could matter, but none has been identified as the cause of the observed failures.
A frozen-checkpoint diagnostic also rejected the simplest claim that the small task did not use attention routing. Across five saved checkpoints, mean validation loss was 2.22732 with learned routing, 3.65161 after making block 0’s routing uniform, and 2.30671 after doing so in block 1. Values and output paths remained. This intervention measures reliance at those checkpoints. It does not tell us how a retrained uniform-routing model would perform.
The next useful benchmark should first recover a relevant known behavior, then compare native schedules and matched functional steps as separate treatments. Tune rates and decay at the intended training horizon with comparable search budgets. Vary width and depth separately, report paired seeds and learning curves, and measure actual end-to-end compute on the chosen hardware.
More scale can test external validity. It cannot repair an unsupported mathematical implication or turn an unsuccessful prediction into a demonstrated mechanism. Our current record supports a narrower conclusion: the tested explanations and allocations have not established an advantage beyond their stated controls in this regime. The broader training question remains open.

No. Finite-time optimization and statistical effects can differ even within the same generic class.
An overall positive scalar on the complete direction. Relative layer or head allocations generally remain.
An independent before-update prediction, followed by evaluation on disjoint scoring examples.
The probes share trained states. Counting them as independent networks would overstate the replication.

title: What our matched-step experiments actually tested
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
The empirical values come from our archived November 4 functional-step study and later scale audit. This article recomputes their aggregates and checks the displayed algebra. It does not rerun training, tune a new method, or claim a large-model result. The initialization replays, primary KL-controlled trajectories, and later diagnostic probes are separate experiments.
Read Part 12 for the difference between a frozen-feature obstruction and a research claim, Part 17 for a transfer protocol, and Part 18 for the pointwise normalized-head bound.
Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm, Section 4, asks a broader scaling question than our fixed-width custom angular comparison. Its experiments provide a reference behavior to reproduce in a suitable benchmark, rather than an outcome established or refuted by these local controls.

title: How normalization can favor lower sharpness
section: Fix the curvature measurement before comparing flatness
text:
Fix the curvature measurement before comparing flatness
For a twice differentiable scale-invariant loss,
\[
L(cw)=L(w),
\quad \nabla L(cw)=c^{-1}\nabla L(w),
\quad \nabla^2L(cw)=c^{-2}\nabla^2L(w).
\]
An ordinary Hessian eigenvalue can therefore be made arbitrarily small by increasing the radius, without changing the predictor. Raw parameter-space flatness is not an invariant ranking of functions.
One way to remove this particular ambiguity is to examine curvature on the unit sphere. At a unit stationary point \(u\), restrict the Hessian to tangent directions \(v\perp u\) with \(\|v\|=1\). Define the local spherical sharpness by the largest eigenvalue of this restriction.
At a scaled stationary point \(w=ru\), the equivalent radial correction is \(r^2\) times the corresponding Euclidean curvature. This removes global radius scaling. It does not remove every other reparametrization of a network or turn sharpness into a universal generalization metric.

title: How normalization can favor lower sharpness
section: Exact gradient flow gives a useful control
text:
Exact gradient flow gives a useful control
Consider
\[
\dot w=-\nabla L(w)-\lambda w.
\]
Since \(w^\top\nabla L(w)=0\), its radius obeys \(r(t)=e^{-\lambda t}r(0)\). Setting \(z(t)=e^{\lambda t}w(t)\) gives
\[
\dot z=-e^{2\lambda t}\nabla L(z).
\]
Thus \(z(t)\) follows the no-decay gradient-flow path with a faster clock, on intervals where the solutions exist away from zero. This exact continuous-time identity does not provide a new directional bias by itself.
The finite-step update contains a different ingredient. Let \(a=1-\eta\lambda>0\), \(w=ru\), and \(g=\nabla L(u)\). Then
\[
u^+=\frac{u-qg}{\sqrt{1+q^2\|g\|^2}},
\qquad q=\frac{\eta}{ar^2}.
\]
Near a stationary direction, decay shrinks \(r\) and can raise \(q\). Discrete normal motion becomes important when this coefficient approaches a local stability threshold.

title: How normalization can favor lower sharpness
section: A valley with different transverse curvatures
text:
A valley with different transverse curvatures
For \(u=w/\|w\|\in\mathbb S^2\), define
\[
L(w)=\frac12\left[2+0.8(u_x^2-u_y^2)\right]u_z^2.
\]
This loss is smooth away from \(w=0\) and scale invariant. Its bracket lies between 1.2 and 2.8, so every equatorial direction \(u_z=0\) is a global minimizer.
Parametrize a neighborhood of that equator by
\[
u=(\sqrt{1-z^2}\cos\phi,\sqrt{1-z^2}\sin\phi,z).
\]
Then
\[
L=\tfrac12 A(\phi)z^2-0.4\cos(2\phi)z^4,
\qquad A(\phi)=2+0.8\cos(2\phi).
\]
The equatorial sharpness is \(A(\phi)\). Motion along the equator has zero curvature, while the unit transverse direction has curvature \(A(\phi)>0\). The sharpest equatorial points have \(A=2.8\), and the least sharp have \(A=1.2\). All have the same training loss.

title: How normalization can favor lower sharpness
section: Oscillations can create a one-way drift
text:
Oscillations can create a one-way drift
For small \(z\), the transverse update is
\[
z^+=(1-qA(\phi))z+O(z^3).
\]
The local linear stability condition is \(0<qA<2\). Above one, the sign alternates while the magnitude contracts if the product remains below two. Near two, the normal motion is weakly damped and can interact with the changing radius.
The longitudinal gradient depends on \(z^2\), not on the sign of \(z\). To make this precise, put
\[
D(\phi,z)=A(\phi)-1.6\cos(2\phi)z^2.
\]
The horizontal part of \(u-qg\) is the original horizontal vector multiplied by \(1+qDz^2\), plus a rotated component with coefficient \(-qA'(\phi)z^2/2\). Consequently the exact longitude change, on a continuous local angle branch, is
\[
\phi^+-\phi
=\operatorname{atan2}\left(-\tfrac12qA'(\phi)z^2,\ 1+qD(\phi,z)z^2\right).
\]
For bounded \(q\) and small \(z\),
\[
\phi^+-\phi=-\tfrac12qA'(\phi)z^2+O(z^4).
\]
Flipping \(z\) does not flip the leading drift. When \(A'(\phi)<0\), repeated small excursions push \(\phi\) toward lower \(A\). A vanishingly small transverse displacement would stop that motion, while persistent excursions can accumulate an effect.
This is why an oscillating coordinate can produce a consistent longitudinal bias. It is not necessary to insert an explicit sharpness penalty into the loss.

title: How normalization can favor lower sharpness
section: A finite calculation, with the controls visible
text:
A finite calculation, with the controls visible
Use \(\eta=0.1\), \(\lambda=0.01\), \(\phi_0=0.3\), and \(z_0=0.03\). Choose the initial radius to make \(q_0=2/A(\phi_0)\). Compare the same initial weight vector with and without decay for 3000 float64 updates.
In the decayed run, the equatorial curvature at the current longitude falls from approximately 2.66027 to 1.43613. Without decay, it ends near 2.65708. In the displayed decayed run, \(|z_t|\) stays below 0.037. These are finite calculations of the stated loss, rather than neural-network training measurements.



An explicit scale-invariant valley shows declining equatorial curvature with decay and persistent sign-alternating normal motion. The no-decay control remains near its starting longitude.


The plotted curvature belongs to the equatorial minimizer at longitude \(\phi_t\). It is not being substituted for the full off-equator Hessian at \(w_t\). The experiment illustrates a local mechanism over a declared horizon, without proving an infinite-time outcome or a generalization benefit.

title: How normalization can favor lower sharpness
section: What the published theorem adds
text:
What the published theorem adds
Understanding the Generalization Benefit of Normalization Layers: Sharpness Reduction, Section 4.2, analyzes a smooth scale-invariant loss near a regular manifold \(\Gamma\) of spherical minimizers. Its assumptions include nondegenerate transverse curvature, a unique largest Hessian eigenvalue, sufficiently small intrinsic rate, and a specified perturbed initialization near the stability boundary.
Under those conditions, the normalized discrete trajectory tracks a slow flow on the minimizer manifold. If \(S\) denotes its spherical sharpness, that flow is
\[
\frac{d\zeta}{d\tau}
=-\frac{2\nabla_\Gamma\log S(\zeta)}
{4+\|\nabla_\Gamma\log S(\zeta)\|^2},
\qquad\tau=t\eta\lambda.
\]
The chain rule gives
\[
\frac d{d\tau}\log S(\zeta)
=-\frac{2\|\nabla_\Gamma\log S(\zeta)\|^2}
{4+\|\nabla_\Gamma\log S(\zeta)\|^2}\leq0.
\]
The theorem supplies a controlled connection between discrete dynamics and this flow. Our explicit valley calculation explains one source of its directional sign, without replacing that connection or its initialization requirements.

title: How normalization can favor lower sharpness
section: An exact minimizer is a revealing exception
text:
An exact minimizer is a revealing exception
If we start exactly on the equator, \(g=0\). Gradient descent with decay then simply rescales \(w\) at every step. Its direction stays fixed, even at an equatorial point whose neighboring minimizers have lower sharpness.
Thus proximity to a minimizer manifold alone does not force the selection mechanism. A suitable transverse component matters. In the paper, the initialization scheme handles exceptional directions with a small random perturbation. It is not minibatch noise inserted throughout training.
Likewise, a repeated top eigenvalue changes the regularity of the sharpness function, and moving far from the local manifold leaves the stated approximation regime. Fixed norms, different tangent oracles, or coordinatewise adaptive states create different dynamics and need their own analysis.

title: How normalization can favor lower sharpness
section: Lower sharpness still needs a task-dependent interpretation
text:
Lower sharpness still needs a task-dependent interpretation
Our example has no test distribution or notion of generalization. Its minimizers agree on the constructed training objective, while their transverse curvatures differ. Showing that an optimizer moves between them establishes a selection bias in this model.
Whether that bias helps a real task requires more: an appropriate curvature definition, a relationship to the predictor, and a controlled evaluation. A sharpness change caused only by parameter rescaling would not be such evidence. Nor would a lower Hessian number under a different normalization convention.
The useful conclusion is more specific. Redundant scales can change finite-step dynamics, and those dynamics can prefer different solutions even when the direct radial change leaves the represented function unchanged.

title: How normalization can favor lower sharpness
section: Try separating scale from selection
text:
Try separating scale from selection

Multiply a stationary weight vector by three. How does its raw Hessian change? What happens to the radius-corrected curvature?
For transverse curvature \(A=2\), which effective rates give linear contraction of the normal coordinate?
Why does alternating the sign of \(z\) not cancel the leading longitude drift?
What happens if the valley experiment starts with \(z_0=0\) exactly?

The Hessian is divided by nine, while multiplying by the new squared radius cancels that factor.
\(0<q<1\). For \(1/2<q<1\), the sign alternates while contracting in the linear approximation.
The drift is proportional to \(z^2\), which has the same sign on both sides of the valley.
The gradient is zero, so decay changes only the radius. There is no motion along the equator.

section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Understanding the Generalization Benefit of Normalization Layers: Sharpness Reduction, Assumptions 4.5 and 4.6, Equation 3, and Theorem 4.7, states the local sharpness-reduction result and initialization scheme. Its Section 5 studies a particular normalized regression model. Neither statement is a universal generalization theorem for fixed-norm adaptive matrix optimizers.
An Exponential Learning Rate Schedule for Deep Learning, Section 4, gives the gradient-flow time-change perspective. The polynomial-on-the-sphere example above is our own explicit calculation. It is not a reproduction of the sharpness paper’s figure or its neural-network experiments.

title: What a noisy matrix update does on average
section: Smooth the update by averaging over noise
text:
Smooth the update by averaging over noise
Flatten a matrix gradient into a vector when necessary. Let \(D:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^p\) be the map producing the proposed update direction, with the descent step taken as \(-\eta D\). Examples include a linear map, coordinatewise signs, a normalized vector, or a matrix polar factor followed by an explicit scaling convention.
Write the input as \(s+\xi\), where \(s\) is the signal and
\[
\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,C),\qquad C\succ0.
\]
Define
\[
F(s)=\mathbb E D(s+\xi),\qquad J(s)=DF(s).
\]
The matrix \(J(s)\) describes how the mean proposal changes under a small common perturbation of the signal. It is not the covariance of the proposal or the derivative of one arbitrarily selected noisy update.
For measurable maps of at most polynomial growth, Gaussian convolution makes \(F\) smooth. This includes bounded discontinuous maps such as a sign, so we do not need to differentiate the map at its exceptional points.

title: What a noisy matrix update does on average
section: Differentiate the Gaussian density
text:
Differentiate the Gaussian density
Write \(F(s)\) as an integral over the actual input \(x\):
\[
F(s)=\int D(x)\,\varphi_C(x-s)\,dx.
\]
The derivative of the density with respect to its mean is
\[
\nabla_s\varphi_C(x-s)=\varphi_C(x-s)C^{-1}(x-s).
\]
Differentiate under the integral, justified by Gaussian tails and the growth assumption. Substituting \(x=s+\xi\) gives
\[
\boxed{J(s)=\mathbb E[D(s+\xi)\xi^\top]C^{-1}.}
\]
Centering \(D\) by \(F(s)\) does not change the right side because \(\mathbb E\xi=0\). This is a Gaussian score identity, used for general nonlinear update maps in Muon Under Gradient Noise, Theorem 4.1.
It is useful for polar updates because individual derivatives can be delicate near rank loss. The density argument concerns the averaged map. Singular covariance needs a separate treatment on its support, rather than inserting an ordinary inverse into this formula.

title: What a noisy matrix update does on average
section: Match the average response with an affine update
text:
Match the average response with an affine update
At a fixed signal \(s\), define
\[
L_s(x)=F(s)+J(s)(x-s).
\]
It has the same mean proposal at \(s\), and the same first-order change in that mean under a nearby signal perturbation. On the noisy input,
\[
D(s+\xi)=F(s)+J(s)\xi+R_s.
\]
By construction and the score identity,
\[
\mathbb E R_s=0,
\qquad \mathbb E[R_s\xi^\top]=0.
\]
Expanding the covariance therefore gives
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Cov}(D(s+\xi))
=J(s)CJ(s)^\top+\operatorname{Cov}(R_s).}
\]
The residual covariance is positive semidefinite. Among affine functions of this Gaussian input, the matched map is the mean-square projection of the nonlinear proposal. No inverse of \(J\) is required, and the input and output dimensions need not agree.
Uncorrelated does not mean independent. The residual can be a deterministic nonlinear function of the same noise. Nor does the covariance identity compare the realized lengths of every paired update.

title: What a noisy matrix update does on average
section: The scalar sign makes every term explicit
text:
The scalar sign makes every term explicit
Take \(D(x)=\operatorname{sign}(x)\) and scalar noise of standard deviation \(\sigma>0\). Then
\[
F(s)=2\Phi(s/\sigma)-1,
\qquad J(0)=\sqrt{\frac2\pi}\frac1\sigma.
\]
At zero signal, the proposal has mean zero and variance one. The affine matched proposal is \(J(0)\xi\), whose variance is \(2/\pi\). Thus
\[
\operatorname{Var}(R_0)=1-\frac2\pi\approx0.363380.
\]
The residual is not a rounding error. Its covariance remains after we match the derivative of the average update exactly.



The Gaussian-averaged sign saturates away from zero, while its local affine response is linear. At zero signal the nonlinear update has an additional residual variance beyond that of the matched affine map.


The mean is nearly linear only locally. Using the tangent line at zero to describe a large signal would introduce another approximation, distinct from the exact covariance decomposition at the chosen signal.

title: What a noisy matrix update does on average
section: What this means for a polar matrix proposal
text:
What this means for a polar matrix proposal
For square dimension \(d\), define the Frobenius-unit polar proposal
\[
D(N)=\operatorname{polar}(N)/\sqrt d.
\]
A full-rank square input gives \(D(N)^\top D(N)=I_d/d\). With independent centered Gaussian entries, symmetry makes the averaged proposal zero. Each coordinate then has variance \(1/d^2\). The covariance is isotropic in the flattened matrix coordinates at zero signal.
The average response is also a scalar operator under isotropic matrix noise. Its scalar coefficient depends on the expected nuclear norm of the noise, rather than being one merely because the singular values of each polar factor are one.
Anisotropic input noise changes this picture. In the next post, a feature-energy matrix scales the gradient columns differently. The polar proposal still has equal coordinate variances by its symmetries, while its columnwise restoring responses differ. Equal update variance is not equal stationary parameter variance.
All these statements depend on the declared scaling of the polar map. A shape multiplier, norm graft, damping rule, or finite polynomial changes the actual \(D\) whose response must be computed.

title: What a noisy matrix update does on average
section: Extra one-step noise is not a complete loss ranking
text:
Extra one-step noise is not a complete loss ranking
Suppose a frozen scalar surrogate has the same restoring coefficient \(c>0\) in two comparisons:
\[
x_{t+1}=(1-\eta c)x_t-\eta\zeta_t,
\qquad \mathbb E\zeta_t=0,
\quad\operatorname{Var}(\zeta_t)=v.
\]
With independent innovations and \(0<\eta c<2\), its stationary variance is
\[
\mathbb E x^2=\frac{\eta v}{2c-\eta c^2}.
\]
In this surrogate, increasing \(v\) increases the stationary quadratic loss. For the scalar sign and its matched affine control at zero signal, the ratio of their innovation variances is \(\pi/2\).
This is not an exact stationary-loss ratio for the full sign recursion. There, the state changes the signal seen by the nonlinearity. Momentum also introduces temporal correlations, so one-step covariance alone does not determine accumulated variance. Muon Under Gradient Noise explicitly separates its frozen-residual surrogate from the full feedback-dependent recursion.

title: What a noisy matrix update does on average
section: Do not use the Gaussian identity as a universal regression rule
text:
Do not use the Gaussian identity as a universal regression rule
Let \(\xi\) instead take values \(-1\) and \(1\) equally, and let \(D(x)=x^3\). Direct calculation gives
\[
F(s)=s^3+3s,
\qquad J(0)=3.
\]
The linear regression coefficient of \(D(\xi)\) on \(\xi\) is instead
\[
\frac{\mathbb E[D(\xi)\xi]}{\mathbb E\xi^2}=1.
\]
Both computations are correct. The derivative of a mean under a common shift and a regression on an arbitrary noise law are different objects. Gaussian integration by parts is what identifies them in the earlier setting.
A finite set of minibatches is generally non-Gaussian. With 12 possible batches, centered gradient noise has covariance rank at most 11, regardless of the matrix’s parameter dimension. A regression on those outcomes cannot recover an unrestricted full response operator in a larger space.
One direct alternative is
\[
J=\frac1K\sum_{i=1}^K D'(g_i),
\]
where each derivative concerns a common perturbation of the batch gradient, with model parameters held fixed. This requires the derivatives to exist or a justified numerical evaluation. It matches the local mean response, without inheriting the Gaussian covariance ordering automatically.

title: What a noisy matrix update does on average
section: Matching the norm can change the response again
text:
Matching the norm can change the response again
If an affine proposal \(L(g)\) has variable length, normalizing it to match another method’s angle changes its derivative:
\[
D\left(\frac{L}{\|L\|}\right)[h]
=\frac{I-qq^\top}{\|L\|}DL[h],
\qquad q=L/\|L\|.
\]
The projection and inverse length both matter. Equal angles and equal response are separate targets. After a graft or normalization, measure the response of the applied update, including retraction where appropriate.
This gives us three useful controls: match step size, match the mean response, and inspect the remaining update noise. The next two posts use them to distinguish a valid constructed mechanism from a stronger claim about independently learned features.

title: What a noisy matrix update does on average
section: Try separating response from variance
text:
Try separating response from variance

For sign updates with \(\sigma=2\), what is \(J(0)\)? What is the proposal variance at zero signal?
Is the Gaussian residual independent of the input noise merely because it is uncorrelated with it?
In the two-point cubic example, what does a noise regression miss?
Does normalizing an affine proposal preserve its fitted Jacobian automatically?



Answer sketches


\(J(0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}/2\approx0.398942\), while the sign variance remains one.
No. The residual can be a deterministic nonlinear function of that noise.
The mean response derivative is three, while the regression coefficient is one.
No. The derivative acquires a tangent projection and a factor inverse to the proposal length.

text:
Yo twin, go read…
Muon Under Gradient Noise and the Limits of Orthogonalization Near Optima, Proposition 3.1, Theorem 4.1, and Sections 5 and 6, develops Gaussian response, the residual decomposition, temporal effects, and a frozen-residual surrogate. The density calculation and scalar example above make the local identity explicit. They do not establish a general optimizer ranking or reproduce a training benchmark.
Return to Part 14 for the difference between averaging before and after a nonlinear direction map, and Part 13 for why finite polar evaluation changes the proposal being analyzed.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: Remove the deliberately shared feature parameter
text:
Remove the deliberately shared feature parameter
The network was
\[
f(x)=V\tanh\left(\gamma\odot\operatorname{LayerNorm}(Wx+b)+\beta\right)+c.
\]
It had six inputs, 12 hidden units, two outputs, and 134 independently trained parameters. Both matrices, all biases, and both LayerNorm parameter vectors learned. No scalar tied a feature energy to a separate nonlinear output term.
The nonlinear teacher depended on the first three inputs. Each dataset had 384 training examples. In one distribution, nuisance coordinates were independent. In the other, two nuisance coordinates correlated with the teacher outputs, creating spurious shortcuts. Evaluation included clean labels on an independent-input distribution where those correlations disappeared.
In the main grid, label noise of standard deviation 0.25 was added once to the training labels. It was not refreshed each update. A fixed partition supplied 12 blocks of 32 examples, sampled uniformly with replacement. Their gradients were unbiased for the finite-data training objective, with genuine non-Gaussian minibatch noise.
This differs from the fresh Gaussian target noise in Part 26. Later controls removed the fixed observational label noise as well.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: Match the quantities the original explanation might hide behind
text:
Match the quantities the original explanation might hide behind
Every paired continuation began from the same checkpoint after 2000 Adam steps and lasted 1024 updates. The grid used four independent dataset and initialization seeds, two matrix step sizes, zero or positive decay, zero momentum, and float64 arithmetic.
The polar reference applied an exact rectangular polar map to matrix gradients. The angular-gradient comparison used ordinary gradient tangent directions while copying the reference’s actual matrix angle and radius at each step. Vector parameters used the same rule across arms.
For a matrix treated as a vector under the Frobenius inner product, write \(u=W/\|W\|_F\) and choose unit \(q\perp u\). The explicit sphere step
\[
W^+=r^+\left(\cos\alpha\,u-\sin\alpha\,q\right)
\]
has prescribed radius \(r^+\) and angle \(\alpha\) with \(W\). This makes clear what the angular control does: it fixes displacement scale on the sphere while allowing the tangent direction to differ.
Matching those quantities does not match the response of the mean update to changing gradients. Part 25 showed why that distinction matters near a fitted model.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: Fit the actual finite-minibatch response
text:
Fit the actual finite-minibatch response
At a calibration checkpoint, enumerate all 12 batch gradients \(g_i\) and their unit polar tangent directions \(q_i\). Let
\[
\bar g=\frac1{12}\sum_i g_i,
\qquad\bar q=\frac1{12}\sum_i q_i,
\qquad J=\frac1{12}\sum_i Dq(g_i).
\]
The global affine control is
\[
L(g)=\bar q+J(g-\bar g).
\]
At calibration, it matches the expected tangent direction and its derivative under a common perturbation of the gradient input. The full block Jacobian was obtained by finite differences, with a two-scale numerical check.
This is not a Gaussian approximation or a regression on the 12 noise samples. Such a regression would not generally identify the same derivative, and its centered input covariance has rank at most 11.
An affine proposal has variable length. Renormalizing it to restore an exact common angle changes its response through the derivative of normalization. The experiment retained both versions and measured their realized errors. It did not declare simultaneous response and angle matching merely because both were intended.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: Preserve more than the mean with a local control
text:
Preserve more than the mean with a local control
A stronger diagnostic kept a separate affine expansion for each batch:
\[
L_i(g)=q_i+J_i(g-g_i),\qquad J_i=Dq(g_i).
\]
At calibration, it reproduces every discrete proposal and its first derivative. It therefore preserves the batchwise update distribution at that point, before the subsequent declared angular step. It is a minibatch-conditioned model, rather than one global linear preconditioner.
As features evolve, both fitted controls can become stale. Recalibration interval and measured response error are part of the comparison. These are expensive diagnostic oracles, not proposed faster optimizers.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: Features differed after angle and radius matching
text:
Features differed after angle and radius matching
For spurious training inputs and decay 0.1, the refreshed control recalibrated every eight steps. Averaging the two step sizes within each independent seed gave:

Positive polar-minus-comparator loss differences mean higher error for polar. The paired mean difference against angular gradient was \(0.012163\), with standard error \(0.003785\) across four seeds. Against affine response, it was \(-0.000010\), with standard error \(0.000453\).
The geometry-dependent observation survived matching angles and norms. The affine response control reproduced most of its held-out error and spurious-input sensitivity. This is evidence against treating the contrast as a phenomenon beyond the measured local response description in this setting.
The hidden rank was the entropy effective rank of the feature covariance. For eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) and \(p_j=\lambda_j/\sum_k\lambda_k\), it is
\[
r_{\rm eff}=\exp\left(-\sum_j p_j\log p_j\right).
\]
The polar-minus-angular-gradient rank difference was \(+0.0959\) with standard error \(0.1175\), and its sign varied across seeds. That does not support a robust extra-collapse prediction. A feature difference, a rank decrease, and a useful predictor are three distinct claims.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: Removing label noise did not remove the response explanation
text:
Removing label noise did not remove the response explanation
The final strict control used deterministic teacher labels, the smaller prescribed matrix angle 0.003, positive decay, and affine recalibration at every step. Polar and angular gradient shared their prescribed angles and radius profile.
