The paired polar-minus-gradient error difference was \(0.006329\pm0.002593\). The polar-minus-affine difference was \(0.000247\pm0.000407\), with signs differing across seeds. Here the plus-minus terms are one standard error, not confidence intervals or a proof of equivalence.



Paired seed comparisons show a consistent difference from angular gradient but much smaller differences from affine response in the two archived controls.


Fixed observational label noise was therefore unnecessary for the contrast with angular gradient. Minibatch noise remained. The clean-label control also changed the clock and recalibration protocol, so the difference between the two tables cannot isolate the effect of removing label noise alone.
The affine arm’s angular RMS was about 1.082 times the prescribed polar angle in the strict control. It was response matched rather than exactly angle matched. A separate normalized-affine control restored angles but retained response error. This limits any claim of exact simultaneous global affine-response and angular equivalence.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: Stale controls can manufacture a misleading gap
text:
Stale controls can manufacture a misleading gap
With 128 steps between calibrations, the batchwise local model’s independent-input MSE in the same spurious, positive-decay setting was about 0.18915, compared with 0.08083 for polar. Its midpoint median response error was about 28 percent over the main grid.
Recalibrating every eight steps reduced its error to 0.08242. The midpoint median response error still reached about 10.3 percent over that refreshed grid. A shorter interval helped, but did not certify uniform accuracy.
Thus a bad result from an outdated local approximation is not evidence that a valid response control fails. Conversely, close losses from an approximate control are not an exact equivalence theorem. The every-step affine experiment was added to probe this distinction directly.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: Keep the statistical unit visible
text:
Keep the statistical unit visible
The noisy-label summary averages step sizes within each seed before computing paired differences and standard errors. Four seeds remain four independent dataset and initialization draws. Repeated conditions and many continuation arms do not turn into additional independent datasets.
Likewise, the hidden features were not frozen: they moved from the common checkpoint, and linear probes and sensitivities changed. That fact establishes an ordinary learned-feature experiment. It does not establish that the specific two-feature collapse mechanism from Part 26 describes those changes.
The benchmark was small, synthetic, finite-horizon, and used exact polar evaluation without momentum. It does not establish an optimizer ranking on natural datasets, Transformers, practical finite polar routines, or the asymptotic time scale of a minimizer-manifold theorem.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: What changed in the research conclusion
text:
What changed in the research conclusion
The appropriate conclusion was to demote the proposed collapse mechanism as the main submission hypothesis. The constructed calculation still illustrates a valid possible bias. The network experiment still shows features can differ after angular matching. The stronger claim that these observations reveal a new useful effect beyond response and minibatch noise did not earn support.
A future proposal needs a prediction that distinguishes it from the strongest accurate controls, survives independently learned features, and improves a declared task outcome under fair tuning and compute comparisons. The present experiment helps specify that target by showing which explanations were insufficient.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: Try checking the control
text:
Try checking the control

Does matching matrix angle determine the expected update Jacobian?
Why is averaging all 12 batch derivatives different from regressing on their gradient noise?
What should happen before interpreting a large loss gap from a stale local approximation?
Why are eight step-size conditions in the refreshed setting still summarized with four independent seeds?



Answer sketches


No. Angle fixes a geometric step size, while response describes how the mean proposal changes with its input.
The derivative concerns a common perturbation of each input. A finite non-Gaussian regression need not recover that operator.
Measure its current response error and recalibrate or otherwise validate the approximation.
Two step sizes share each dataset and initialization draw. Average within those draws before reporting uncertainty across them.

title: Why matching the angle did not explain the features
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
The empirical values come from our archived untied LayerNorm-network study, including its refreshed, deterministic-label, and every-step response controls. This article recomputes selected aggregates and checks the displayed identities. It does not rerun the continuations or claim a new network result.
Muon Under Gradient Noise and the Limits of Orthogonalization Near Optima, Sections 4 through 6, motivates separating response from remaining fluctuations under its Gaussian and surrogate assumptions. Our finite-batch controls instead enumerate the actual gradient outcomes and evaluate the response directly.
Read Part 25 for why the Gaussian score formula is not a universal empirical regression rule, and Part 26 for the constructed model whose extrapolation this experiment tested.

title: How oscillations push back on sharpness
section: A third derivative links oscillation to curvature
text:
A third derivative links oscillation to curvature
At a reference point \(w\), let \(H=\nabla^2L(w)\) have a simple leading eigenvalue \(S\) with unit eigenvector \(u\). Write \(T=\nabla^3L(w)\), viewed as a symmetric trilinear form. Part 28’s eigenvalue derivative gives
\[
a:=\nabla S=T[u,u],
\]
where the vector on the right is defined by \(v^\top T[u,u]=T[v,u,u]\).
For a small displacement \(\delta\), Taylor expansion gives
\[
\nabla L(w+\delta)
=g+H\delta+\tfrac12T[\delta,\delta]
+O(\|\delta\|^3),
\]
provided a fourth-derivative bound controls the remainder locally. A displacement \(xu\) contributes the quadratic gradient term
\[
\tfrac12x^2a.
\]
Its descent contribution is \(-\eta x^2a/2\). The corresponding first-order change of sharpness is
\[
-\frac{\eta x^2}{2}\|a\|^2.
\]
It has the same sign for positive and negative \(x\). Alternating directions cancel in a mean displacement, but their squared amplitude can leave a persistent curvature-reducing effect.
This calculation isolates one term. For a general displacement \(xu+v\), there are also \(xT[u,v]\), \(T[v,v]/2\), moving-eigenvector effects, and Taylor errors. Dropping those terms needs a regime in which they are controlled.

title: How oscillations push back on sharpness
section: See both updates in one mixed monomial
text:
See both updates in one mixed monomial
Suppose, locally, the retained loss contains
\[
\frac{x^2}{\eta}+\frac b2yx^2-cy,
\qquad b,c>0.
\]
The mixed term gives \(bxy\) in the \(x\) gradient and \(bx^2/2\) in the \(y\) gradient. Thus
\[
x^+=-(1+\eta by)x,
\qquad
y^+=y+\eta c-\frac{\eta b}{2}x^2.
\]
Positive \(y\) makes the oscillation grow. The growing squared amplitude then opposes the upward drift of \(y\). Omitting either derivative of the mixed term destroys this feedback loop.
This is the explanatory structure developed in Self-Stabilization, Section 4. Its more general analysis tracks a moving reference and additional terms. Progressive sharpening enters as an assumption, rather than a consequence of the curvature-reduction calculation.

title: How oscillations push back on sharpness
section: An explicit loss with a restoring curvature coordinate
text:
An explicit loss with a restoring curvature coordinate
For our worked example, use
\[
L(x,y)=\tfrac12(a+by)x^2+\tfrac\gamma2(y-y_0)^2.
\]
Here \(x\) is the oscillating coordinate. The quadratic penalty pulls \(y\) toward \(y_0\), while \(y\) controls the curvature in \(x\). Choose
\[
\eta=1,\qquad a=b=1,\qquad\gamma=0.2,
\qquad y_0=1.1.
\]
Exact simultaneous gradient descent is
\[
x^+=(1-\eta(a+by))x,
\]
\[
y^+=(1-\eta\gamma)y+\eta\gamma y_0
-\frac{\eta b}{2}x^2.
\]
The coordinate curvature \(\kappa(y)=a+by\) reaches \(2/\eta\) at
\[
y_c=\frac{2/\eta-a}{b}=1.
\]
Without oscillations, the restoring term would move \(y\) toward 1.1 and the \(x\) curvature toward 2.1. With sufficiently large squared amplitude, the last term pushes \(y\) back.
This polynomial is a local model. It is not globally bounded below over all \((x,y)\), and the calculation does not claim global convergence from arbitrary starting points. We analyze a specified trajectory and a neighborhood of its cycle.

title: How oscillations push back on sharpness
section: Solve the two-cycle before simulating it
text:
Solve the two-cycle before simulating it
Seek a cycle \((A,y_c)\mapsto(-A,y_c)\mapsto(A,y_c)\). The \(x\) update flips sign exactly because \(a+by_c=2/\eta\).
The \(y\) update stays fixed when
\[
\gamma(y_0-y_c)=\frac b2A^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{A^2=\frac{2\gamma(y_0-y_c)}b=0.04,\qquad A=0.2.}
\]
The center is \((0,1)\), but neither cycle point equals the center. Both have loss
\[
L(\pm0.2,1)=0.041,
\]
while \(L(0,1)=0.001\). The additional loss is the cost of the persistent oscillation. A stable training trajectory need not converge to a stationary parameter vector.

title: How oscillations push back on sharpness
section: Check that the cycle attracts nearby points
text:
Check that the cycle attracts nearby points
Existence of a cycle alone does not establish stability. Let \(F\) be the one-step map. At \((A,y_c)\) its Jacobian is
\[
DF(A,y_c)=
\begin{pmatrix}
-1&-k\\
-k&1-h
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad k=\eta bA,\quad h=\eta\gamma.
\]
At \((-A,y_c)\), both off-diagonal signs reverse. Multiplying in trajectory order gives the two-step Jacobian
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
1-k^2&k(2-h)\\
-k(2-h)&(1-h)^2-k^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For \(k=h=0.2\),
\[
M=\begin{pmatrix}0.96&0.36\\-0.36&0.60\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its eigenvalues are \(0.78\pm0.311769i\), each of modulus 0.84. The cycle is locally attracting. A one-step Jacobian at only one cycle point would not be the relevant return map.
This is a mathematical property of the displayed example. It is not an application of a neural-network coupling theorem to unchecked assumptions.

title: How oscillations push back on sharpness
section: Follow the full recurrence
text:
Follow the full recurrence
Starting at \((x_0,y_{\mathrm{init}})=(0.001,0.4)\), evaluate 400 simultaneous updates in float64. The small oscillation initially shrinks. The restoring force raises \(y\), the multiplier crosses its threshold, and the oscillation grows until its squared amplitude regulates \(y\) near one.



An exact two-variable gradient-descent recurrence approaches a locally attracting two-cycle, with squared oscillation amplitude opposing the force that increases curvature.


By update 400, the trajectory is numerically at the predicted cycle. This is a cheap evaluation of an explicit polynomial, with no neural-network training, data fitting, or random noise.
The initial loss is about 0.0490. It falls close to zero before the instability becomes visible, rises as the oscillation develops, and approaches 0.041. The curve illustrates why a short loss window and eventual bounded motion are different diagnostics.

title: How oscillations push back on sharpness
section: The full sharpness is not exactly the coordinate curvature
text:
The full sharpness is not exactly the coordinate curvature
The Hessian is
\[
H(x,y)=
\begin{pmatrix}
a+by&bx\\bx&\gamma
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
At the cycle center it has eigenvalues two and 0.2. At either actual cycle point, its largest eigenvalue is
\[
S_{\mathrm{cycle}}
=\frac{2+0.2+\sqrt{(2-0.2)^2+4(0.2)^2}}2
\approx2.021954.
\]
So the full instantaneous sharpness remains slightly above \(2/\eta\), even though the two-step orbit attracts. There is no contradiction: the two changing one-step maps have a stable product. The frozen-quadratic calculation does not describe that product.
Calling \(a+by\) the full sharpness away from \(x=0\) would erase this distinction. For smaller cycle amplitudes, the difference is quadratic in amplitude when the center eigengap stays positive, but it is visible at the finite values used here.

title: How oscillations push back on sharpness
section: A perturbation and an averaging window both matter
text:
A perturbation and an averaging window both matter
If \(x_0=0\) exactly, the recurrence preserves \(x=0\). Then \(y\) approaches 1.1 without any oscillation-induced correction. The resulting fixed point is transversely unstable, but exact arithmetic does not invent a displacement.
A tiny nonzero initial \(x\) can take many steps to regrow after an initial contraction. The onset delay depends on that amplitude. A model that immediately imposes the eventual equilibrium variance will miss this transient, even if it predicts the final cycle center correctly.
Likewise, averaging two adjacent iterates cancels an exact two-cycle. It need not eliminate a changing envelope, curvature-coordinate drift, or a burst. A smooth curve should identify what was averaged and over which time window.

title: How oscillations push back on sharpness
section: What the general theory does and does not give
text:
What the general theory does and does not give
Self-Stabilization’s Theorem 1 is a finite-horizon local coupling to a constrained reference plus a predicted oscillatory displacement. Its hypotheses include an eigengap, positive sharpening alignment, controlled higher derivatives and transverse terms, a small error parameter, and a nonvanishing oscillatory component over the stated horizon. It is not global convergence or a proof that every loss progressively sharpens.
Our example verifies a local cycle directly. The paper supplies a broader conditional analysis. Both support keeping the feedback term. Neither establishes that a larger learning rate always improves generalization or that stochastic momentum training has the same reduced dynamics.
The next post asks what survives after the fast phase is removed: a covariance that still contributes to the center’s motion.

title: How oscillations push back on sharpness
section: Try following the feedback
text:
Try following the feedback

Why does the curvature-reducing term survive a sign flip of \(x\)?
What return map checks local stability of the displayed cycle?
Is the full Hessian’s largest eigenvalue exactly two at the actual cycle points?
Why does the initial state \(x_0=0\) need separate treatment?



Answer sketches


It depends on \(x^2\).
The product of the two one-step Jacobians, in trajectory order.
No. It is about 2.021954 because the off-diagonal Hessian entries are nonzero.
That coordinate remains zero exactly, so the instability is never excited.

section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Self-Stabilization: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability, Lemma 2, Sections 4 and 5.3, and Section 8.3, gives the cubic feedback, conditional coupling, and unresolved sharpening question. The polynomial, cycle, return-map calculation, and figure here are independent worked examples. They do not reproduce its experiments or certify all of its assumptions.
Part 28 derives the frozen boundary. Part 30 retains the effect of the oscillations through their covariance.

title: Averaging the steps without losing their effect
section: Define the average before replacing it with a flow
text:
Define the average before replacing it with a flow
For saved iterates \(w_t\), one concrete offline average is
\[
c_t=\sum_{j=-m}^{m}a_jw_{t+j},
\qquad a_j\ge0,
\qquad\sum_ja_j=1.
\]
Freeze this center within the window and write \(\delta_{t,j}=w_{t+j}-c_t\). Then \(\sum_ja_j\delta_{t,j}=0\) exactly, and
\[
\Sigma_t=\sum_ja_j\delta_{t,j}\delta_{t,j}^\top\succeq0.
\]
This describes a particular filter applied to an existing trajectory. It uses future observations when the window is centered. A flow predicted from the objective is a different object.
To connect them, we would need enough averaging to suppress oscillation, little center drift over that window, controlled derivative variation, and a justified replacement of smoothed finite differences by derivatives. At the birth of an oscillation or during a large spike, those requirements can fail.
A moving average is also not generally idempotent. Subtracting a changing smoothed trajectory does not automatically give a residual whose moving average is exactly zero. The frozen-window construction makes clear which elementary centering identity is exact.

title: Averaging the steps without losing their effect
section: Average gradients, rather than differentiating the average loss blindly
text:
Average gradients, rather than differentiating the average loss blindly
At a frozen center \(c\), let \(g=\nabla L(c)\), \(H=\nabla^2L(c)\), and define
\[
\mathcal T[v]=DH(c)[v].
\]
Its adjoint maps a symmetric matrix \(X\) to a vector, with
\[
\langle v,\mathcal T^*[X]\rangle
=\langle\mathcal T[v],X\rangle_F.
\]
Averaging the gradient Taylor expansion for centered \(\delta\) gives
\[
\mathbb E_{\rm time}\nabla L(c+\delta)
=g+\tfrac12\mathcal T^*[\Sigma]
+\mathbb E_{\rm time}r(\delta).
\]
With a bounded fourth derivative, \(\|r(\delta)\|\le C\|\delta\|^3\) locally. Small average remainder, rather than visual smoothness of the plotted center, is the relevant requirement.
On optimizer-step time \(t\), the resulting model is
\[
\boxed{\dot c=-\eta\left(g+\tfrac12\mathcal T^*[\Sigma]\right).}
\]
Equivalently, the correction is \(\nabla_c\langle H(c),\Sigma\rangle_F/2\) with \(\Sigma\) held fixed during that derivative. Differentiating a state-dependent fitted \(\Sigma(c)\) inside this expression adds terms that were not present in the averaged gradient calculation.
This is the deterministic time-averaging construction in Understanding Optimization in Deep Learning with Central Flows, Section 3 and Appendix A. The discrete-to-flow connection is heuristic and numerically supported, rather than a proved approximation theorem with a general error bound.

title: Averaging the steps without losing their effect
section: Let marginal stability determine one variance
text:
Let marginal stability determine one variance
Suppose the center has one simple critical eigenpair,
\[
Hu=Su,\qquad S=2/\eta,\qquad\|u\|=1.
\]
Model the covariance as \(\Sigma=q uu^\top\), where \(q\ge0\). Let \(a=\nabla S=\mathcal T^*[uu^\top]\). Then
\[
\dot c=-\eta(g+qa/2),
\]
\[
\dot S=\eta\left(r-\frac q2\|a\|^2\right),
\qquad r=\langle a,-g\rangle.
\]
If free descent pushes outward, \(r>0\), remaining on the stability boundary requires
\[
q=\frac{2r}{\|a\|^2}.
\]
If \(r\le0\), zero variance is enough and the center can move inward. A negative variance is never an admissible way to enforce equality. Thus, for \(a\ne0\), the boundary rule is
\[
q=\left[\frac{2r}{\|a\|^2}\right]_+.
\]
In the strict stable interior, the model sets \(q=0\). At \(a=0\), this formula is undefined and a higher-order or degenerate analysis is needed. It does not determine onset phase or the time required for a tiny displacement to grow.

title: Averaging the steps without losing their effect
section: Recover the cycle balance from Part 29
text:
Recover the cycle balance from Part 29
At the center \((0,1)\) of that example,
\[
H=\operatorname{Diag}(2,0.2),\qquad
u=(1,0),\qquad a=(0,1),\qquad g=(0,-0.02).
\]
Hence \(r=0.02\) and \(q=0.04\). This equals the squared cycle amplitude derived directly from the recurrence. No measured trajectory amplitude was fitted to get the prediction.
For centers \((0,y)\) below \(y_c=1\), ordinary gradient flow gives
\[
\frac{dy}{d\tau}=0.2(1.1-y),
\qquad \tau=\eta t.
\]
The constrained center follows that flow until it reaches one, then stays there. Starting from \(y(0)=0.4\),
\[
y_{\rm central}(\tau)
=\min\{1,\ 1.1-0.7e^{-0.2\tau}\}.
\]
The contact time is \(\tau_c=5\log7\approx9.72955\). Ordinary gradient flow instead approaches 1.1. Both flow curves start at the axis center \((0,0.4)\). The discrete comparison retains Part 29’s nonzero initial \(x=0.001\), so it can develop the oscillation that the center model replaces by a variance.



The constrained center captures the long-time cycle center but does not capture the delayed growth of oscillation amplitude. At equilibrium the raw loss includes a fluctuation contribution absent from the center loss.


The figure deliberately retains the transient mismatch. The pair average removes the two-step carrier, not its evolving envelope. Agreement of the eventual center and variance does not make the displayed flow an exact description of the entire recurrence.

title: Averaging the steps without losing their effect
section: The center loss and average raw loss are different observables
text:
The center loss and average raw loss are different observables
The loss Taylor expansion gives
\[
\mathbb E_{\rm time}L(c+\delta)
\approx L(c)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(H\Sigma).
\]
If covariance is supported on GD-critical directions, \(H\Sigma=(2/\eta)\Sigma\), so
\[
\overline L\approx L(c)+\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma}{\eta}.
\]
For the explicit cycle, this is exact: \(0.001+0.04=0.041\). Comparing a center-loss curve directly with smoothed raw losses would therefore create a discrepancy even at the perfectly balanced cycle.
Likewise, a decreasing center loss does not imply decreasing fluctuation variance. The average raw loss can rise while the center continues to descend. A useful prediction needs both components.

title: Averaging the steps without losing their effect
section: More than one critical mode needs a matrix condition
text:
More than one critical mode needs a matrix condition
Let
\[
A_s=\frac2\eta I-H(c)\succeq0.
\]
The model requires \(\Sigma\succeq0\) and \(\langle A_s,\Sigma\rangle_F=0\). For positive semidefinite matrices this implies \(A_s\Sigma=0\), so the covariance lies in the critical subspace.
These static conditions do not fix its magnitude. Zero covariance satisfies them even when free descent points out of the stable region. We also need future feasibility.
With \(U\) an orthonormal critical basis, write \(\Sigma=UXU^\top\). Differentiating the slack along the proposed flow gives
\[
\dot A_s
=\eta\mathcal T[g]
+\frac\eta2\mathcal T\mathcal T^*[UXU^\top].
\]
At a regular contact, the critical block must obey a complementarity condition
\[
X\succeq0,\qquad
Y:=U^\top\left(\mathcal T[g]
+\tfrac12\mathcal T\mathcal T^*[UXU^\top]\right)U\succeq0,
\qquad\langle X,Y\rangle_F=0.
\]
Off-diagonal entries of \(X\) can matter. Rotating a repeated-eigenvalue basis changes those entries while preserving the ambient covariance. Solving unrelated scalar balances in an arbitrary basis need not preserve that geometry.
Positive definiteness of the associated operator gives a unique covariance solution. Mere positive semidefiniteness does not. Degenerate feedback can leave the covariance ambiguous or make the balance infeasible, so existence and uniqueness require hypotheses.

title: Averaging the steps without losing their effect
section: The projection interpretation gives a precise conditional statement
text:
The projection interpretation gives a precise conditional statement
At a regular stable center, the feasible velocity cone is
\[
C_c=\{v:U^\top\mathcal T[v]U\preceq0\}.
\]
Under the conditions identifying this linearized cone with the actual tangent cone, the GD central velocity is
\[
\dot c=\eta\Pi_{C_c}(-g).
\]
Let \(p=\Pi_{C_c}(-g)\). Projection onto a closed convex cone gives \(g^\top p=-\|p\|^2\), hence
\[
\frac{d}{dt}L(c(t))=-\eta\|p\|^2\le0.
\]
This is a property of the defined constrained flow. The stable region itself need not be globally convex. Neither the projection identity nor monotone center loss proves that arbitrary discrete GD tracks the flow.

title: Averaging the steps without losing their effect
section: This covariance is not the noise from Part 25
text:
This covariance is not the noise from Part 25
Here \(\Sigma\) has units of squared parameter displacement and can arise in deterministic full-batch training. Part 25’s gradient-noise covariance has squared gradient units. They are not interchangeable inputs to the same formula.
Stochastic gradients can contribute to displacement fluctuations, but deriving their covariance needs a dynamical calculation. Momentum adds temporal state. Adaptive methods add preconditioning history and change the effective stability geometry. None follows by inserting an SGD noise matrix into the deterministic closure unchanged.
The central-flows paper studies deterministic GD and RMSProp variants. Its limitations include costly numerical evaluation, reduced accuracy around large excursions and nonsmooth architectures, and the absence of a stochastic or momentum extension. Its predictive success remains distinct from a uniform approximation guarantee.

title: Averaging the steps without losing their effect
section: Try reading the averaged state
text:
Try reading the averaged state

Why does averaging away the sign of an oscillation leave a gradient correction?
At the boundary, should an inward free drift be balanced by negative variance?
Why can the center loss differ from average raw loss?
Do stability support conditions alone determine the covariance magnitude?



Answer sketches


The quadratic displacement term survives and contracts the loss’s third derivative with the covariance.
No. Zero variance is admissible and lets the center move inward.
The raw trajectory carries a quadratic fluctuation loss, approximately \(\operatorname{tr}\Sigma/\eta\) on critical directions.
No. Future feasibility and a nondegenerate response are needed to close the balance.

section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Understanding Optimization in Deep Learning with Central Flows, Section 3, Appendix A.1.5, Appendix A.2, and Section 8, develops the averaging, complementarity, projection, and scope qualifications. The two-variable evaluation here is an independent illustration, including its onset mismatch. It is not a reproduction of the paper’s neural-network comparisons.
Part 29 supplies the exact cycle. Part 25 supplies the separate Gaussian gradient-response calculation whose covariance has a different meaning.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: Hold the input fixed and look at the output
text:
Hold the input fixed and look at the output
Let \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(y=Wx\). Change the weights by a matrix \(\Delta W\), keeping the input fixed. The activation change is
\[
\Delta y=(W+\Delta W)x-Wx=\Delta W x.
\]
This is exact. There is no neglected higher-order term because the layer is linear in \(W\) at a fixed \(x\).
Suppose we measure input and output size with norms \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_X\) and \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_Y\). The induced operator norm is
\[
N_{X\to Y}(\Delta W)
=\sup_{x\ne0}\frac{\lVert\Delta W x\rVert_Y}{\lVert x\rVert_X}.
\]
It gives the bound
\[
\lVert\Delta y\rVert_Y
\leq N_{X\to Y}(\Delta W)\lVert x\rVert_X.
\]
If inputs have norm at most one, the matrix norm is a worst-case activation-change budget. The choices of input and output norms specify what that promise means.
This is the starting point of Bernstein and Newhouse’s treatment of layer geometry, especially Sections 3.3 and 4.1. The semantics of the layer determine which operator norm is worth considering.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: Equal Frobenius size can hide different worst cases
text:
Equal Frobenius size can hide different worst cases
With Euclidean norms on both activation spaces, the induced norm is the spectral norm:
\[
N_{2\to2}(\Delta W)=\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
=\sigma_{\max}(\Delta W).
\]
Compare two perturbations in two dimensions:
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both have Frobenius norm one. But \(A\) can move the output by one on a unit input, while \(B\) moves every unit input by \(1/\sqrt2\). Thus
\[
\lVert A\rVert_F=\lVert B\rVert_F=1,
\qquad
\lVert A\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=1,
\qquad
\lVert B\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}=1/\sqrt2.
\]



Images of the Euclidean unit input circle under two perturbations with Frobenius norm one. A maps the circle to a line segment reaching radius one. B maps it to a circle of radius one over square root two.


The distinction grows with width. In \(n\) dimensions, a rank-one matrix with its only nonzero singular value equal to one has the same Frobenius norm as \(I/\sqrt n\). Their operator norms are one and \(1/\sqrt n\).
Frobenius size adds energy across singular directions. Spectral size asks for the largest response in any one direction. Neither description is meaningless. They answer different questions.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: An average asks a different question again
text:
An average asks a different question again
Suppose \(x\) is uniformly distributed on the Euclidean unit sphere in \(\mathbb R^n\). Then \(\mathbb E[xx^\top]=I/n\), and
\[
\mathbb E\lVert\Delta W x\rVert_2^2
=\frac1n\operatorname{tr}(\Delta W^\top\Delta W)
=\frac1n\lVert\Delta W\rVert_F^2.
\]
For our two-dimensional \(A\) and \(B\), this mean squared activation change is \(1/2\) in both cases. Their worst cases differ, but this particular average agrees.
More generally, if \(C=\mathbb E[xx^\top]\) is the input second-moment matrix,
\[
\mathbb E\lVert\Delta W x\rVert_2^2
=\operatorname{tr}(\Delta W C\Delta W^\top).
\]
This formula uses the second moment, not necessarily the covariance. They agree when the input mean is zero.
A weight perturbation can be large on a direction the data rarely uses. Conversely, a modest-looking change can align with a frequently amplified feature. The uniform-sphere calculation does not establish what is typical under an arbitrary training distribution.
Before debating which matrix norm is best, decide whether the goal is a worst-case guarantee, a distributional average, or another functional quantity. The matrix entries alone do not make that choice for us.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: RMS measurements introduce an explicit width factor
text:
RMS measurements introduce an explicit width factor
For a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), define
\[
\lVert x\rVert_{\mathrm{RMS}}=\frac{\lVert x\rVert_2}{\sqrt n}.
\]
This measures a typical coordinate scale. A vector with all coordinates equal to one has RMS norm one at every width, while its Euclidean norm grows as \(\sqrt n\).
Use RMS norms on the input and output of \(y=Wx\). Substituting their definitions into the operator norm gives
\[
N_{\mathrm{RMS}\to\mathrm{RMS}}(\Delta W)
=\sqrt{\frac n m}\,\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}.
\]
The factor is \(\sqrt{n/m}\), with input width in the numerator. A budget \(N(\Delta W)\leq\epsilon\) therefore allows
\[
\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
\leq\epsilon\sqrt{\frac m n}.
\]
For a map from four inputs to sixteen outputs, a perturbation with spectral norm one has RMS-to-RMS norm \(1/2\). For a map from sixteen inputs to four outputs, the same spectral norm corresponds to RMS-to-RMS norm two. The worst-case RMS responses differ by a factor of four.
These are choices of measurement for the same forward expression \(y=Wx\). RMS is a ruler here, not an extra RMSNorm operation inserted into the network. Conventions that rescale the forward function itself can move width factors elsewhere, so the forward equation and the norm must be read together.
This width factor will reappear in the next post’s update direction. It comes from the activation geometry before we choose an optimizer.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: A lookup table has different input semantics
text:
A lookup table has different input semantics
A dense layer may receive mixtures of input coordinates. An embedding lookup receives a one-hot vector \(e_j\), and its output is simply column \(j\) of the embedding matrix \(E\).
If we want every lookup to have a bounded Euclidean output change, the relevant quantity is
\[
\max_j\lVert\Delta E[:,j]\rVert_2.
\]
This is also the induced \(\ell_1\)-to-Euclidean norm. Indeed,
\[
\lVert\Delta E x\rVert_2
\leq\sum_j |x_j|\lVert\Delta E[:,j]\rVert_2
\leq\lVert x\rVert_1\max_j\lVert\Delta E[:,j]\rVert_2.
\]
Equality is attained by choosing a one-hot input for a largest column. With an RMS output ruler, divide the column lengths by \(\sqrt m\).
The same matrix can look different under the dense-layer question. Take
\[
\Delta E=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Each lookup changes the Euclidean output by one. But the Euclidean unit input \((1,1)/\sqrt2\) combines the columns and produces an output of length \(\sqrt2\). The spectral norm sees that mixture, while the lookup budget need not.
The distinction is what the input can be. Matrix shape does not tell us whether the module is a dense transformation or a categorical lookup. Bernstein and Newhouse make this explicit in their Linear and Embed examples in Section 4.1.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: Let the input move and a second term appears
text:
Let the input move and a second term appears
So far, we have held \(x\) fixed. If upstream parameters also change the input by \(\Delta x\), then
\[
(W+\Delta W)(x+\Delta x)-Wx
=\Delta W x+W\Delta x+\Delta W\Delta x.
\]
The first two terms form the differential. The final term is a finite-step interaction. For Euclidean measurements, for example,
\[
\lVert\Delta y\rVert_2
\leq\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lVert x\rVert_2
+\lVert W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lVert\Delta x\rVert_2
+\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lVert\Delta x\rVert_2.
\]
A local weight-update budget controls the first contribution. It does not erase input sensitivity or the interaction term. Shared normalization gains from Part 2 also belong in the joint perturbation when they move.
This is why a layerwise measurement is a starting point for network geometry. Composing modules requires accounting for how one module’s output perturbation becomes another’s input perturbation. We will reach that question in Part 7.
For now, the layer’s role gives us a constraint set for its update. The next question is how to choose a direction within that set to reduce the loss.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: Try changing the ruler
text:
Try changing the ruler

In four dimensions, compare the Frobenius and operator norms of \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,0,0,0)\) and \(B=I/2\). What is their common mean squared response on uniformly distributed unit inputs?
For a layer with nine input and four output coordinates, what spectral update budget gives an RMS-to-RMS budget of \(0.1\)?
For the two-column lookup example above, compare the largest column’s RMS change with the RMS-to-RMS operator norm of the same matrix.



Answer sketches


Both Frobenius norms are one. The operator norms are one and \(1/2\). The common mean squared response is \(1/4\).
\(\lVert\Delta W\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\leq0.1\sqrt{4/9}=1/15\approx0.066667\).
The largest column RMS is \(1/\sqrt2\). Since input and output dimensions are both two, the RMS-to-RMS norm equals the spectral norm, \(\sqrt2\). Their input unit sets differ, so this is not a contradiction.

title: What counts as a small layer change?
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Jeremy Bernstein and Laker Newhouse, Modular Duality in Deep Learning (ICML 2025), Definition 3, Examples 3 and 4, and Section 4.1, derives the dense and embedding operator norms used here. Its Linear module uses the forward convention \(y=Wx\), matching this post.
Tim Large and collaborators, Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm (NeurIPS 2024), Section 3 and Appendix B, develops the module-level bounds that let local measurements compose. Its appendix also illustrates why forward scaling conventions matter when comparing norm formulas. The examples in this post are direct calculations about activation perturbations, not evidence that a particular layer budget yields more useful features.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: Begin with a bound on the computation
text:
Begin with a bound on the computation
Suppose local perturbation analysis gives
\[
\lVert\delta f\rVert_Y\leq\sum_{i=1}^k c_i N_i(\delta W_i),
\]
where \(N_i\) measures a module’s weight perturbation and each \(c_i>0\) accounts for its downstream sensitivity. This is a bound on the differential at the point under discussion. A finite-step bound needs the corresponding remainder control.
For a composition \(f_2\circ f_1\), for example, a sensitivity bound \(s_2\) for the second module leads to contributions of the form
\[
\lVert\delta f\rVert_Y\leq s_2N_1(\delta W_1)+N_2(\delta W_2),
\]
assuming the module norms and input domain make those local bounds valid. The earlier module pays for amplification through the later one.
We now want a single norm on the whole update tuple. Choose positive masses \(m_i\) summing to one, and set
\[
N_{\max}(\delta W)=\max_i\frac{c_iN_i(\delta W_i)}{m_i}.
\]
If \(N_{\max}(\delta W)\leq\epsilon\), then \(c_iN_i(\delta W_i)\leq m_i\epsilon\) for each module. Adding these inequalities proves
\[
\lVert\delta f\rVert_Y\leq\epsilon.
\]
Mass is a share of this bound. It is not a claim that each layer will learn equally useful features, or that the assigned share is always fully used by the true output change.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: The maximum creates a product of local balls
text:
The maximum creates a product of local balls
The global unit ball is exactly
\[
\{\delta W:N_{\max}(\delta W)\leq1\}
=\prod_i\{\delta W_i:N_i(\delta W_i)\leq m_i/c_i\}.
\]
The constraints are independent once their radii are chosen. One layer does not consume another’s radius simply by taking a nonzero step. That product structure is the key geometric property.
Let \(G_i\) be the loss differential for block \(i\), represented through its usual coordinate pairing. Maximizing the global linear functional separates into one support problem per block:
\[
N_{\max}^*(G)=\sum_i\frac{m_i}{c_i}N_i^*(G_i).
\]
If \(D_i\) is a unit-ball support maximizer for \(G_i\), one globally steepest fixed-radius descent update is
\[
\delta W_i=-\epsilon\frac{m_i}{c_i}D_i.
\]
Every block with nonzero gradient can saturate its assigned local radius at once. Zero gradients and ties permit nonunique choices. Choosing zero on an inactive block is convenient.
This is parallel budget use, not a guarantee that all blocks make comparable progress. Sensitivity and gradient geometry still differ.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: A two-module calculation
text:
A two-module calculation
Take two scalar blocks with \(c=(2,1)\), masses \(m=(1/4,3/4)\), and gradient coordinates \(G=(6,1)\). The global norm is
\[
N_{\max}(d)=\max(8|d_1|,\,4|d_2|/3).
\]
The positive support maximizer is \(d=(1/8,3/4)\). It has
\[
G^\top d=6/8+3/4=3/2,
\qquad 2|d_1|+|d_2|=1.
\]
The actual descent update is \(-\epsilon d\). The first block receives a smaller parameter displacement because its output effect is amplified by a factor of two and its mass is smaller.
There is no missing global rescaling to divide the remaining budget between these two directions. The maximum already allocated both radii.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: A sum asks the optimizer to make a different allocation
text:
A sum asks the optimizer to make a different allocation
The functional bound also suggests the valid norm
\[
N_{\mathrm{sum}}(d)=\sum_i c_iN_i(d_i).
\]
Its dual norm is
\[
N_{\mathrm{sum}}^*(G)=\max_i\frac{N_i^*(G_i)}{c_i}.
\]
With a unique largest ratio, a support maximizer can spend the entire budget on that block. In our example, the ratios are three and one. The sum-budget maximizer is \((1/2,0)\), with support value three.
A weighted quadratic aggregation gives an intermediate geometry:
\[
N_2(d)=\left[\sum_i m_i
\left(\frac{c_iN_i(d_i)}{m_i}\right)^2\right]^{1/2},
\]
\[
N_2^*(G)=\left[\sum_i m_i
\left(\frac{N_i^*(G_i)}{c_i}\right)^2\right]^{1/2}.
\]
Here its support value is \(\sqrt3\), attained at approximately \((0.216506,0.433013)\). The three norms control the same stated linearized feature bound, but their feasible sets and allocations differ.



Three ways to allocate the two-module budget. A weighted maximum gives a rectangle, a quadratic aggregation an ellipse, and a weighted sum a diamond. Their support maximizers for the same gradient occur at different points.


The larger support value of the sum budget is not an optimization victory over the maximum. Its unit ball is larger here. The question is which allocation describes the changes we want to permit.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: What recursive modular geometry adds
text:
What recursive modular geometry adds
In a network, the coefficients are not a list of independent tuning constants pasted onto unrelated layers. Composition propagates input sensitivity through downstream modules. Concatenation combines outputs under a specified output-space norm. The module tree determines how those rules are applied.
Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm develops this recursive construction. Modular Duality then derives the corresponding support directions. The distinction parallels Part 6: normalizing a proposal in a norm and solving the norm’s support problem are different operations.
Our simple product-ball derivation explains one important property of the weighted maximum. It does not by itself establish all the curvature bounds or learning-rate transfer results of the modular framework. Those require the papers’ module assumptions and composition arguments.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: Where the choice still needs judgment
text:
Where the choice still needs judgment
The norm depends on the chosen module boundary. If a gain and several matrices jointly determine an effective map, treating each matrix as an independent atom may leave out part of the perturbation. A different outer aggregation cannot repair that missing dependency.
Masses also encode priorities. They can reserve more possible feature motion for one part of the computation, but a bound on motion is not a bound on its usefulness. Task progress still depends on gradients, data, and nonlinear interactions.
The maximum earns its place because it gives explicit local radii and parallel support problems. It is a design with consequences, not a uniqueness theorem. Changing it is mathematically possible. A useful alternative needs a reason for its different allocation.
Next we add a distinct kind of restriction: the weights themselves may have to remain on a constraint set. That restriction changes which directions are admissible even before we choose their size.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: Try allocating the budget
text:
Try allocating the budget

In the two-module example, verify that the maximum-budget support direction obeys the unit feature bound.
Keep \(c=(2,1)\) but use equal masses. What local radii and support value does the maximum give for \(G=(6,1)\)?
Why does the sum budget admit an optimizer that changes only the first block in the original example?



Answer sketches


\(2(1/8)+3/4=1\), while the gradient pairing is \(3/2\).
The radii are \(1/4\) and \(1/2\). The support value is \(6/4+1/2=2\).
Its dual compares \(6/2=3\) with \(1/1=1\). The first block offers more linear decrease per unit of that sum budget, so \((1/2,0)\) is a support maximizer.

title: How Modula combines layer budgets
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Tim Large and collaborators, Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm (2024), Sections 2.2 and 3, defines the modular norm and its composition rules while acknowledging other aggregations.
Jeremy Bernstein and Laker Newhouse, Modular Duality in Deep Learning (ICML 2025), Sections 3.4 and 4.2, connects recursive modular norms to dualization. The scalar example and alternative-ball calculations above are direct support calculations under explicitly stated coefficients.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: Write down the wrapper exactly
text:
Write down the wrapper exactly
The Hyperball paper defines a Frobenius normalization \(\operatorname{Normalize}(X)=X/\lVert X\rVert_F\) and a fixed radius \(R>0\). Given a nonzero base proposal \(u_t\) and step parameter \(\eta_t\geq0\), its update is
\[
W_{t+1}=R\operatorname{Normalize}
\left(W_t-\eta_tR\operatorname{Normalize}(u_t)\right).
\]
The matrix starts on the radius-\(R\) sphere. The trial displacement has Frobenius length \(\eta_tR\). The return map restores the weight norm to \(R\).
The final chord \(W_{t+1}-W_t\) need not have length \(\eta_tR\). This difference is visible even before considering what base optimizer produced \(u_t\).
The normalization requires nonzero arguments. A zero proposal needs a defined no-step convention. A zero trial point also needs an implementation guard rather than division by its norm.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: Two fixed norms leave one angle unfixed
text:
Two fixed norms leave one angle unfixed
Write \(E=W/R\) and \(U=u/\lVert u\rVert_F\), so both have Frobenius norm one. Let
\[
\rho=\langle E,U\rangle_F,
\qquad U_T=U-\rho E,
\qquad\lVert U_T\rVert_F=\sqrt{1-\rho^2}.
\]
The trial direction is
\[
E-\eta U=(1-\eta\rho)E-\eta U_T.
\]
Radial renormalization preserves that direction. For a nonzero trial point, the actual rotation is therefore
\[
\theta=\operatorname{atan2}
\left(\eta\sqrt{1-\rho^2},\,1-\eta\rho\right).
\]
When \(\rho=0\), this reduces to \(\theta=\arctan\eta\). Otherwise, the same value of \(\eta\) can give a different angle. For \(\eta=1/2\), the tangent proposal gives approximately \(26.57^\circ\), while \(\rho=-0.8\) gives approximately \(12.09^\circ\).
The final chord length is
\[
\lVert W_{t+1}-W_t\rVert_F=2R\sin(\theta/2).
\]
If \(U=E\) and \(0<\eta<1\), the trial point shrinks along the radius and renormalization returns exactly to the starting weight. There was a nonzero proposal budget and no final motion.



For a fixed normalized proposal length of one half of the weight radius, the actual rotation varies with the weight-proposal correlation. The tangent case is about 26.57 degrees, while a correlation of minus 0.8 gives about 12.09 degrees.


Fixed norms make the geometry more explicit. They do not make the remaining variable disappear. This is controlled length, not automatically a fixed angular step.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: A one-step schedule match we can derive exactly
text:
A one-step schedule match we can derive exactly
Compare a free-radius update at \(w=R_tE\):
\[
w^+=aR_tE-\alpha U,\qquad a>0.
\]
If the unit proposal \(U\) is the same in both comparisons, choosing
\[
\alpha=aR_t\eta
\]
gives \(w^+=aR_t(E-\eta U)\). The free-radius update and the Hyperball update have exactly the same next direction. Their radii differ.
This equality holds for radial as well as tangent proposals. It is a conditional one-step identity: we assumed the same current direction and the same normalized proposal. Those conditions do not automatically persist when optimizer states, scale-sensitive parameters, or data-dependent proposal directions evolve differently.
Part 3 gave a whole-trajectory equivalence under its own assumptions. Part 4 showed why optimizer memory must also transform. A schedule intervention in a real matrix optimizer should not silently inherit either theorem.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: What the two papers establish
text:
What the two papers establish
Hyperball Optimization studies the fixed-radius wrapper with base optimizers and reports benefits in its pretraining comparisons. Its Section 4 separates an expressivity argument from a model of radius and angular dynamics. The stationary analysis assumes an infinite optimizer history and iid isotropic Gaussian optimizer inputs. Its angular interpretation uses an ansatz, rather than a pathwise theorem for every training run.
Hyperball May Not Be a Free Lunch explicitly includes the parameter-proposal angle and tests schedule interventions. In its tested settings, aligning angular effective steps reproduces a substantial part of the validation-loss behavior. That result motivates a control, not a universal equality of all optimizer trajectories.
The productive question is whether a claimed benefit survives comparisons that account for the induced schedule. Simply giving both methods the same nominal learning rate does not answer it.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: Separate the interventions before comparing them
text:
Separate the interventions before comparing them
For a useful experiment, distinguish the base proposal rule, weight-radius constraint, proposal normalization, and external schedule. Changing all four at once makes the source of an improvement ambiguous.
Start with a common base optimizer and a fully specified state initialization. Compare decay and fixed-radius versions under their tuned schedules. Measure the true angle, proposal-weight correlation, radius, effective map change, and final task loss. A matched-angle control is useful even if it does not reproduce every feature of the trajectory.
If one method needs extra matrix operations, report that work. If a correction depends on a reference run’s recorded angles, identify the reference information it uses. An intervention that diagnoses a mechanism is not automatically a deployable tuning rule.
Completed-budget outcomes matter. A method can look slower early because its effective step remains large, then behave differently during decay. An early curve alone is an incomplete comparison.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: The forward function remains a separate question
text:
The forward function remains a separate question
The geometric derivation above works for any matrix proposal. Interpreting its radius as redundant requires a statement about the forward function.
A normalization gain can compensate one matrix’s scale through a joint transformation. That is not the same as independently scaling that matrix with every other parameter fixed. If a gain is shared, compensating it changes every consuming branch. We will examine that compatibility explicitly in Part 11.
Fixed-norm optimization and learned forward scales are therefore not inherently opposed. A method can constrain a directional matrix while another parameter controls a meaningful amplitude. The next post asks which of those amplitudes should remain available.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: Try holding the norms fixed
text:
Try holding the norms fixed

For a unit weight, a tangent unit proposal, and \(\eta=1/2\), compare the trial displacement length with the final chord length.
What is the rotation when \(U=E\) and \(\eta=1/2\)?
A free-radius update has \(R_t=3\), shrinkage \(a=0.9\), and the same normalized proposal as Hyperball with \(\eta=0.2\). Which proposal length \(\alpha\) matches its next direction?



Answer sketches


The trial length is \(0.5\). The angle is \(\arctan(0.5)\) and the chord is approximately \(0.459506\).
Zero. The trial point is \(E/2\), which renormalizes back to \(E\).
\(\alpha=aR_t\eta=0.54\). This matches one direction under the stated common-proposal assumption.

title: Fixed norms and the schedule question
section: Yo twin, go read…
text:
Yo twin, go read…
Kaiyue Wen and collaborators, Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them II: Hyperball Optimization, inspected v2, Section 2 and Sections 4.1 and 4.2, gives the wrapper and distinguishes its expressivity and stationary-model arguments.

title: Free probability
text:
Writing

Free probability


In process of rewriting…

These are working drafts, not finished posts.



Knowing the eigenvalues of two matrices does not determine the eigenvalues of their sum or product.


This series studies what happens when their eigenvectors are randomly oriented, then develops the tools that make the limiting calculations possible.

Why crossings disappear


Organizing mixed moments with partitions, then deriving the free central limit theorem in moments.

Derive the Cauchy-transform equation and calculate why two free sign variables have an arcsine sum.

Rotate the eigenvectors

Multiplying matrices

Multiplying positive matrices


Define multiplicative free convolution, derive the S-transform convention, and work through free projections.

Covariance matrices and their products

From edge directions to node featuresThe magnetic Laplacian attaches a complex phase to an edge according to its direction. The charge parameter q controls that phase. Its low-frequency eigenvectors supply positional information to the model.I used four charges (0.025, 0.05, 0.075 and 0.1), taking 16 real-valued channels from each. I concatenated those 64 channels with the node features.I used three layers of PyG TransformerConv neighborhood attention, with four heads and hidden width 64. Message passing sees symmetrized edges. Only the magnetic encoding gets the original edge directions.
How much was just extra width?My first seven-seed test comparison gave the magnetic encoding a +0.727 percentage-point gain. But I had compared 64 magnetic channels with 16 ordinary Laplacian channels. More features and more input parameters could explain some of that advantage.I reran the comparison with 64 channels and 65,832 parameters on both sides. In this validation experiment, the mean magnetic advantage fell from +0.569 points against LapPE-16 to +0.275 points against LapPE-64.

I would not compare the old test score directly with these validation scores: the seeds and splits differ. Within the new experiment, widening the baseline clearly matters to the mean gap. Three seeds leave me unsure about the remaining gain. They do not establish that the encodings are equivalent, either.
A negative follow-upI also tried choosing charges with a cheap ridge-regression proxy. The idea was to propagate features through the graph before scoring them, so the proxy would behave a little more like the GNN. I used training labels only.The extra propagation did not earn its keep. Its charge ranking agreed less with the historical GNN validation results: Spearman correlation 0.476, compared with 0.691 for the simple proxy. All three policies picked the same charge pair anyway.Aaand that’s where I stopped.
One graph is not enoughMatching the number of channels fixes one problem. It does not make the spectral features identical apart from direction. My model is also sensitive to the eigenvector coordinates, including their complex phases.So far I have one real graph, charges explored during earlier experiments, and a test set that has already influenced the work. Next I would fix a minimum useful gain before running more paired seeds, then try an independent directed task. I want to know whether the extra structure helps beyond this particular graph.
